However, we acknowledge that our ebullition evidence is a gross observation, as the pathway has been reported in several lakes in cold months (Walter, Zimov, Chanton, Verbyla, & Chapin, 2006; Wik, Crill, Bastviken, Danielsson, & Norbäck, 2011). In our study, we exclusively sampled on 1 day each month, which is not sufficient to accurately estimate this emission pathway. In the future, higher temporal resolution of sampling (by diurnal sampling, sampling several days per month and spatial analysis) is required to reduce uncertainties in CH₄ ebullition from aquatic ecosystems, as previously recommended by Wik, Thornton, et al. (2016). However, other methods used in the literature contain large uncertainties; DelSontro et al. (2011) indicated that the acoustic technology has large coefficients of variation that exceed 100%, while the classic randomised bubble trap method is highly biased and underestimates results (Walter Anthony & Anthony, 2013). Newer gas analysers and the combination with established techniques may help to determine CH₄ diffusion and ebullition in freshwater ecosystems. Zhao et al. (2015) suggested such a method as a tool for assessing diffusion and ebullition, while Grasset et al. (2016) was one of the first studies to include ebullition data from these newer gas analysers. In the context of CO₂, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle can be classified as an acidic lake, in which CO₂ is the major inorganic carbon species (Cole & Prairie, 2009) and where the availability of allochthonous and autochthonous inorganic carbon is in some ecosystems a very important driver of CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere (Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). During turnover events, with the exception of spring in the SW basin, peaks of CO₂ fluxes were detected jointly with high CO₂ stored in the water column. The surplus CO₂ for both basins likely did not completely originate from surficial (0–20 cm, data not shown) sediments (1.0 ± 0.5 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average), as stored quantities were one order of magnitude lower than the mass of CO₂ emitted (13.0 ± 4.6 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average) and dissolved in the water column (9.3 ± 4.3 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This suggests inputs of CO₂ directly from external sources of inorganic carbon and indirectly from mineralisation of internal or external DOC (Brothers et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly et al., 2013; Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The reduction in DOC in the NE basin potentially accounted for the 41% reduction in total annual CO₂ emissions. Moreover, CH₄ emissions decreased to a similar extent (53%), but cannot, as previously discussed, be adequately explained by the reduced availability of DOC to the pelagic community. Ducharme-Riel, Vachon, Del Giorgio, and Prairie (2015) remarked on the complexity of lake dynamics since interaction between physical and biological factors regulates CO₂ dynamics. Sources of CO₂ and contributions by different sources need to be elucidated (Drake et al., 2018; Engel et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). It is important to note that we could not observe any CO₂ ebullition with the new gas analyser used in this study, but we acknowledge that our device was not sensitive enough to confirm CO₂ in bubbles for several reasons: (a) CO₂ is highly soluble in water, and therefore, bubbles trapped in sediments might have had low CO₂ concentration; (b) the remaining CO₂ concentration in gas bubbles could have been re-dissolved through the water column before bubbles were emitted to the atmosphere (McGinnis et al., 2011); (c) there was a high CO₂ concentration inside the chamber (atmospheric concentration, ca. 380 ppm) at the initial time of sampling (to observe CO₂ bubbles it would be necessary to exceed this threshold). Similarly, the analyses of Casper et al. (2000) and Sepulveda-Jauregui et al. (2015) determined that only 1% of CO₂ was emitted by ebullition and 99% by diffusion in small shallow lakes. Together, our results may help to identify the environmental factors that regulate carbon emissions in small lakes. In freshwater systems, temperature controls the biological activity across food webs, the length of stratification periods and gas solubility. High temperatures amplified CH₄ emissions (Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018), which led to markedly higher amounts of CH₄ stored and emitted from the basins in the hotter summer of 2014 with a clear correlation between CH₄ emissions and temperature. Similar responses to regional temperature have been shown in ponds, in small shallow, and medium-sized lakes (Bartosiewicz, Laurion, & Macintyre, 2015; Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Liikanen, Huttunen, Valli, & Martikainen, 2002; Miettinen et al., 2015; Natchimuthu et al., 2014; Room et al., 2014) and in enclosure experiments (Audet et al., 2017; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017), suggesting that in predicted warming scenarios, an increase in carbon greenhouse gas emissions can be expected in lake ecosystems regardless of DOC inputs and their biogeochemical effects in the water column (e.g., in stratification, temperature regimes, pH, microbial metabolism and CO₂ dynamics). Despite the long-term division of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle that created two very different stable ecosystems with regard to carbon supply, the CH₄ and to some extent CO₂, emissions to the atmosphere were mainly determined by DOC-independent environmental conditions, as suggested by direct correlations between gas flux and temperature and between pH and dissolved gases. However, pH is an indirect factor associated with DOC correlation with dissolved gas concentrations. Therefore, the correlation between pH and dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ in the SW basin implied that DOC can play an important role in greenhouse gas emissions (Drake et al., 2018). In the case of CH₄, previous studies on methanogenesis in sediments of this acidic bog lake showed that the pathways to form CH₄ were similar to those in pH-neutral lakes (Conrad et al., 2010). Therefore, the reduction in DOC inputs to aquatic ecosystems would benefit several ecological and environmental issues, but in the context of CH₄ and CO₂ emission to the atmosphere from small lakes, the lake size and warming are probably the key factors for determining CH₄ and CO₂ emissions (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Kankaala, Huotari, Tulonen, & Ojala, 2013; Room et al., 2014; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). 4.2 | O₂ dynamics governing carbon greenhouse gas storage and emission Higher CH₄ emission periods coincided with the presence of extensive anoxic hypolimnia (in summer and fall). In contrast, low CH₄ emission periods were observed when the water column was oxygenated (in winter and early spring). We suggest that the presence of O₂ in the surficial sediment layers led to a decrease in methanogenic activity by inhibition because it is a strictly anaerobic process. Also, aerobic CH₄ oxidation likely occurred in the superficial sediment layers, further reducing the amount of CH₄ released to the water column. The reciprocal gradient between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ present during the stratification period suggested that CH₄ oxidation in the water column may have regulated diffusive CH₄ emission in stratification periods, but had little effect during mixing periods, as previously reported for lakes (Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Casper et al., 2005; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2006; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Ricao Canelhas et al., 2016; Utsumi et al., 1998). The correlation analyses of dissolved gases (CH₄, CO₂ and O₂) showed that CH₄ and CO₂ are stored in anoxic layers and that they are indicators of high net heterotrophy (Borges et al., 2015; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2015). The weaker correlation between CO₂ and O₂ (when compared to CH₄ and O₂) was consistent with previous reports of dissolved CO₂ patterns in acidic lakes (e.g., Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle) that are being strongly influenced by catchments rich in organic and inorganic carbon (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). However, the reciprocal correlation between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ or CO₂ suggests that dissolved O₂ in the water column is an important indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ storage. Total carbon storage (calculated from dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ concentrations) followed dissolved O₂ changes over the seasons (Figure 7), with higher CH₄ and CO₂ emissions occurring when anoxic conditions predominated (maximum of 71 ± 13%, mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This may have been the result of higher microbial activity in the summer compared to colder periods of mixing; the reduction in the aerobic zone of the water column may have led to a decrease in aerobic methane oxidation activity. For more than 2 months during the winter, the water column was well oxygenated in both basins, and when temperature increased in spring, O₂ was quickly consumed in the newly established hypolimnia. Bartosiewicz et al. (2016) and Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) also found dissolved O₂ in the water column to be an indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ dynamics in summer. Moreover, Sabrekov et al. (2017) pointed out that O₂ patterns were among the major factors that controlled the dynamics of CH₄ and CO₂ in Siberian lakes, based on regional model development. Therefore, dissolved O₂ can be used as a tracer of biological activity associated with temperature and stratification changes during the seasons. Interestingly, we did not find any relationship between dissolved CH₄ or CO₂ and T or pH, when data from both basins were grouped. Instead, we found a positive correlation between pH and CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations when solely assessed in the water column of the SW basin. This correlation may indicate a higher microbial activity in all trophic levels (from primary production to heterotrophy) and not an intrinsic effect of recalcitrant DOC in the sediments (indicated by the low pH in the SW basin) on CH₄ and CO₂. Moreover, only the western basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle receive inflow from an adjacent peat bog (Burkert et al., 2004; Koschel, 1995), which may supply CH₄ and CO₂ and explain the positive correlation between pH and both gases. Such external sources have been suggested as an important source of both gases for freshwater ecosystems (Garcia-Tigreros Kodovska et al., 2016; Tank et al., 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). FIGURE 7 Per cent of carbon stored (sum of CH₄–C and CO₂–C) in the anoxic (grey) and oxic (white) water layers in the water column during the time of the study in both basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle beginning in August 2014 and ending in July 2015 5 | CONCLUDING REMARKS In the artificially divided Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, the reduction in DOC inputs over 30 years to one of the studied basins was not the factor dominating CH4 and CO2 dynamics. Instead, seasonal changes in ambient temperature, O2 and stratification periods determined the relative contribution of cumulative carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Despite significant differences in pH and DOC developed between the two basins, CH4 and CO2 emissions were in the same order of magnitude over the year. The latter result shows the knowledge gap regarding the mineralisation processes of DOC in small acidic lakes. Therefore, the effect of DOC inputs to these types of lakes, including on CH4 and CO2 emissions, is still unclear. Further studies in various types of lakes are needed in order to better identify the effects of DOC on small and shallow lakes, which are a key component in global carbon greenhouse gas emissions. 1 | INTRODUCTION

Even though lakes cover a small proportion of the global land masses (ca. 4%), they are considered a major component in the global carbon cycle (Cole et al., 2007), emitting significant amounts of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Saunois et al., 2016). From those ecosystems, small lakes with surface areas <1 km2 comprise the major proportion of lakes (Cael & Seekell, 2016; Verpoorter, Kutser, Seekell, & Tranvik, 2014). With respect to the amount of the Earth's surface that they cover, small lakes emit disproportionately high amounts of CH4 and CO2, and their projected contribution to global warming is still under investigation (Audet et al., 2017; Downing, 2010; Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Wik, Varner, Walter Anthony, Macintyre, & Bastviken, 2016; Yvon-Durocher, Hulatt, Woodward, & Trimmer, 2017).

Because small lakes are commonly shallow, the sediments and water column interact strongly with the air temperature (Bar-tosiewicz, Laurion, Clayer, & Maranger, 2016; Heslop et al., 2015). Therefore, carbon mineralisation from allochthonous and autochthonous sources increases in warmer seasons, resulting in higher production of CH4 and CO2 (Gudasz, Sobek, Bastviken, Koehler, & Tranvik, 2015; Schulz, Matsuyama, & Conrad, 1997; Sobek, Tranvik, & Cole, 2005). Although CH4 and CO2 productions are temperature dependent in lakes, their emission pathways are not identical. CH4 is mainly produced in anoxic sediments, with a lower amount derived from terrestrial inputs (Paytan et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2016) and oxic layers (DelSontro, del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2017); it is released primarily by ebullition and, to a lesser extent, by diffusion (Casper, Maberly, Hall, & Finlay, 2000; DelSontro, Boutet, St-Pierre, Del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2016; Wik, Varner, et al., 2016). CO2 is produced along the water column and in sediments (biologically and abiotically), or is derived from terrestrial inputs, and is released primarily by diffusion due to its high solubility (24 times more soluble than CH4) (Battin et al., 2009; Casper et al., 2000; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly, Barker, Stott, & De Ville, 2013; Tank, Fellman, Hood, & Kritzberg, 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015).

The delivery of fresh dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from the catchment is among the key drivers that have been shown to increase the magnitude of CH4 and CO2 emissions (Drake, Raymond, & Spencer, 2018), especially from small lakes (Chmiel et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Valencia et al., 2014; West, Creamer, & Jones, 2015). However, DOC can comprise different proportions of fresh (ready bio-labile) and more recalcitrant fractions, the latter being older in age, highly aromatic (and thus coloured) and regularly referred to as “humic-like” (Raeke, Lechtenfeld, Wagner, Herzsprung, & Reemtsma, 2016). Small lakes that receive large quantities of recalcitrant DOC generally feature the following: reduced metabolism, lower pH and O2 availability, altered contaminant toxicity, lowered light penetration, longer stratification periods and disfavoured food for fish and benthic communities (Brothers et al., 2014; Hessen & Tranvik, 1998; Wetzel, 2001; Williamson, Morris, Pace, & Olson, 1999). It has been regularly reported that, in small lakes with high DOC load, respiration dominates over primary production, resulting in CO2 supersaturation (Cole & Prairie, 2009; Kortelainen et al., 2006; Tranvik et al., 2009) and attenuated CH4 production (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper, Chan, Furtado, & Adams, 2003). Alternatively, parts of the loaded DOC can be incorporated into higher trophic levels, photochemically degraded or absorbed to mineral surfaces (Brothers et al., 2014; Riedel, Zak, Biester, & Dittmar, 2013; Vachon, Lapierre, & del Giorgio, 2016). The cumulative effects of DOC on carbon greenhouse gas emissions from lakes are therefore highly complex and under ongoing debate (Casper et al., 2003; Kankaala, Taipale, Nykanen, & Jones, 2007; López Bellido, Tulonen, Kankaala, & Ojala, 2013; Miettinen et al., 2015; Peura et al., 2014).

The current and projected increase in delivery of terrestrial carbon to freshwater ecosystems and the accompanying socio-ecological challenges (e.g., drinking water and fishery services) are some of the most pressing topics in limnology (Clark et al., 2010; Drake et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). One topic with several uncertainties is how the ecosystems will recover after the reduction and/or blocking of DOC inputs from the catchment. One method used for assessing this question is the use of experimental enclosures in the ecosystems; they can achieve a realistic manipulation of the ecosystem (Giling et al., 2017) to obtain insights into the functioning of lake metabolism at the ecosystem level, such as CH4 and CO2 cycling (Audet et al., 2017; Bogard et al., 2014; Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005; Davidson et al., 2015; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). Audet et al. (2017) and Davidson et al. (2015, 2018) found that biotic interactions influenced greenhouse gas emissions more strongly than warming effects, while Yvon-Durocher et al. (2017) showed that long-term effects of warming increased CH4 and CO2 emissions derived from the change in microorganism metabolism and ecosystem dynamics. In Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, an acidic lake rich in DOC, CH4 and CO2 dynamics have been examined in sediments. Similar methanogenic communities and dissolved gases were found in contrasting basins (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005).

In this study, we assessed the balance between CO2 and CH4 accumulated and emitted in two contrasting basins in a long-running whole-lake experiment. In 1986, experimental Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was first divided into two basins by a plastic curtain (Kasprzak, 1993), and later, in 1989, it was subdivided into four basins (Figure 1). The two western basins receive allochthonous DOC inputs from an adjacent peat bog (Sachse, Babenzien, Ginzel, Gelbrecht, & Steinberg, 2001), keeping the pH at 4.4. Meanwhile, the two eastern basins have remained unaffected by DOC inputs from the adjacent peat bog, favouring a pH increase up to 6.5. Besides this pH increase, biomass and biological activity across all trophic levels in the eastern basins were higher compared to those in the western basins (Hehmann, Krienitz, & Koschel, 2001). Our aim was to evaluate how long-lasting (nearly 30 years) modification of DOC input to a small lake alters its CH4 and CO2 dynamics. The experimental whole-lake enclosure allowed the manipulation of nonartificial DOC inputs for almost 30 years, which provided a unique opportunity to assess the effect of DOC reduction on carbon greenhouse gas emission in lakes. Independent from intersystem variations
pages.2:
in climatic or land-use conditions, this work closely examined whether reduced DOC inputs could be a means for greenhouse gas mitigation in lakes.

2 | METHODS

2.1 | Study site and sampling strategy

Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is a small naturally acidic bog lake, located in a forested area in the Mecklenburg-Brandenburg Lake District in north-eastern Germany at an altitude of 59 m a.s.l. and about 100 km north of Germany's capital Berlin. The landscape, consisting of end moraine, outwash plain and glacial spillways, formed during the Weichsel glacial period (Burkert, Ginzel, Babenzien, & Koschel, 2004). At present, water supplies are provided by ground water and precipitation (Casper & Koschel, 1995). Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was divided by plastic curtains in 1986 into two basins (east and west), and into four compartments by a second east–west separation in 1990. Initially, the division was conducted to enable whole-lake experiments in food-web manipulation (Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995). Over the decades of division, research in Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle has covered several other topics: plankton studies (Glöckner et al., 2000; Hehmann et al., 2001; Macek, Simek, & Bittl, 2001), microorganisms and microbial activity (Grossart et al., 2008; Kanaparthi, Pommerenke, Casper, & Dumont, 2013; Simek et al., 1998), basic limnology and geographical settings (Burkert et al., 2004; Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995; Richter, 1997; Succow & Jeschke, 1986), and CH4 and CO2 cycle (Casper et al., 2003; Chan, Wolf, Hepperle, & Casper, 2002; Conrad, Claus, & Casper, 2010), among others. The two most contrasting basins, namely south-west basin (SW) (characterised by a low pH of 4.4 and DOC of 37.3 mg/L) and the north-east basin (NE) (with a pH of 6.5 and DOC of 16.4 mg/L), were selected for this study (Figure 1). The main limnological characteristics of the original lake, NE and SW basins are summarised in Table 1. The catchment areas draining the eastern basins provided mainly inflow, while the catchment area adjacent to the western basins was only outflow (Figure 1). Generally, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is stratified during the summer stagnation period, and anoxic hypolimnia are usually found in all basins from May to September or October (Casper et al., 2003). Both basins were sampled monthly over 1 year from August 2014 to July 2015. All measurements were made during daylight hours between 9:00 hr and 14:00 hr CEST.

2.2 | Physicochemical analysis in water

All physical and chemical parameters in water were measured from a sampling platform in the centre of the lake (Figure 1). Vertical depth profiles in both basins included temperature (T, °C), O2 (mg/L) and pH (–), which were measured using oxy-197 and pH-196T probes (WTW GmbH, Weilheim, Germany). Additionally, we collected water samples at 0.5-m depth intervals using a 2-L-Limnos sampler (Limnos, Turku, Finland) for ex situ determination of dissolved CH4 and CO2, ions, and DOC. Temperature data loggers (Tinytag Aquatic 2, Gemini Data Loggers Ltd., Chichester, UK) were installed at four depths (0, 1 and 2 m water depth, and just above the sediment) in both basins to record water temperature year-round at 15-min intervals.

Water samples for nitrate (NO3– ), sulphate (SO42– ), soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) and DOC measurements were filtered through 0.45-mm filter. Water samples for these analyses were collected in September 2014, January 2015 and June 2015. Sulphate was analysed using ion chromatography (electrical conductivity detector; Dionex Corp., Sunnyvale CA, USA), NO3– and SRP were analysed spectrophotometrically by flow injection analysis (FIAstar 5000, Foss Analytical, Hilleroed, Denmark), and DOC was measured using a total carbon analyser (Shimadzu TOC-Vcsh, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan).

2.3 | Dissolved CH4 and CO2 in the water column

Monthly water samples were collected at 0.5-m depth intervals using a 2-L-Limnos sampler to measure dissolved CH4 and CO2 concentrations. We subsampled from the port of the Limnos sampler with a 60-ml syringe and gently transferred the sample into 20-ml headspace vials until the water overflowed (performed in duplicate). We then sealed the vials with silicone/PTFE stoppers and magnetic crimp caps. In the laboratory, a headspace was created by displacing water with He (99.999%; Air Liquide, Düsseldorf, Germany) using a two-way needle system. Approximately 40% of the water was replaced, and volumes of sample and headspace were calculated by weight.

Biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment Chorng-Bin Hsu a, Hwey-Lian Hsieh b, Lei Yang c, Sheng-Hai Wu a, Jui-Sheng Chang d, Shu-Chuan Hsiao a, Hui-Chen Su e, Chao-Hsien Yeh e, Yi-Shen Ho f, Hsing-Juh Lin a,b,* a Department of Life Sciences, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung 40227, Taiwan b Biodiversity Research Center, Academia Sinica, Taipei 11529, Taiwan c Department of Marine Environment and Engineering, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan d Department of Leisure Management, Yu Da University, Miaoli 36143, Taiwan e Department of Water Resources Engineering and Conservation, Feng Chia University, Taichung 40724, Taiwan f Wild Bird Society of Taipei, Taipei 10664, Taiwan A R T I C L E I N F O Article history: Received 7 October 2010 Received in revised form 15 April 2011 Accepted 6 June 2011 Available online 2 July 2011 Keywords: Free-water-surface (FWS) constructed wetlands Subtropics Richness Diversity Community A B S T R A C T Constructed wetlands are often built for wastewater treatment to mitigate the adverse effects of organic pollution in streams and rivers caused by inputs of municipal wastewater. However, there has been little analysis of biodiversity and related factors influencing the ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the biodiversity of two free-water-surface integrated constructed wetlands in subtropical Taiwan by analyzing the water quality, habitat characteristics, and biotic communities of algae, macrophytes, birds, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the treatment cells. Our results indicated that the two integrated constructed wetlands (Hsin-Hai II and Daniaopi Constructed Wetlands) achieved good performance in reducing the concentrations of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP), and loadings of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) from municipal sewage. In total, 58 bird species, 7 fish species, and 34 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded in the two wetlands. The results of stepwise multiple regressions showed that the richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentrations. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Ordination analyses indicated that variations in the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were respectively best explained by water temperature, wetland area, and species richness of fish. Our results suggest that wetland area, cover of aquatic macrophytes, and water quality were the most important factors governing the diversity in the constructed wetlands, and that the factors influencing community structures varied among different taxonomic groups. In addition to improving water quality, this study implied that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. © 2011 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Due to increasing population densities and impacts from human activities, pollution remains an essential issue for water quality protection and conservation of biodiversity in urban areas. There is a wide range of treatment technologies that can be used to improve the quality of wastewater to meet effluent standards. Many regions, however, do not have purification plants or lack sufficient capacity to treat all effluents due to the high costs of treatment processes (Kivaisi, 2002). The low coverage of sewage systems often results in municipal sewage and industrial wastewater being directly discharged into aquatic environments with no treatment (Jing et al., 2008). Wetlands are well known as one of the most productive ecosystems in the world (Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007). Countless species of birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, and invertebrates depend on the water and vegetation in wetland habitats (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Wetlands also directly and indirectly support people by providing ecosystem services such as flood abatement, food, a clean water supply, esthetic beauty, educational and recreational benefits, and carbon sinks (Zedler, 2003; Zedler and Kercher, 2005). The ability to simultaneously achieve water quality improvement and enhance biodiversity has generated increasing interest in constructing and restoring wetlands for wastewater treatment (Kivaisi, 2002). Constructed wetlands are artificial wetlands designed to intercept wastewater and remove a wide range of pollutants before discharge into natural water bodies. They mimic natural wetland ecosystems that combine physical, chemical, and biological processes to purify the water quality in more-controlled and efficient ways (Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands are widely used as low-cost alternatives to conventional tertiary municipal wastewater treatment worldwide (Kivaisi, 2002; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Researchers have demonstrated that constructed wetlands are effective for the onsite management of municipal and agricultural wastewater and can remove various nutrients, including suspended solids (SS), biological oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), nitrogen, phosphorus, trace elements, and microorganisms contained in the wastewater (Rousseau et al., 2004; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The success of constructed wetlands is frequently assessed based on the performance of pollution reduction (Rousseau et al., 2004; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands can also enhance various ecosystem services (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Vymazal, 2011). Of the ecosystem services provided by wetlands, the biodiversity of constructed wetlands has attracted relatively less attention. Despite the rapid loss in wetland area and function (Zedler and Kercher, 2005), wetland biodiversity has been overlooked until recent decades (Denny, 1994). Wetland biodiversity is considered to have substantial conservation (Zedler and Kercher, 2005) and economic value (Costanza et al., 1997), and is also used as an indicator to assess ecosystem integrity (Mayer and Galatowitsch, 2001). Most studies addressing the biodiversity of constructed wetlands focused on a single taxonomic group (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Benyamine et al., 2004; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010; Korfel et al., 2010). Although faunal diversity is thought to remain high in wetlands constructed for water treatment (Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), previous studies showed that high nutrient concentrations in wastewater are directly detrimental to wetland fauna (Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006) and to aquatic macrophyte communities, and, in turn, to the fauna that relies on macrophytes (Zhang et al., 2010). Although many studies have focused on the design of constructed wetlands to increase the pollutant removal efficiency (e.g., Thullen et al., 2005; Nahlil and Mitsch, 2006; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), designing constructed wetlands it is more difficult to enhance biodiversity than to improve water quality, since there is a limited understanding of the factors that affect biodiversity (Zedler, 2003). There is an increasing trend to design multi-purpose treatment wetlands to enhance ancillary wildlife and human use benefits (Knight, 1992, 1997). An increasing number of studies have explored aquatic communities and factors influencing them in constructed wetlands (Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Balcombe et al., 2005; Canonico et al., 2005; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010). However, the richness and diversity of different taxonomic groups in wetlands were determined by different factors in different regions (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Therefore, it is imperative for wetland managers to examine the relationship between environmental variables and biotic communities. Hansson et al. (2005) indicated the possibility of improving the design of wetlands in terms of both biodiversity and nutrient retention. The knowledge of relationships between environmental variables and biodiversity, especially in constructed wetlands, is of great value, not only because it is important in assessing ecosystem services provided by constructed wetlands, but also because it provides an essential tool for designing and managing wetlands in order to maintain and enhance biodiversity. In Taiwan, the water quality in many streams near urban areas is severely impacted by municipal wastewater, only <15% of which enters wastewater treatment plants (Jing et al., 2008). Under governmental support, constructed wetlands were widely built along riparian zones for on-site water treatment (Taiwan EPA, 2007). There are currently about 100 wetlands installed or under construction in Taiwan. Most of these constructed wetlands are located in riparian areas between levees and the river and are used to treat urban wastewater. Monitoring data show that these wetlands achieve an acceptable wastewater treatment performance (Jing et al., 2008). However, the biodiversity of these constructed wetlands is poorly understood. We investigated the effects of a number of environmental factors that may affect the diversity and community structures of wetland birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment. Understanding driving factors will be of benefit to managers involved in enhancing freshwater biodiversity on a large landscape scale. The objectives of this study were to (1) evaluate the biodiversity of different biotic communities, including aquatic macrophytes, birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates among treatment cells in two free-water-surface (FWS) integrated constructed wetlands along the riparian zone of the Da-Han River in subtropical Taiwan, (2) identify major factors influencing changes in the biodiversity of the constructed wetlands, and (3) examine relationships between the biotic community structure and environmental variables. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study sites The Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN) are five-cell FWS integrated wetlands, located in the riparian zone on the eastern bank of the Da-Han River in Taipei County (Fig. 1a). The HS2 and DN were respectively completed in September and November 2006. The DN covers a larger area with a higher flow rate and shorter hydraulic retention time than HS2 (Table 1). These two integrated wetlands have similar configurations, with each comprised of five treatment cells. The five sequential cells are a depositional pond, heavily vegetated pond I, open-water pond, heavily vegetated pond II, and ecological pond in the HS2 (cells HS2-1–HS2-5) (Fig. 1b and Table 2). The wastewater effluent from the ecological pond of HS2 flows directly into the Da-Han River after treatment. In the DN, the depositional pond (DN1) is followed by an open-water pond (DN2). The heavily vegetated pond I (DN3) is divided into four parallel sub-cells (DN3-A–DN3-D), each of which receives wastewater from the open-water pond and discharges outflow into the heavily vegetated pond II (DN4) and then into the ecological pond (DN5). After treatment, the wastewater effluent flows from the ecological pond (DN5) into a drainage channel and then into the Da-Han River (Fig. 1c and Table 2). We conducted water sampling and surveyed aquatic macrophytes and macroinvertebrates, fishes, and birds in the two constructed wetlands in February (winter) and June (summer) 2009, and bi-monthly from October 2009 to August 2010. Low-elevation aerial photos were also taken in February and June 2009 and January 2010. C.-B. Hsu et al. / Ecological Engineering 37 (2011) 1533–1545 1535 Fig. 1. (a) Locations and configurations of (b) the Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and (c) Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN). 2.2. Environmental variables The wetland area of each treatment cell was estimated based on aerial photographs using the software package, Image Pro 4.0 (Media Cybernetics, Silver Spring, MD). Water variables were measured in the field using portable instruments, such as water temperature (WTW LF196, Weilheim, Germany), dissolved oxygen (WTW oxi 3302), conductivity (WTW Cond 330i), and pH (WTW pH340). Water samples were taken from the outflow of each cell, immediately placed on ice in a cooler, and brought back to the laboratory for analyses of BOD, COD, nitrate (NO3⁻), nitrite (NO2⁻), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), suspended solids (SS), and phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl)-a concentration following standard methods of the APHA (Clesceri et al., 1998). 2.3. Biotic samples Aquatic macrophytes were surveyed using transects across treatment cells. Six transects were set up in each treatment cell, and all aquatic macrophytes on the transects were identified to species level. To determine the cover of aquatic macrophytes, we overlaid a grid of 2.5-m plots onto an enlarged aerial photo of each treatment cell, and the cover of each species was determined by estimating the fractions of vegetation in each grid and summing up all grids. When areal photos were not available, the cover of aquatic macrophytes was estimated on each transect in the field. We used a D-net sweep (Model 7412D, BioQuip, Rancho Dominguez, CA) to collect aquatic invertebrates modified from a procedure of the USEPA (2002). During each sweep, the D-net was placed on the wetland bottom and pushed horizontally into the vegetation, if available, for a distance of 1 m to cover an area of about 0.3 m², while bouncing the net into the sediment at least twice. The distance between locations of adjacent sweeps was at least 1 m. Two sweeps were combined into one sample, and three samples (six sweeps) were taken in each treatment cell. Materials collected in the net were poured into a 0.5-mm-mesh sieve. After elutriation and removal of large debris, samples retained on the sieve were preserved in 70% ethanol. Aquatic macroinverte-

Nematodes and zooplankton taxa including cladoceran, copepods, and ostracods were excluded from further analyses. Major classes or orders were described for those specimens for which the species could not be determined. We used a cast net (2 m in radius with a 2-cm mesh size) and shrimp traps (15 cm in diameter) to collect fish from the constructed wetlands. The cast net was deployed three times in treatment cells where the method was applicable except in cells HS2-1, HS2-2, DN1, DN2, DN3-A, and DN3-D. Ten shrimp traps were also set up in each treatment cell. Caught fish were chilled on ice and transported back to the laboratory. A bird survey was conducted by three trained persons on three consecutive days, one for each constructed wetland. Observers patrolled the shores of treatment cells on foot during the first 3 h of daylight, and species and abundances in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands were determined with the aid of binoculars. The habitats where the birds were observed were also recorded. 2.4. Biotic metrics We assessed the biodiversity of constructed wetlands using two common measures of richness and the Shannon–Wiener index. Species richness (the number of species) was selected to represent the richness of birds, fishes, and aquatic macrophytes, whereas taxon richness (the number of taxa) was selected for aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands. The Shannon–Wiener index (H') was calculated using the following equation: H' = - \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i; where $p_i$ is the proportion of individuals found of the ith species (taxon) or the percent coverage of the ith aquatic macrophyte species. 2.5. Statistical analysis Variables were first examined to see if they were normally distributed. DO, SS, BOD, COD, and NO$_x^-$ (NO$_2^-$ + NO$_3^-$) concentrations were log-transformed, while wetland areas and TN, TP, and phytoplankton Chl-a concentrations were square-root-transformed to improve the normality. Abundances of birds and fishes were square-root-transformed, and the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates was log(x + 1)-transformed. An arcsine-square-root transformation was used for the percent cover of aquatic macrophytes (Zar, 1996). We used multiple regressions to develop the most appropriate statistical models to predict biodiversity measures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the constructed wetlands. Species or taxon richness, abundance (density), and Shannon diversity (H') of biotic communities were used as dependent variables, while wetland attributes, including wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics, were used as independent variables in a stepwise regression model (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Variables with a significance level of <0.05 were included in the regression models. We did not examine the diversity of aquatic macrophytes because most of the aquatic macrophyte species were artificially introduced when constructing the wetlands. Rare species (taxa) were excluded from the analyses to reduce their influence on the ordinations (ter Braak, 1995). Only taxa constituting more than 0.5% of the total abundances for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were included in the multivariate analyses. Totals of 33 species of birds, 4 species of fishes, and 13 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were used in the analyses (Appendix A). A prior detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was separately conducted on the bird, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrate data to assess the gradient length of the first DCA axis. The lengths of the gradients were 3.957, 2.869, and 2.871 (in SD units) for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates, respectively. Therefore, the unimodal model (e.g., the canonical correspondence analysis, CCA) was more appropriate for birds, and a linear model (e.g., the redundancy analysis, RDA) was better for fishes and aquatic macroinvertebrates (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). In the ordination models, wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics were used as explanatory variables. We ran the analysis using the automatic forward-selection mode, and only variables explaining a significant proportion of the remaining variation were included (based on a Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations at \( p < 0.1 \)). Biodiversity measures were calculated using the PRIMER vers. 5 computer software (Clarke and Gorley, 2001). Multiple regression analyses were produced using the software package SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2003). Ordination analyses were performed using CANOCO for Windows vers. 4.52 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables Areas of treatment cells varied within and between constructed wetlands. The depositional ponds of the two constructed wetlands were small, at <0.2 ha. Areas of other treatment cells ranged 0.55–0.83 ha in the HS2 and 0.26–1.86 ha in the DN (Fig. 2). The cover of aquatic macrophytes was the highest in heavily vegetated ponds of each constructed wetland, i.e., HS2-2, HS2-4, DN3-A, DN3-B, and DN3-D (Fig. 2). Water quality widely varied among treatment cells in each constructed wetland. DO was low, generally <6 ppm except in the ecological ponds, and showed an increasing trend along the sequential treatment cells in both constructed wetlands (Table 2). In contrast, conductivity and concentrations of TN and TP showed a decreasing trend along sequential treatment cells, suggesting reductions in the pollutant concentrations of wastewater after passing through these constructed wetlands (Table 2). Other variables, however, fluctuated along the sequential treatment cells. The overall system performance of pollutant removal based on the reduction in concentrations in the water column is shown in Table 3. Removal of BOD and COD was higher in the HS2 with respective removal rates of 58.8% and 51.1%, and the outflow concentration was reduced to <11 and 30 mg L\(^{-1}\), respectively (Tables 2, 3). Concentrations of TN and TP were substantially reduced in the DN with respective removal rates of 51.4% and 52.3%, and the outflow concentrations were 8.4 and 0.5 ppm, respectively.

3.2. Biotic metrics The average species richness of aquatic macrophytes in each treatment cell ranged 4.5–14.3 in the HS2 and 1.4–14.4 in the DN. Table 4 lists the vegetation and average percent cover in each cell. The dominant macrophytes in the HS2 were water spinach (*Ipomoea aquatica*), southern cutgrass (*Leersia hexandra*), *Ludwigia x taiwanensis*, common reed (*Phragmites australis*), and common cattail (*Typha orientalis*) (Table 4). The DN was dominated by *Cyperus imbricatus* subsp. *imbricatus*, water hyacinth (*Eichhornia crassipes*), Chinese water chestnut (*Eleocharis dulcis*), and water spinach. In total, 429 individuals belonging to 33 bird species and 1233 individuals belonging to 57 bird species were respectively recorded in the HS2 and DN. The average species richness of birds in treatment cells ranged 0–7.3 in the HS2 and 0.9–12.3 in the DN (Table 5).

Wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes (means ± SE) in each treatment cell of the Hsin-Hai II (HS2) and Daniaopi (DN) constructed wetlands. The average bird abundance and Shannon diversity (\( H' \)) were highest in the ecological ponds and lowest in the depositional ponds of both wetlands (Table 5). The dominant species was Chinese Bulbul (Pycnonotus sinensis), respectively accounting for 18.4% and 18.7% of the total abundances in the HS2 and DN. Only seven fish species were recorded in the two wetlands, and four of them, including tilapia (Oreochromis hybrid), topmouth gudgeon (Pseudorasbora parva), striped snakehead (Channa striata), and predatory carp (Erythrocultter erythropterus) are exotics. Levels of fish species richness were low in the two constructed wetlands with mean values ranging 0–1.6 in the HS2 and 1.0–2.4 in the DN (Table 5). Higher abundances and lower \( H' \) values were observed in treatment cells of the HS2 than in those of the DN (Table 5). The dominant species in the HS2 was blue gourami (Trichogaster trichopterus), which accounted for 91.3% of the total abundance. The DN was dominated by tilapia and goldfish (Carassius auratus auratus), accounting for 63.2% and 35.0% of the total abundance, respectively. The mean taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell ranged 7.1–10.8 in the HS2 and 7.3–15.0 in the DN (Table 5). In the HS2, densities of aquatic macroinvertebrates were higher in HS2-2 and HS2-3 with mean values of 210.0 and 248.2 individuals m\(^{-2}\), respectively. Densities in the DN were higher in DN2 and DN1 followed by DN3-B and DN3-A (Table 5). Mean \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell was similar, ranging 1.20–1.73 in the HS2 and 0.85–1.67 in the DN. The dominant taxa in the HS2 were mosquitoes (Culex spp.) and non-biting midges (Chironomidae), which respectively accounted for 33.4% and 13.6% of the total abundance. The DN was dominated by oligochaetes and chironomids, which respectively accounted for 59.0% and 8.0% of the total abundance. 3.3. Factors affecting biotic metrics in the constructed wetlands Results from stepwise multiple regressions showed that the biodiversity and abundance of different taxonomic groups were affected by different environmental variables (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds were positively related to the wetland area, while \( H' \) was also correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Table 6). Species richness of fishes was positively related to the wetland area and negatively related to conductivity and \( H' \) of aquatic macrophytes. Fish abundance was positively related to DO, while \( H' \) was negatively related to the TP concentration (Table 6). For aquatic macroinvertebrates, taxon richness and density were positively correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes and negatively with COD. \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates was positively related to the wetland area, although the \( R^2 \) value was low (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds increased with wetland area up to about 2 ha (Fig. 3). Species richness of fishes and the taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes, respectively. However, relations between environmental variables and other biotic metrics of fish and aquatic macroinvertebrates were not clear. 3.4. Seven variables explained 46.4% of the total variation in abundances of four dominant fish species (\( F = 5.57, df = 6 \) and 44, \( p = 0.0010 \), Monte Carlo permutation test with 999 permutations; Table 8). The RDA plot showed that goldfish, tilapia, and topmouth gudgeon were more abundant in treatment cells with a larger area, higher concentrations of SS and COD, and a low density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 5). The blue gourami was more abundant in treatment cells with a higher \( H' \) value of macrophytes and TP concentrations (Fig. 5). For the distribution of aquatic macroinvertebrates, the RDA using automatic forward selection retained seven variables: fish species richness, richness and cover of aquatic macrophytes, water temperature, and values of conductivity, pH, and DO (\( p < 0.1 \), Monte Carlo permutation with 999 permutations; Table 7). The first four axes in the RDA model explained 21.3% of the total variation in abundance of the 13 most dominant aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa, 94.1% of which was significantly related to the measured variables (\( F = 3.80, df = 6 \) and 89, \( p = 0.0010 \), Monte Carlo permutation test with 999 permutations; Table 8). The RDA ordination plot indicated that narrow-winged damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Diplonychus sp.) and leaf beetle larvae (Chrysomelidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Apple snails (Pomacea canaliculata) and mayflies (Cloeon sp.) were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 6). Dipteran species such as mosquitoes (Culex spp.), brine flies (Ephydridae), and non-biting midges (Chironomidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high values of conductivity and low values of DO (Fig. 6). 4. Discussion 4.1. Performance of pollutant removal The construction of wetlands is an alternative measure to conventional water treatment, which provides a potentially more environmentally friendly and economical treatment system to mitigate the negative effects of domestic wastewater and urban runoff (Scholz et al., 2007). Our study showed that the two constructed wetlands were effective in nutrient removal, although the performances varied between the constructed wetlands and also among nutrients. Wetland design, water quality, hydraulics, soil chem- istry, microbial communities, macroinvertebrates, and vegetation each may greatly affect the performance of constructed wetlands. The main removal mechanisms of BOD and COD include microbial degradation and settling of colloidal particles (Vymazal et al., 1998). Nitrogen is primarily removed through microbial nitrification and denitrification in most constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998). Phosphorus removal in constructed wetlands occurs from absorption and precipitation by soil particles (Vymazal, 2010). The amount of nutrients such as phosphorus removed by plant uptake generally accounts for a small fraction of total nutrients removed in constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998), and may be released back into the water after plants decay (Vymazal, 2010). Small and deep wetlands increase phosphorus retention by increasing particle sedimentation, while large surface areas may maximize nitrogen removal (Hansson et al., 2005; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The removal rates in this study were similar compared to nearby constructed wetlands (Fan et al., 2009). 4.2. Biodiversity of constructed wetlands Along with treating wastewater, there is an increasing trend in designing constructed wetlands to restore degraded habitats for wildlife. However, different ecological functions of wetland systems are thought to be conflicting. High nutrient loadings that surpass a critical level may cause dramatic shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning (Verhoeven et al., 2006). Some potential problems, including bioaccumulation of toxic materials, transmission of disease, and environmental hazards, might result from the use of wetlands for wastewater treatment (Knight, 1992). Benyamine et al. (2004) indicated that the typical single-objective focus of scientific studies has led to contradictions in recommendations for the design and management of constructed wetlands for multiple uses. Nevertheless, this study combined with others (e.g., Knight, 1997; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006) suggest that constructed wetlands can provide attractive habitats for various kinds of wildlife. Meanwhile, after reviewing the North American Treatment Wetland (NADB) Database, Knight et al. (2001) indicated that there were no detrimental effects on wildlife caused by the pollution-cleansing function of treatment wetlands. Due to a lack of data in nearby freshwater habitats, the contribution of constructed wetlands to landscape biodiversity could not be determined in this study. Nevertheless, in addition to water quality improvement, this study suggests that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. This study further demonstrated that the biodiversity of different taxonomic groups in constructed wetlands is governed by various factors. 4.3. Factors affecting wetland biodiversity Our results suggest a positive relationship between the area of a constructed wetland and the biodiversity and abundance of birds, which is in accordance with other studies on wetlands (Zedler, 2003; Hansson et al., 2005). In addition to wetland area, bird biodiversity was found to be affected by adjacent and regional land uses, such as road density and connectedness (Whited et al., 2000). Ordination results suggested that bird communities were mainly determined by seasonal patterns, as well as food availability and nesting requirements for brood rearing. Bird species such as the Dusky Thrush, Teal, and Yellow Wagtail were winter visitors (Shiu et al., 2005), and, therefore, were negatively correlated with water temperature. Members of the Ardeidae such as Little Egrets and Black-crowned Night Herons, and the Recurvirostridae like Black-winged Stilts were found to be associated with the species richness and abundance of fishes (Fig. 4). A number of studies indicated that they feed on a wide variety of prey types but mainly on fish (Fasola, 1994; Kazantzidis and Goutner, 2005). The association of White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) with aquatic macrophytes can be attributed to nest-site selection for brood rearing (Gopakumar and Kaimal, 2008). Aquatic invertebrates are primary food resources for many wintering waterbirds. Wallau et al. (2010) indicated that the Common Moorhen feeds on pieces of aquatic macrophytes and removes macrophytes to search for invertebrates which utilize macrophytes as habitats. The Cattle Egret was found to rely heavily on various invertebrates as their main food sources (Lombardini et al., 2001), and its number was positively correlated with the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 4). Teal and Spot-billed Duck (Anatidae) may also compete with fish for the same food resources (invertebrates) and are thus found in lower densities at wetlands with fish compared to those without fish (e.g., Eriksson, 1979). Our study showed that fish biodiversity was low in these young (<5 years) constructed wetlands. Hansson et al. (2005) also found similar results and indicated that natural wetlands aged more than 100 years showed considerably higher fish species richness than young constructed wetlands. In constructed wetlands, possible sources of the fish are limited to those from nearby streams during floods and mercy releases, and, therefore, the biodiversity of fish is unlikely to increase over a short time period. This study showed that a wetland’s area is also important in determining the species richness of fishes. All treatment cells in our study were <2 ha (Fig. 2). Søndergaard et al. (2005) found that fish species richness was low, typically 1–3 species, in Danish ponds and lakes with areas of <1 ha, and gradually increased with lake size. Scheffer et al. (2006) proposed that fish are rare in small, isolated lakes, probably as a result of a higher likelihood of fish kills combined with their low colonizing ability. Moreover, fish biodiversity appeared to be most affected by the water quality in constructed wetlands. Fish species found in constructed wetlands appeared to be tolerant of high nutrient levels and low DO conditions. Blue gourami is an obligate air-breathing fish (Burggren, 1979), which means that it can adapt to changing DO levels in constructed wetlands. The dominant blue gourami and tilapia in constructed wetlands are exotics, but not the goldfish. Tilapia (Cichlidae) are among the most widely distributed exotic fishes in the world (Canonico et al., 2005). Studies found that they are able to respond to environmental changes by rapidly altering their life history characteristic and trophic levels (Bowen and Allanson, 1982), which may benefit their invasion into new environments (Holway and Suarez, 1999). The exotic species introduced to these wetlands either on purpose or accidentally may also threaten populations of native species. Our results suggest close relationships of the richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates with the coverage of aquatic macrophytes. The abundance and diversity of aquatic invertebrates were found to be associated with the vegetated area of wetlands (Gee et al., 1997). The presence of aquatic macrophytes might affect the distributions of aquatic macroinvertebrates and thus their biodiversity in several ways. Submerged vegetation in aquatic ecosystems forms complex structures, which may be used as habitats (Gee et al., 1997) or as refuges to reduce the foraging efficiency of predators (Diehl, 1992). Because there is more space for food attachment and collection, aquatic macrophytes provide additional resources such as epiphytes to the macroinvertebrate community, especially for grazers and thus may indirectly favor detritivores and predators (Diehl, 1992). Positive relationships between the abundance of aquatic macroinvertebrates and cover of aquatic macrophytes were reported elsewhere (de Szalay and Resh, 2000). In constructed wetlands, excessive nutrient loadings, high toxic pollutant levels, and anaerobic conditions often prevent aquatic macroinvertebrates from using wetlands as habitats (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Hence, our results indicated a negative relationship of COD with the taxon richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates. Decreases in richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates were shown to be related to changes in water quality in various aquatic ecosystems (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Jurado et al., 2010). The community structure of aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands was influenced by the presence of predators and suitable habitats. Fish are often the top predators in wetland ecosystems and can impact aquatic macroinvertebrates in terms of species richness, density, diversity, and community structure (Diehl, 1992). Ordination analyses indicated that the major dipteran taxa in these constructed wetlands, such as non-biting midges (Chironomidae), mosquitoes (Culicidae), and brine flies (Ephydridae), were negatively associated with the species richness of fish and dissolved oxygen. Most of the fish species in our study sites rely on aquatic invertebrates as their main food sources. The diet of the blue gourami mainly consists of aquatic invertebrates and algae-based foods (Syarifuddin and Kramer, 1996). Although goldfish predominantly eat non-animal food, studies showed that they also feed on a wide range of food resources, including various zooplankton and aquatic insects (e.g., Peterson et al., 2005). Numerous studies demonstrated that the presence of fish may reduce the density and biomass of certain taxa of aquatic invertebrates (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000) and change the community structure of aquatic invertebrates in wetlands (Tarr et al., 2005). Moreover, many species of these dipteran families are tolerant of low DO and polluted water (Courtney et al., 1996). Relationships of damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Belostomatidae), and leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) with the cover of aquatic macrophytes suggest that the vegetation is used as food and perch sites (Cloarec, 1990; Gibbons et al., 2002; Fernandez and Hilker, 2007). The amount of unexplained variation in our models suggests that some other unmeasured variables play certain roles in regulating communities in these constructed wetlands. Keddy and Fraser (2000) suggested that variations in water depth were the most important factor governing communities in shoreline wetlands. Increases in habitat heterogeneity or complexity (Hansson et al., 2005) and age (Fairchild et al., 2000) may increase the biodiversity of wetlands. In addition, the richness of aquatic invertebrates increases with the hydroperiod, i.e., the length of time that a wetland holds water (Tarr et al., 2005). In highly connected wetlands, aquatic invertebrate richness may also increase through dispersal from areas with different environmental conditions (e.g., Cottenie and De Meester, 2003). These factors could be constructed and manipulated through proper design and management of constructed wetlands, and can therefore be used to increase biodiversity. 4.4. Implications for the design and management of constructed wetlands Previous studies examined the impacts of environmental factors on biodiversity across various taxonomic groups in lentic ecosystems (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Results from those studies as well as ours reveal that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. In order to maximize biodiversity in constructed wetlands, the factors involved in each taxonomic group should be taken into consideration in wetland design and management from a holistic view. According to our results, wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes appeared to be the two most important factors affecting biodiversity in the constructed wetlands. A wetland constructed with the aim of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Findlay and Houlahan (1997) found that species richness of all taxa in their study, including birds, mammals, herptiles and plants, increased with wetland area. Whatever other considerations may be taken into the wetland design, from a biodiversity conservation perspective, bigger is indeed better, although the maximum richness of some taxa might be encountered at a certain area (e.g., 4–5 ha for birds, Hansson et al., 2005). Changes in macrophyte composition and cover are among the most important ecological successions in constructed wetlands (Mitsch et al., 2005). Although high macrophyte cover may increase taxa richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates, problems can arise as a result of the presence of dense vegetation in wetlands such as consumption of DO and contribution to nutrient loadings as plants decompose (Sartoris et al., 2000). For wastewater treatment, a high cover of aquatic macrophytes was designed as one of the important factors facilitating N retention (Thiere et al., 2011). For wildlife management, a 50:50 ratio of open water to emergent vegetation, i.e., hemi-marshes, was recommended to attract wildlife (Murkin et al., 1997). de Szalay and Resh (2000) indicated that the cover of aquatic macrophytes increased the abundances of some dipteran taxa, which might cause serious nuisance problems in wetlands. Our results also show that taxa responded differently to changes in the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Since the vegetation has both positive and negative effects on the performance of constructed wetland for wastewater treatment, a proper vegetation balance is needed for optimal treatment performance through vegetation management (Thullen et al., 2005). It is widely accepted that created wetlands, whether for wastewater treatment or not, may never express the full range of ecological variability found in natural wetlands (Brooks et al., 2005). However, as water quality improves due to sequential purification along the treatment cells, the last ponds in a constructed wetland may be capable of supporting biodiversity similar to that of natural wetlands (Jurado et al., 2010). 5. Conclusions Although characterized by high nutrient loadings, constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment are able to support various wildlife and enhance biodiversity. This study indicated that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. The richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with the wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentration. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Therefore, a wetland constructed with the aims of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Our results imply that ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands, used primarily for wastewater treatment or created for new wetland areas, can be managed to enhance biodiversity. Nematodes and zooplankton taxa including cladoceran, copepods, and ostracods were excluded from further analyses. Major classes or orders were described for those specimens for which the species could not be determined. We used a cast net (2 m in radius with a 2-cm mesh size) and shrimp traps (15 cm in diameter) to collect fish from the constructed wetlands. The cast net was deployed three times in treatment cells where the method was applicable except in cells HS2-1, HS2-2, DN1, DN2, DN3-A, and DN3-D. Ten shrimp traps were also set up in each treatment cell. Caught fish were chilled on ice and transported back to the laboratory. A bird survey was conducted by three trained persons on three consecutive days, one for each constructed wetland. Observers patrolled the shores of treatment cells on foot during the first 3 h of daylight, and species and abundances in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands were determined with the aid of binoculars. The habitats where the birds were observed were also recorded. 2.4. Biotic metrics We assessed the biodiversity of constructed wetlands using two common measures of richness and the Shannon–Wiener index. Species richness (the number of species) was selected to represent the richness of birds, fishes, and aquatic macrophytes, whereas taxon richness (the number of taxa) was selected for aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands. The Shannon–Wiener index (H') was calculated using the following equation: H' = - \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i; where $p_i$ is the proportion of individuals found of the ith species (taxon) or the percent coverage of the ith aquatic macrophyte species. 2.5. Statistical analysis Variables were first examined to see if they were normally distributed. DO, SS, BOD, COD, and NO$_x^-$ (NO$_2^-$ + NO$_3^-$) concentrations were log-transformed, while wetland areas and TN, TP, and phytoplankton Chl-a concentrations were square-root-transformed to improve the normality. Abundances of birds and fishes were square-root-transformed, and the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates was log(x + 1)-transformed. An arcsine-square-root transformation was used for the percent cover of aquatic macrophytes (Zar, 1996). We used multiple regressions to develop the most appropriate statistical models to predict biodiversity measures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the constructed wetlands. Species or taxon richness, abundance (density), and Shannon diversity (H') of biotic communities were used as dependent variables, while wetland attributes, including wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics, were used as independent variables in a stepwise regression model (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Variables with a significance level of <0.05 were included in the regression models. We did not examine the diversity of aquatic macrophytes because most of the aquatic macrophyte species were artificially introduced when constructing the wetlands. Rare species (taxa) were excluded from the analyses to reduce their influence on the ordinations (ter Braak, 1995). Only taxa constituting more than 0.5% of the total abundances for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were included in the multivariate analyses. Totals of 33 species of birds, 4 species of fishes, and 13 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were used in the analyses (Appendix A). A prior detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was separately conducted on the bird, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrate data to assess the gradient length of the first DCA axis. The lengths of the gradients were 3.957, 2.869, and 2.871 (in SD units) for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates, respectively. Therefore, the unimodal model (e.g., the canonical correspondence analysis, CCA) was more appropriate for birds, and a linear model (e.g., the redundancy analysis, RDA) was better for fishes and aquatic macroinvertebrates (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). In the ordination models, wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics were used as explanatory variables. We ran the analysis using the automatic forward-selection mode, and only variables explaining a significant proportion of the remaining variation were included (based on a Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations at \( p < 0.1 \)). Biodiversity measures were calculated using the PRIMER vers. 5 computer software (Clarke and Gorley, 2001). Multiple regression analyses were produced using the software package SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2003). Ordination analyses were performed using CANOCO for Windows vers. 4.52 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables Areas of treatment cells varied within and between constructed wetlands. The depositional ponds of the two constructed wetlands were small, at <0.2 ha. Areas of other treatment cells ranged 0.55–0.83 ha in the HS2 and 0.26–1.86 ha in the DN (Fig. 2). The cover of aquatic macrophytes was the highest in heavily vegetated ponds of each constructed wetland, i.e., HS2-2, HS2-4, DN3-A, DN3-B, and DN3-D (Fig. 2). Water quality widely varied among treatment cells in each constructed wetland. DO was low, generally <6 ppm except in the ecological ponds, and showed an increasing trend along the sequential treatment cells in both constructed wetlands (Table 2). In contrast, conductivity and concentrations of TN and TP showed a decreasing trend along sequential treatment cells, suggesting reductions in the pollutant concentrations of wastewater after passing through these constructed wetlands (Table 2). Other variables, however, fluctuated along the sequential treatment cells. The overall system performance of pollutant removal based on the reduction in concentrations in the water column is shown in Table 3. Removal of BOD and COD was higher in the HS2 with respective removal rates of 58.8% and 51.1%, and the outflow concentration was reduced to <11 and 30 mg L\(^{-1}\), respectively (Tables 2, 3). Concentrations of TN and TP were substantially reduced in the DN with respective removal rates of 51.4% and 52.3%, and the outflow concentrations were 8.4 and 0.5 ppm, respectively.

3.2. Biotic metrics The average species richness of aquatic macrophytes in each treatment cell ranged 4.5–14.3 in the HS2 and 1.4–14.4 in the DN. Table 4 lists the vegetation and average percent cover in each cell. The dominant macrophytes in the HS2 were water spinach (*Ipomoea aquatica*), southern cutgrass (*Leersia hexandra*), *Ludwigia x taiwanensis*, common reed (*Phragmites australis*), and common cattail (*Typha orientalis*) (Table 4). The DN was dominated by *Cyperus imbricatus* subsp. *imbricatus*, water hyacinth (*Eichhornia crassipes*), Chinese water chestnut (*Eleocharis dulcis*), and water spinach. In total, 429 individuals belonging to 33 bird species and 1233 individuals belonging to 57 bird species were respectively recorded in the HS2 and DN. The average species richness of birds in treatment cells ranged 0–7.3 in the HS2 and 0.9–12.3 in the DN (Table 5).
