The share of the total variability accounted for by each of the first two axes of the compromise was 38.4 and 27.3%, respectively (Fig. 1B). Out of the 13 environmental factors taken into account, only a few were found to be correlated with the structure of macroinvertebrate assemblages (Fig. 1B). The first axis described a positive association with the sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies, and a negative association with the altitude. The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 1 for the environmental abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_370_180_1407_1207.png) study, however, we found that the distributions of the chironomids and tubificids were mostly associated with the pond size and pond depth, respectively. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. First record of the endemic phytophilous cladoceran Celsinotum candango Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro, 2010, in Minas Gerais state, in a threatened shallow lake at Serra do Gandarela Francisco Wagner Moreira¹, Emerson Silva Dias¹ & Eneida Maria Eskinazi Sant’Anna¹,² ¹Universidade Federal de Ouro Preto, Instituto de Ciências Exatas e Biológicas, Departamento de Biodiversidade, Evolução e Meio Ambiente. Laboratório de Ecologia Aquática. Campus Morro do Cruzeiro, CEP 35400000, Ouro Preto, MG, Brazil. ²Corresponding author: Eneida Maria Eskinazi Sant’Anna, e-mail: eskinazi@iceb.ufop.br MOREIRA, F.W., DIAS, E.S., SANT’ANNA, W.M.E. First record of the endemic phytophilous cladoceran Celsinotum candango Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro, 2010, in Minas Gerais state, in a threatened shallow lake at Serra do Gandarela. Biota Neotropica. 15(4): e0052. http://dx.doi.org/10.1590/1676-0611-BN-2015-0052 Abstract: This study describes the occurrence of the phytophilous cladoceran Celsinotum candango, which has been considered, up to now, an endemic species of the Brazilian Cerrado, with only two previous records in the wetlands of Brasilia, Federal District. The cladoceran has now been registered at Coutos Lake (“Lagoa dos Coutos”), an altitudinal, temporary shallow lake, located in ironstone outcrops at Serra do Gandarela, Minas Gerais state. This mountain ridge was recently turned into an integral protection conservation unit, the Gandarela National Park. However, many shallow lakes, including this one, were excluded from the delimited area of the park, and are now at risk of disappearing due to expansion of mining activities. The information provided here reveals the importance of these shallow lakes to aquatic biodiversity, and reinforces the need for the inclusion of these rare aquatic ecosystems into the recently created Gandarela National Park. Keywords: Cladoceran, Celsinotum, occurrence, shallow lake, Serra do Gandarela, Minas Gerais. MOREIRA, F.W., DIAS, E.S., SANT’ANNA, W.M.E. Primeiro registro do cladóbero fitófilo endêmico Celsinotum candango Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro, 2010, no estado de Minas Gerais, em uma lagoa ameaçada da Serra do Gandarela. Biota Neotropica. 15(4): e0052. http://dx.doi.org/10.1590/1676-0611-BN-2015-0052 Resumo: O objetivo deste estudo foi descrever a ocorrência do cladóbero fitófilo Celsinotum candango, uma espécie considerada, até o momento, endêmica do cerrado brasileiro, com registros anteriores em apenas duas áreas úmidas de Brasília (Distrito Federal). O cladóbero foi agora encontrado na Lagoa dos Coutos, uma lagoa temporária de altitude, localizada em área de afloramento ferruginoso da Serra da Gadarela, no estado de Minas Gerais. A Serra foi recentemente transformada em uma unidade de conservação (Parque Nacional do Gandarela). Entretanto, esta lagoa, além de outras, foi excluída da área delimitada para o Parque, e está agora sob risco de desaparecer, em função da expansão da atividade de mineração. As informações fornecidas no presente estudo revelam a importância dessas lagoas para a biodiversidade aquática, e reforçam a necessidade de inclusão desses raros ecossistemas aquáticos na recém-criada unidade de conservação do Parque Nacional do Gandarela. Palavras-chave: Cladóbero, Celsinotum, lagoa, Serra do Gandarela, Minas Gerais. Introduction Small lakes are vital inland bodies of freshwater, representing around 30 percent of the global surface area of standing water (Downing et al. 2006; Ewald et al. 2012). These wetlands are recognized as ecosystems of extreme ecological importance, but are nevertheless still neglected in terms of conservation (Maltby 1991; Downing 2010). Altitudinal shallow lakes have also been considered crucial, not only because of the exclusive species they can support, but also due to the suitable environment they provide for the interaction amongst distinct animal groups such as insects, amphibians, birds, mammals, and several others, hence contributing to the maintenance of local and regional diversity (Wiggins et al. 1980; Williams 2006). These shallow environments are usually colonized by aquatic macrophytes, which contribute to their high environmental heterogeneity by diversifying habitats and ecological niches (Drew et al. 2005, Van Der Valk 2012, Lukacs & Finlayson 2010). When compared to the organisms associated to the macrophytes in these humid areas, the phytophilous cladoceran can be considered a group of exceptional diversity. Although they harbor up to 70% of the known cladoceran species (Elmor-Loureiro 2000, Forró et al. 2008), it was only recently that wetlands of the Brazilian Cerrado were added to research aimed at taxonomic knowledge for these organisms. As a result, new species were described and new geographic patterns were established for the phytophilous cladoceran (Sinev & Hollwedel 2002, Serafim-Junior et al. 2003, Elmoor-Loureiro 2007, Elmoor-Loureiro et al. 2009, Sousa et al. 2014 and others). The freshwater cladoceran Celsinotum candango was described very recently (Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro 2010), having its first occurrence in Brazil attributed to a phytophilous community in a shallow pond in Brasília, Federal District. So far, there is only one more record of the species, also in a shallow pond from the Cerrado wetlands (Sousa et al. 2013). In our study, we describe the presence of this species in a temporary shallow lake, “Lagoa dos Coutos” (Lake Coutos), located in ironstone outcrops at Serra do Gandarela (southern portion of the Espinhaço mountain range). This is the third record in Brazil and first in Minas Gerais of the cladoceran Celsinotum candango. Serra do Gandarela is one of the most important synclines of the Minas Gerais central region and it houses several springs that supply water to the Belo Horizonte metropolitan region, including streams and creeks of special class water (ICMBio 2010). Serra do Gandarela is also an important ecological corridor, joining the Caraça region to two important basins: Rio Doce/Piracicaba and São Francisco/Rio das Velhas. According to Jacobi and Carmo (2008a), there is a very high level of plant diversity at Serra do Gandarela. This is a result of mineral and topographical heterogeneity of the outcrops, which creates distinct microhabitats, resulting in a unique association of extremely adapted plants. These adaptations can include metallophytes or, at least, metal-tolerant plant species (Jacobi et al. 2007). Due to the occurrence of these unique environments, high biodiversity and endemic levels, and imminence of impact associated with mining activity, in addition to other anthropic activities, the creation of the National Park of the Serra do Gandarela was proposed and then promulgated on October 13th, 2014 through a Decree-Law. However, only 31.4 out of the 38 hectares initially proposed by the Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade (ICMBio) were considered, excluding rare shallow lakes from complete protection, among them, the Coutos Lake. Mining activity has expansion projects in these unprotected areas, which will inevitably result in the extinction of these aquatic ecosystems. We hope that the information of our study will contribute to reinforce the need to prioritize the preservation of such unique aquatic ecosystems that are still not very well known, but potentially relevant to aquatic biodiversity. Material and Methods The Coutos Lake (19°59’6.54" S; 43°33’4.75" W), is a temporary shallow lake (as described by Williams 2006), located in an ironstone outcrops area, in the municipality of Barão dos Cocais, at about 100km from the state capital, Belo Horizonte. This lake is located in the Rio Doce basin, at 1072m above sea level, under highland subtropical climate with dry winters and rainy summers. It is a shallow pond with 0.65 cm depth average, reaching 1.5 m during the rainy period, until complete dryness in August. Figure 1. During our study (from January to June/2013), water temperature ranged from 29 to 18 °C, presenting higher variation during the summer (25.6 ± 1.4). The Coutos Lake can be considered oligotrophic (chlorophyll \( a \) averaging < 5 g.\( \mu \)L\(^{-1} \)), with neutral to acid waters (pH ranging from 7.46 to 4.77), and low conductivity (from 70 to 120 \( \mu \)S.cm\(^{-1} \)) (Dias, 2014). Since it is a shallow lake, it presents dense macrophyte banks throughout its whole extension, with patches dominated by Eleocharis minima. Several other species of macrophytes have also been found in Coutos Lake, such as Nymphoides indica, Polygonum mesneirianum, Helanthium tenellum, Utricularia sp., and Egeria najas (Dias 2014). Specimens of the cladoceran Celsinotum candango were found among samples of macrophytes collected in January 15th, February 15th and June 19th 2013, during a decomposition experiment. The macrophytes samples were collected through the use of “litter bags”, with dimensions of 10x20 cm (Petersen & Cummins 1974). The specimens were extracted from the samples under a stereomicroscope, preserved in 70% alcohol, and identified according to description given by Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro (2010). All specimens were measured using an eyepiece-micrometer and deposited in the aquatic invertebrate collection of Aquatic Ecology, Evolution and Conservation Laboratory at the Federal University of Ouro Preto. Water temperature (°C), conductivity (\( \mu \)S.cm\(^{-1} \)) and pH were obtained with a Horiba (model U-50) analyzer. Results and Discussion The genus Celsinotum was initially considered endemic to Australia (Frey, 1991); however, it has been registered in other places lately, amplifying its distribution. In Brazil, C. laticaudatum had only been found in the Northern part of the Brazilian Amazon (Smirnov & Santos-Silva 1995), while C. candango had only been found in the Brazilian Cerrado (Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro 2010, Sousa 2013). This paper now presents the first record of C. candango in the state of Minas Gerais and, furthermore, its first record in an altitudinal temporary lake on ironstone outcrops. According to the description of Sinev and Elmoor-Loureiro (2010), Celsinotum candango clearly differs from all other species of the genus in proportions of the postabdomen, as the postanal portion is only 1.2–1.3 times longer than anal one in all other species. C. candango also differs from the other Brazilian species C. laticaudatum Smirnov and Santos-Silva 1995 in longer spine on basal segment of antenna exopodite (about 2/3 length of middle segment of antenna), in the shape of the postabdomen (it is only weakly narrowing distally, distal part of postanal portion is almost rectangular) and in the postabdominal denticles, in this species distalmost denticles are long and single (Sinev & Elmoor-Loureiro 2010). The four C. candango individuals found in Coutos Lake (adult parthenogenetic females) were small, with a maximum length of 0.65 mm. The individuals were found in water temperature ranging from 24.7 to 18°C, conductivity from Figure 1. Map of Gandarela Ridge location and Lagoa dos Coutos. Gandarela Ridge location (A). Coutos Lake panoramic view during rainy period (January/2012) (B). Coutos Lake during dry period (August/2013) (C). 109 to 91 µS.cm⁻¹ and lake water with acid feature (pH from 6.4 to 5.3) Table 1. The specimens presented the characteristic postabdomen, with postabdominal claw from 65-70 µm in length and postanal margin with clusters of small distalmost denticles in each, besides the spine on basal segment of exopodite of antenna as shown in Figure 2. We did not find ephippial forms from C. candango, in spite of the occurrence of other cladocerans resting eggs, and the temporary characteristic of Coutos Lake. The species is considered endemic to the Brazilian Cerrado wetlands (Sousa et al. 2014), and presents restricted geographic distribution with ecological preference for shallow environments, dominated by macrophytes. Traditionally, most studies in aquatic ecology have been directed to ‘permanent’ (i.e., hydroperiod > 1 year) lentic and lotic systems. As a result, we know more about communities in permanent waters than we do about those in temporary ones and have less evidence to protect these unique, endangered habitats than for other systems (Schwartz & Jenkins 2000). The results of our study reinforce the importance of small ponds to aquatic biodiversity, by congregating plants diversity, environmental heterogeneity, and invertebrate assemblages with specific habitat requirements, such as phytophilous cladocerans. All these features can enhance the occurrence of exclusive species in these temporary aquatic ecosystems. Coutos Lake can nowadays be considered a threatened aquatic ecosystem in the Gandarela ridge. The intense expansion of mining activity in the region is considered one of the greatest threats to the integrity of Serra do Gandarela ecosystems (Jacobi & Carmo 2008b, Carmo et al. 2012). The creation of the Gandarela National Park did not reach these areas of extreme relevance to the preservation of species and ecosystems in ironstone outcrops of the Serra, not even shallow lakes that still deserve further research in order to describe their biodiversity. The record of this recently discovered cladoceran species reveals that there probably is still much more to find in these unique ecosystems that are now critically threatened of disappearing.

Fish assemblages in floodplain lakes in a Neotropical river during the wet season (Magdalena River, Colombia) Carlos Granado-Lorencio*,†, Alejandra Gulfo†, Frank Alvarez†, Luz Fernanda Jiménez-Segura†, Juan David Carvajal-Quintero† and Andrés Hernández-Serna† * Department of Plant Biology and Ecology, Faculty of Biology, University of Sevilla, Box 1095, 41080 Sevilla, Spain † Ichthyology Group, Sciences Institute, University of Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia (Accepted 20 February 2012) Abstract: A number of studies have pointed out that abiotic factors and recolonization dynamics appear to be more important than biotic interactions in structuring river–fish assemblages. In this paper, we studied the fish assemblages in 27 floodplain lakes, with perennial connection to the river, in the middle section of the Magdalena River (Colombia), to examine spatial pattern in freshwater fish diversity in relation to some environmental parameters. Our objective was to examine relationships between floodplain-lake fish communities and environmental variables associated with lake morphology, water chemistry and river–floodplain connectivity in a large river–floodplain ecosystem. During the study, a total of 18 237 fish were caught from 50 species (regional richness; 17 were migrants and 33 residents). In the present study, the most diverse order was Characiformes with 20 species, followed by Siluriformes, with 19 species. Characidae and Loricariidae were the richest families. The range of species richness (local richness) varied between five and 39 species. Similarity of local assemblages (using the presence–absence data) depends on the distance between lakes. A positive relationship was observed between the Ln of the total abundance of each species and the number of lakes where they were found. Out of all the environmental parameters taken in the lakes, only the size (Log Area) and relative perimeter length are significantly related to local assemblage species richness. It has not been possible to demonstrate that the connectivity (distance) from lakes to the main river can be considered a predictor of the local richness. Key Words: distance decay, fish, floodplain lakes, local richness, river INTRODUCTION Patterns of species co-occurrence have been widely investigated by ecologists (Jackson et al. 1992, Peres-Neto 2004). Fish communities are structured by effects working at a regional scale, where abiotic factors limit the species distributions; and at a local scale, where biotic factors determine species survival within a system (Gaston 2000, Thompson 2009). However, in highly variable aquatic systems, abiotic factors appear to be more important with little or no influence of biotic factors (Fisher & Lindenmayer 2002, Granado-Lorencio et al. 2007, Snodgrass et al. 1995, Suárez et al. 2004, Taylor & Warren 2001). In large tropical rivers, rainfall-driven hydrology is a key factor in the seasonality of aquatic environments (Sanderson et al. 2005). The flood-pulse concept (FPC) identifies seasonal hydrology as the major force structuring stream–fish assemblages (Araújo et al. 2009, Junk et al. 1989). During the flood pulse, the majority of water bodies become interconnected (floodplains) and the fish are free to disperse throughout the floodplain (Godoy et al. 1999). Floodplain lakes connected with the river by channels are open systems (Saint-Paul et al. 2000), and are typical ecotopes of large lowland rivers (Schomaker & Wolter 2011). In Neotropical floodplains, the flood cycle (pulse) associated with alteration of dry and rainy seasons produces major changes in fish communities (Rodríguez & Lewis 1994), and it acts as an intermediate disturbance. Because of high environmental variability, species assemblage organization has been portrayed as highly stochastic, without any apparent overall organizational pattern (Lowe-McConnell 1987, Lowe et al. 2006). However, more recent studies have seemingly found non-random associations of fishes within the floodplain (Petry et al. 2003, Winemiller 1996). Studies on the structure and dynamics of fish assemblages of permanent water bodies in different floodplain river systems indicate that these assemblages are structured by a combination of environmental variables, as well as by the pool of species available during the period in which the water bodies are permanently connected to the river (Fernandes et al. 2010). Certain environmental variables (hypoxia, depth, transparency, local-scale habitat, size and drainage area) have been considered to be good predictors of the richness of local associations of fish, within the floodplain (Montaña & Winemiller 2010). A study of the factors that control species richness in floodplain lakes requires information about the taxonomy and distribution of the species. Information is more extensive on fish species from temperate rivers and big tropical rivers than on fish species of floodplain lakes. Therefore, the first aim of this study was to catalogue fish species (ichthyofauna survey) and examine the fish richness in tropical floodplain lakes, during the high-water season. For this study, we selected 27 lakes from the Magdalena river, which vary in morphological and limnological characteristics. The fish caught were identified taxonomically and the sampling data were used to calculate the total abundance. The second aim was to determine the main factors that control local species richness (lake community). We test the following hypotheses: (1) there is an relationship between abundance and regional occupancy (%) in fish species of the floodplain lakes, (2) the area is related to the species richness of the lake (species–area relationship, SAR), (3) the distance to the main river (connectivity) is a predictive variable of local richness, and (4) the geographical distance between lakes has a relationship to the similarity in fish assemblages found in them (community similarity decay). METHODS The Magdalena River is 1612 km long and drains a 257 438-km² basin. The principal tributaries are the Cauca, Sogamoso, San Jorge and César Rivers. The average precipitation for the valley measured in run-off is 2050 mm y⁻¹. The lowest values are recorded for the December–January and July–August periods, and the highest between April–May and October–November (twice-yearly peak flooding). The annual mean discharge (data for 1975–1995) from the Magdalena River in the locality of Calamar (112 km upstream of the estuary) is 7200 m³ s⁻¹ (Restrepo & Jerfve 2000). The physical structure of the system comprises a meandering river channel with numerous connected and isolated lakes (lakes vary in size and degree of connection). The main types of habitats in floodplain lakes are herbaceous vegetation (aquatic macrophytes) and open water. The relative proportion of the habitats varies both regionally and seasonally. The whole middle and lower Magdalena River is not fragmented by dams and is still characterized by highly variable hydrological conditions. While some floodplain lakes become permanently cut off from the main flow of the river and remain closed (isolated), others remain open with perennial connection with the river. Twenty-seven connected lakes were studied, all in the midsection of the Magdalena River basin, between the localities of Puerto Boyacá and Barrancabermeja (840.92 km; Figure 1). The study area is centred at 6°04′N–7°26′N, 73°57′W–74°31′W (GPS derived). The selection was based on lake surface area and permanent connectivity with the main river. These lakes were selected to represent a range of size (4–2300 ha) and degree of human impact (Table 1). Lakes were sampled during the wet season, because of its near-maximum species richness and stability in water level. Ten lakes were sampled at the beginning of November 2008 (Palagua, Samaria, El Encanto, Rio Viejo, Barbacoas, Chucurí, El Opón, Juan Esteban, Tabacurú, Bija) and the remaining 17 in 2010, at the same month, coinciding with the second peak flooding. The sampling method was the same for all the lakes. Water parameters were measured for 24 h every 4 h. At each fishing site, dissolved oxygen concentration (DO in mg L⁻¹), water temperature (T in °C) and conductivity (μS) were measured in situ. DO (dissolved oxygen) and temperature were measured in the water column every metre. The maximum depth (m) of lakes was determined by sonar. For each lake, the area and perimeter length were calculated for the period of high water level. An index used to quantify this is called the shoreline development (DI). This index compares the minimum possible circumference of the lake, given a specific surface area (i.e. a perfect circle), to the actual circumference of the lake and its surface area. A value of 1 for shoreline development is a perfect circle and a larger value means that the shoreline is highly dissected. Lakes with high shoreline development are often naturally productive relative to those with low shoreline development. The shortest distance between lakes and the river were measured on maps (1: 100 000) from Google Earth. We use the length of the channel (measured in the field) that links the lake to the main river as a measure of connectivity; Tockner et al. (1999) consider that this distance is a good predictor for this structural variable. Prior to statistical analyses, all variables except pH and temperature were logarithmically transformed in order to approximate normal distributions. The measurements for environmental variables were analysed using a one-way ANOVA with the aim of discovering differences between periods, as well as between habitats for each period (Bonferroni correction included). In order to estimate the total species richness, sampling was designed for each of the various existing habitats. In all the lakes, one sampling station was chosen within each of these four macrohabitats: littoral with trees, littoral without trees, open water, and the connecting channel between the lake and main river. All were sampled simultaneously. Because sampling effort was constant across samples, it was not necessary to adjust richness estimates using rarefaction or other techniques to account for different sampling techniques or sample sizes. The fish were collected using experimental multifilament gillnets, formed from panels measuring 100 × 3 m, in nine different sizes (from 2 to 10 cm stretched mesh). This kind of technique for capture has been used in the studies of associations of fish in oxbow lakes (Winemiller et al. 2000). The nets were set out for 24 h, and checked every 4 h, with the intention of avoiding phenomena such as predators and decomposition due to the high temperature of the water. Fishes were classified as sedentary or short-distance migrant species based on available regional information. Catch per site was standardized according to the length of bank fished and the catch per unit effort (CPUE) determined as fish caught per 100 m. The standardized fish densities were used to calculate basic fish-assemblage metrics, like relative abundance (%) of species and richness. In all analyses for a lake, only the abundances and richness of taxa present at that lake were used. We used the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to test the occupancy-abundance relationship. We define the richness of species in a lake as local richness (LR, \( \alpha \)-diversity), and the analysis of all the lakes taken together as regional richness (RR, \( \gamma \)-diversity). We analysed the similarities of assemblages using only presence–absence data. Previous studies have shown that taxonomic patterns may differ when using the presence–absence or abundance data (La Sorte & McKinney 2007). In order to analyse whether the geographical distance between lakes has any relationship to the similarity in associations of fishes found in them (community similarity decay; Nekola & White 1999), the Sørensen index was applied (\( S = C/\alpha \); where C represents common species and \( \alpha \) the average richness for the two lakes), and the Figure 2. Distance decay often is examined using linear geographic distance (Maloney & Munguía 2011). Distance decay is used to describe the decay in ecological similarity of assemblages between two sites as a function of their distance apart along an environmental gradient. Regression distance-decay models are fitted by calculating the ecological similarity between each pair of sites on a scatterplot of similarity vs. distance (x-axis). As the pairwise similarity values and distances are not truly independent in a statistical sense (each fish community is used in more than one pairwise comparison), we use average similarity and average distance for each lake. The significance of each regression model was tested using a randomization approach. The general model was conducted using software package Statistica 6.0. The study of species–area relationships (SARs) has a long tradition in ecology and the construction of SARs is one of the most frequently used methods to estimate species number at different spatial scales (Lomolino 2000). In this study, the data were fitted to the power model (ln (S) = z ln (A) + c). RESULTS A total of 18 237 individuals were recorded representing 50 species (regional richness). Characiformes (38%) and Siluriformes (36%) were the best represented orders. We observed 50 fish species (Appendix 1). The most frequent species in all catches were Cyphocharax magdalenae (29.3%) and Roeboides dayi (20.3%), followed by Caquetaia kraussii (14.6%) and Trachelyopterus insignis (12.8%), all of them with a sedentary life style. The range of richness of species (local richness) varied between 9 and 39 species. In Figure 2, the species caught were ordered on the basis of their overall Ln regional abundance and geographical range (% of lakes occupied). We observed 50 species, of which 22 were dominant, two were accidental, three common and 23 were rare (in relation to the mean values of the total number of species and lakes, 3.87% and 42.3%, respectively). The species found in all the lakes studied (100% incidence) were sedentary species: Caquetaia kraussii and Cyphocharax magdalenae. At the local scale, the relationship between migratory and sedentary species was significant and positive in all the lakes in terms of local richness (r = 0.79, P = 0.0009). A significant relationship was observed between the total abundance of each species (ln-transformed) and the number of lakes where they were found (n = 50, r_s = 0.93, P = 0.000001). Out of all the measurements taken in the lakes, only lake size (log(Area) was significantly correlated to the local richness of species (n = 27, r = 0.69, P = 0.0009) (Figure 3). We found that lake shoreline development had significant effect on species richness (n = 27, r = 0.48, P = 0.0068). The other environmental variables (including connectivity) were not significant in any of the multiple regressions; many habitat characteristics were significantly correlated. Similarity in fish communities decreased with distance. A linear regression provided a good fit to these data (averaged for each lake). Our results show that the Figure 3. DISCUSSION The Neotropical region harbours the world’s richest freshwater ichthyofauna, with more than 2500 species (Böhlke et al. 1978). The ichthyofauna of South American rivers is dominated by ostariophysan fishes (Characiformes over Siluriformes and Gymnotiformes). The families Anostomidae, Chilodontidae, Curimatidae and Prochilodontidae inhabit most river systems throughout tropical and subtropical South America and southern Central America (Albert & Reis 2011, Carolsfield et al. 2004). In the present study, the most diverse order was Characiformes with seven families and 20 species, followed by Siluriformes, six families and 19 species. Characidae and Loricariidae were the most diverse (seven genera). It is interesting to observe that there is a maximum of three species within each genus, and that most genera are represented by only one species. Lowe-McConnell (1987) explained high dominance of small characiformes in tropical fish communities mainly by the capacity of these species to use oxygen in the upper portion of the water column. Two variables were consistently related to the species richness: area and shoreline development. Other variables such as depth, DO, conductivity, temperature and distance to the main river were not significant in any of the multiple regressions. The lack of relationship between these variables and the fish richness in floodplain lakes could be accounted for by sampling limitations (type II error) or could represent a real lack of effect. Since we studied 27 lakes, the statistical resolution was reasonable despite the variability in catch. A more probable hypothesis is that these variables had a weak effect, if any, on species richness. Lake depth is often an important variable to explain fish richness and fish abundance. Winemiller et al. (2000) found a direct relationship between these variables in oxbow lakes of the Brazos River, USA. Suárez et al. (2004) and Tejerina-Garro et al. (1998) reported depth as one of the main environmental structuring factors of fish communities of the Pantanal and Araguaia River. Lake depth had a weak effect on the species richness of lakes in our study. Even if the connectivity (distance) to the main channel can be considered a predictive variable, indicating the richness of a lake, or at least in relation to migratory species as has been demonstrated in certain Amazon floodplain lakes (Granado-Lorencio et al. 2005), in our study it has not been possible to demonstrate this. In the lakes studied by Bertolo & Magnan (2006) connectivity had little effect on fish species richness; and Tejerina-Garro et al. (1998) verified that connectivity had no apparent effect on community structure. This may be because of the varying hydrological behaviour of the river, or the different capacities of diverse species to colonize or simply that the range of lengths of the connecting channels was not sufficient. Comparisons of tropical fish community structure in lake surveys conducted at regional or supra-regional scales have detected predictable links between community structure and environmental variation (Tejerina-Garro et al. 1998). Principally, the structure of fish assemblages can be produced by two different processes: species-specific colonization and/or dispersal potential and species-specific vulnerability to extinction. If it was generated through colonization, then species colonize sites located at different distances from the common source (main river). Species with greater capacity for dispersal are able to cover longer distances, and colonize more distant sites, than those which are either less mobile or sedentary. The similarity between species at sites demonstrates a more or less strong negative relationship to the geographical distance between them. This pattern has been observed in freshwater ecosystems (Taylor & Warren 2001). McAbendroth et al. (2005) indicate that the species with more limited capacity for dispersal occupy fewer sites than the migrant species. In our study, the two most abundant species (Caquetaia kraussi and Cyphocharax magdalenae) are present in the 27 lakes in the study; they are floodplain specialists but are not migratory species (both have sedentary behaviour; Galvis & Mójica 2004). This admits the possibility that species-specific, non-biological factors exist. Our results show that the similarity between the local assemblages depends on the distance between lakes; possibly relating to the colonization processes. Thomaz et al. (2007) recorded that during the flood season some fish species migrate from upper reaches to the floodplain after spawning, and fish communities tend to be more similar among the lakes that comprise a floodplain system. The area hypothesis refers to the existence of a positive relationship between the number of species present in a given area and the size of this area (McArthur & Wilson 1963). Lubinski et al. (2008) verified that lake surface area was one of the most important factors in the structuring of fish communities and local richness (Liu & Wang 2010, Minns 1989, Sondergaard et al. 2005). Larger areas have higher rates of speciation and immigration, and lower rates of extinction. Neotropical freshwater faunas conform well to the species–area relationship (Tedesco et al. 2005). In our study, the local richness manifest significant relationships with the size of the lake and shoreline development, possibly indicating that the dispersal assembly (through hydrological connectivity) is an important ecological factor. A pattern consistently shown in biogeographic studies is a decrease in community similarity with increasing distance between two sampled sites (Qian 2010, Rosindell et al. 2011). This decay is a manifestation of processes controlling community composition that operate across a gradient of scales. Community similarity at large scales tends to decrease environmental similarities, dispersal limitation and niche-width differences (Nekola & White 1999). This relationship obtained suggested that seasonal colonization processes play an important role in fish floodplain assembly. Lakes with a larger surface area comprise greater fish richness than smaller ones, and small lakes contain species with ample regional distribution and abundance. As already shown by Taylor & Warren (2001), species with high local abundances were better colonizers. The regularities observed in our study permit introduction of ecological aspects into the communities in these Neotropical floodplain rivers for purposes of development and planning strategies for biodiversity conservation (Gaston & Blackburn 2000). In order to estimate the total species richness, sampling was designed for each of the various existing habitats. In all the lakes, one sampling station was chosen within each of these four macrohabitats: littoral with trees, littoral without trees, open water, and the connecting channel between the lake and main river. All were sampled simultaneously. Because sampling effort was constant across samples, it was not necessary to adjust richness estimates using rarefaction or other techniques to account for different sampling techniques or sample sizes. The fish were collected using experimental multifilament gillnets, formed from panels measuring 100 × 3 m, in nine different sizes (from 2 to 10 cm stretched mesh). This kind of technique for capture has been used in the studies of associations of fish in oxbow lakes (Winemiller et al. 2000). The nets were set out for 24 h, and checked every 4 h, with the intention of avoiding phenomena such as predators and decomposition due to the high temperature of the water. Fishes were classified as sedentary or short-distance migrant species based on available regional information. Catch per site was standardized according to the length of bank fished and the catch per unit effort (CPUE) determined as fish caught per 100 m. The standardized fish densities were used to calculate basic fish-assemblage metrics, like relative abundance (%) of species and richness. In all analyses for a lake, only the abundances and richness of taxa present at that lake were used. We used the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to test the occupancy-abundance relationship. We define the richness of species in a lake as local richness (LR, \( \alpha \)-diversity), and the analysis of all the lakes taken together as regional richness (RR, \( \gamma \)-diversity). We analysed the similarities of assemblages using only presence–absence data. Gas transfer velocities in small forested ponds Meredith A. Holgerson1,2, Emily R. Farr1, and Peter A. Raymond1 1School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA, 2Now at Department of Environmental Science and Management, Portland State University, Portland, Oregon, USA Abstract Inland waters actively exchange gases with the atmosphere, and the gas exchange rate informs system biogeochemistry, ecology, and global carbon budgets. Gas exchange in medium- to large-sized lakes is largely regulated by wind; yet less is known about processes regulating gas transfer in small ponds where wind speeds are low. In this study, we determined the gas transfer velocity, \( k_{600} \), in four small (<250 m\(^2\)) ponds by using a propane (C\(_3\)H\(_8\)) gas injection. When estimated across 12 h periods, the average \( k_{600} \) ranged from 0.19 to 0.72 m d\(^{-1}\) across the ponds. We also estimated \( k_{600} \) at 2 to 3 h intervals during the day and evaluated the relationship with environmental conditions. The average daytime \( k_{600} \) ranged from 0.33 to 1.83 m d\(^{-1}\) across the ponds and was best predicted by wind speed and air or air-water temperature; however, the explanatory power was weak (\( R^2 < 0.27 \)) with high variability within and among ponds. To compare our results to larger water bodies, we compiled direct measurements of \( k_{600} \) from 67 ponds and lakes worldwide. Our \( k_{600} \) estimates were within the range of estimates for other small ponds, and variability in \( k_{600} \) increased with lake size. However, the majority of studies were conducted on medium-sized lakes (0.01 to 1 km\(^2\)), leaving small ponds and large lakes understudied. Overall, this study adds four small ponds to the existing body of research on gas transfer velocities from inland waters and highlights uncertainty in \( k_{600} \), with implications for calculating metabolism and carbon emissions in inland waters. 1. Introduction Inland waters actively exchange gases with the atmosphere, with important consequences for ecosystem dynamics such as carbon emissions [Schilder et al., 2013; Seekell et al., 2014], oxygen availability [Melack and Fisher, 1983; Holgerson et al., 2016], and food web structure [Schindler et al., 1997; Devlin et al., 2015]. For instance, air-water gas exchange rates influence the extent to which greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, are released by inland waters. The gas transfer velocity, \( k \), partly controls the exchange rate and is largely driven by turbulence at the air-water interface [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. In large water bodies, wind speed often drives turbulence because it creates surface waves and shear stress that increase \( k \) [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. As such, wind speed is often used to model \( k \) in lakes [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and the ocean [Wanninkhof, 1992]. However, the relationship between wind speed and \( k \) typically breaks down under low-wind conditions, characteristic of smaller and more sheltered waters [Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998]. Considering that over 90% of lakes and ponds worldwide are less than 1 ha in size [Downing et al., 2006; Verpoorter et al., 2014] and that small ponds play a disproportionately large role in greenhouse gas emissions [Holgerson and Raymond, 2016], it is critical to determine their \( k \). Furthermore, because directly measuring \( k \) is time intensive, it is important to evaluate if any environmental parameters can be used to predict \( k \). Other than wind, environmental factors that influence turbulence and can be readily measured or estimated include surfactants, rainfall, and convection. Surfactants are formed by hydrophobic organic compounds, and they reduce wind stress at the surface, can obstruct molecular diffusion, and ultimately decrease gas transfer [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. Raindrops physically increase turbulence at the air-water interface and increase gas exchange [Ho et al., 1997]. Convection can influence \( k \) through seasonal and diurnal changes in air-water temperature, particularly in small water bodies [Matthews et al., 2003; Poindexter and Variano, 2013]. For instance, convection from cooling surface waters can increase gas transfer velocities by increasing turbulence in the surface mixing layer [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Holgerson et al., 2016]. The importance of convective cooling may be greater in small systems because they exhibit more extreme diurnal temperature changes than larger lakes, which increases sensible heat flux and convective turbulence [Woolway et al., 2016]. The relative importance of convection versus wind on \( k \) may be mediated by lake surface area, with wind dominating in larger systems and convection being more important in smaller, more sheltered lakes and ponds [Read et al., 2012]. There are multiple approaches for estimating \( k \), including whole-lake gas tracers, floating chambers, directly measuring turbulence, meteorological techniques (e.g., eddy flux), and modeling techniques, all of which have limitations [Matthews et al., 2003; Zappa et al., 2007; Cole et al., 2010]. Whole-lake tracers use gases such as sulfur hexafluoride, helium, or propane, which are added to a water body and the gas loss over time is used to estimate \( k \) [e.g., Wanninkhof et al., 1985; Clark et al., 1995; Frost and Upstill-Goddard, 2002; Cole et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2012]. However, this approach can be time-intensive and costly, particularly for large water bodies. Floating chambers are easy to deploy, but they create microenvironments within the chamber that exclude effects of wind and rainfall, generate artificial turbulence, change the atmospheric pressure, and alter the air-water concentration gradient [Matthews et al., 2003; Vachon et al., 2010]. Additionally, there are often high spatial and temporal variabilities that may not be captured by chambers that are only deployed for a short time [Schilder et al., 2013; Vachon and Prairie, 2013]. Flux chambers can also grossly overestimate \( k \) in low-turbulence environments [Vachon et al., 2010], characteristic of smaller water bodies. Directly measuring turbulence and eddy flux techniques works well but requires expensive equipment and is usually employed only in larger water bodies with adequate fetch [e.g., Jonsson et al., 2008]. Models offer the benefit that \( k \) can be estimated for water bodies that were never sampled, thus saving time, money, and allowing for gas exchange estimates to be extrapolated to the regional or global scale. Predictive models were originally based entirely on wind speed [Wanninkhof, 1992; Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998] and more recently, models have included components for other variables such as lake area [Vachon and Prairie, 2013], wave breaking [Soloviev et al., 2007; Winslow et al., 2016], and buoyancy flux to capture convection [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Read et al., 2012]. For instance, the surface renewal model takes into account turbulence generated from both wind and heat loss, which creates instability at the air-water interface, particularly when the water becomes warmer than the air [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. Numerous models are now available for estimating \( k \), with varying data requirements [Winslow et al., 2016]. While these models are useful, they first require field sampling and validation across diverse water bodies. Field studies have shown that the wind speed-gas exchange relationship breaks down under low-wind speeds (\(<3\) m s\(^{-1}\)) [Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998] and models that predict convection will dominate in these low-wind and oftentimes smaller water bodies [Read et al., 2012]. While some field studies have estimated \( k \) in small lakes, we are not aware of any study conducted in ponds smaller than 3000 m\(^2\) [Cole et al., 2010; Schilder et al., 2013]. Considering that there could be as many as 3 billion ponds between 100 and 1000 m\(^2\) globally [Downing, 2010] and that small ponds are hotspots for carbon emissions [Holgerson and Raymond, 2016], it is critical to determine their \( k \). Our study aims to fill this research gap by using whole-pond gas tracer studies to measure \( k \) in four small (<250 m\(^2\)), low-wind ponds. We then compared \( k \) to environmental parameters including wind speed, rain, light, and air and pond temperatures. We expected that pond cooling, indicative of convection, would be more important than wind in predicting \( k \). Lastly, we compiled data from 67 ponds and lakes worldwide where \( k \) was directly measured in order to compare values and variability across a spectrum of lake sizes. We expected that \( k \) would increase with lake size and were curious about variability across lake size classes. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Sites We evaluated the gas transfer velocity, \( k \), in four small, temporary ponds in Yale-Myers Forest in northeastern Connecticut during May and June 2013. The ponds ranged in surface area from 181 to 225 m\(^2\) and in mean depth from 31 to 56 cm (Table 1). The four ponds, Brookside, CH, RH, and Westford, were chosen for their closed basins with minimal emergent vegetation. The closed basin prevents the gas tracer from being diluted by inflow or escaping with outflow. The lack of emergent vegetation ensured that plant matter was not an important factor in regulating \( k \) [Poindexter and Variano, 2013]. During its sampling period, RH had ferns in about 20% of the basin along the edge and about 10 trees in the sides of the basin because it was sampled after a period of rain and therefore had higher water levels. All four ponds are heavily sheltered by the surrounding forest and thus have negligible fetch. Westford and CH are located within the forest directly beside roads, and Brookside and RH are both surrounded entirely by forest approximately 0.5 km from a road. aTemperature and wind speed are averaged across the entire study period (82 or 83 h), while rain is cumulative. 2.2. Environmental Conditions To monitor environmental conditions at each pond, we used a data logger (Campbell Scientific CR300) to log measurements of wind speed (m s−1) and wind direction (degrees), air and water temperature (°C), photosynthetically active radiation (μmol s−1 m−2), and rainfall (mm) at 15 min intervals in each pond. We positioned the anemometer (height above water level: Westford 75 cm, Brookside 77 cm, CH 50 cm, and RH 35 cm), temperature probes, and photometer (LI-190 Quantum Sensor, LI-COR) on a stake at the deepest point of each pond. A tipping-bucket rain gauge located on a separate stake in the least canopy-covered region of each basin measured precipitation. We assessed pond bathymetry by measuring depth every meter along five transects per pond. We assumed that ponds had elliptical basins to estimate surface area and used depth measurements to estimate pond volume. 2.3. Gas Sampling We injected the ponds with propane because it is an inert gas with negligible background concentrations in the air and water. On the first day of sampling, we used an airstone to bubble propane into eight 18.9 L carboys filled with pond water for 10 min each at 13 psi. We added 3 mL of rhodamine to each carboy as a tracer to determine when the pond had completely mixed. The carboys were well mixed, and we sampled each carboy to determine initial propane concentrations. We then poured the carboy mixtures throughout the entire pond basin and walked through the pond to help with mixing. We used a handheld data logger (Turner Designs DataBank™) to measure rhodamine concentrations twice a day for the first 2 days to verify that the propane concentration mixed throughout the pond. We took our first measurements 6 h after the propane addition, which is when rhodamine concentrations indicated that the propane had mixed evenly throughout the pond basin. We measured propane concentrations from surface waters (~13 cm below the surface) at the deepest point of each pond by using a peristaltic pump (Cole-Parmer Masterflex E/S™ portable sampler 115 VAC). We took occasional samples manually without the pump as a result of instrument malfunction. We sampled every 2 h for the first 24 h, then every 3 h for the remaining 72 h, excluding the interval between 20 h and 08 h due to daylight constraints. We measured propane concentration by using a headspace equilibration technique [Raymond et al., 1997]. Briefly, we filled a beaker with water from the peristaltic pump and allowed it to flush for several volumes. We took three replicate 40 mL water samples from the beaker by using an airtight 60 mL syringe, then immediately drew in 20 mL of ambient air. We shook the syringe vigorously for 2 min in order to equilibrate the air and water phases. Samples of the headspace were then stored and transported to the laboratory in airtight, evacuated glass vials (Labco Limited, UK). We measured propane concentrations using a gas chromatograph (GC) (SRI 310C) with a 3.5 mm column. The GC temperature settings were as follows: detector temperature to 150°C and oven temperature to 100°C, resulting in a propane retention time of ~4.08 min. We injected all propane samples in 1 mL quantities with a 1 mL syringe. We also ran propane samples taken from the eight carboys for each pond on the GC with equivalent initial temperature settings but injected 0.5 mL volumes. PeakSimple 4.09 software measured the propane peak area in each sample, which we converted to concentration (ppmv) by using propane calibration curves. In order to obtain pond propane concentrations, we multiplied measured propane concentrations by 3/2 to correct for the dilution with ambient air during headspace equilibration. HOLGERSON ET AL. GAS EXCHANGE IN SMALL PONDS 1013 2.4. Estimating Gas Transfer Velocity Gas transfer between aquatic surfaces and the atmosphere is described by the equation: \[ F = k (C_{\text{sur}} - C_{\text{eq}}) \] (1) where \( F \) is the gas flux (mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)), \( k \) is the gas transfer velocity (m d\(^{-1}\)), \( C_{\text{sur}} \) is the gas concentration in the surface water, and \( C_{\text{eq}} \) is the gas concentration when in equilibrium with the atmosphere. For the propane additions, we directly measured \( F \), \( C_{\text{sur}} \), and \( C_{\text{eq}} \), allowing for the derivation of \( k \). To derive \( k \), we first used a Grubbs outlier test to discount any erroneous propane concentrations that resulted from sampling error. We then converted the average propane concentrations (ppm\(_v\)) of the triplicates at each time point to units of mol L\(^{-1}\) by using Henry’s law constants [Mohebbi et al., 2012; Sander, 2015]. We calculated \( k \) across two different time scales: (1) for each 12 h sampling interval and (2) for each 2 or 3 h sampling period during the day. Longer time scales may more accurately reflect the overall ecosystem gas transfer velocity [Wanninkhof et al., 1987], while shorter time periods better allow for comparisons to be made to environmental conditions. To calculate \( k \) (m d\(^{-1}\)), we used the following equation [Wanninkhof et al., 1987]: \[ k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i - C_o}{C_f - C_o} \] (2) where \( h \) is the average depth of the pond, \( \Delta t \) is the time interval, \( C_i \) and \( C_f \) are the initial and final propane concentrations in the pond, respectively, and \( C_o \) is the background concentration of propane in the water. We computed average pond depth, \( h \), by taking the mean of the measured depths for each square meter measured in each pond. Since \( C_o \) of propane is negligible in this experiment, equation (2) becomes \[ k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f} \] (3) Because we measured propane concentrations multiple times during the day, to estimate \( k \) for 12 h daytime periods, we performed a linear regression to determine the slope of concentration change over time for each 12 h daytime interval of sampling, and this slope replaced \( \frac{1}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f} \) in equation (3). We did not take any gas samples between 20 h and 08 h during the experiment, so we calculated the \( k \) values for each night of sampling by using \( C_f \) from the previous day as the initial propane concentration and \( C_i \) from the following day as the final propane concentration. We normalized \( k \) values to a \( k_{600} \) for propane by using the following equation [Jähne et al., 1987]: \[ \frac{k_{600}}{k_{\text{gas2}}} = \left( \frac{600}{\text{Sc}_{\text{gas2}}} \right)^n \] (4) where \( k_{600} \) is the \( k \) for propane at 20°C and corresponds to a Schmidt number of 600, which can be related to the \( k \) for any other gas [Raymond et al., 2012]. Sc denotes the Schmidt number for the particular gas of interest, and \( n \) is the Schmidt exponent, which varies from –0.5 to –0.67 depending on the boundary conditions. In low-wind environments (<3 m s\(^{-1}\)), \( n \) can be assumed to equal –0.67 [Jähne et al., 1987]. Occasionally, our measurements indicated that propane concentrations increased between sampling times, which likely resulted from spatial heterogeneity in the pond. We only report estimates of \( k \) for periods of time where propane concentrations decreased and indicate net propane evasion from the pond. 2.5. Comparison Across Lake Sizes We conducted a meta-analysis to compare our results to other water bodies where \( k_{600} \) was directly measured. We identified 18 studies, including ours, representing 67 ponds and lakes ranging in size from 181 m\(^2\) to 520 km\(^2\) (Data Set S2 in the supporting information). With this data set, we examined the mean and variability of \( k_{600} \) across lake sizes and also explored the relationship between surface area and gas exchange rate. 2.6. Data Analysis To evaluate if \( k_{600} \) was influenced by environmental variables, we used linear mixed-effects models with pond as a random effect. Models were created in R (R version 3.2.4, R Core Team) by using the “lme4” package [Bates et al., 2014]. Models were constructed by using daytime 2 or 3 h estimates of \( k_{600} \), only including Figure 1. Estimating Gas Transfer Velocity Surface water propane concentrations decreased exponentially over the sampling period in all four ponds (Figure 1), indicating continuous propane evasion from the ponds to the atmosphere. Initial concentrations of propane measured in the ponds ranged from 89 nmol L\(^{-1}\) in CH to 283 nmol L\(^{-1}\) in Westford and decreased between 51% and 93% during the sampling periods (Table 2). For 12 h periods, \( k_{600} \) averaged between 0.22 and 0.72 m d\(^{-1} \), with considerable variability within and among ponds (Table 2). For instance, estimates of \( k_{600} \) in CH differed by as much as 1.21 m d\(^{-1} \) among days. The maximum variability among ponds was 1.23 m d\(^{-1} \), with a minimum of 0.07 m d\(^{-1} \) in Westford and a maximum of 1.30 m d\(^{-1} \) in CH. There were no significant differences in average \( k_{600} \) during the day versus night (t test, \( t = 0.84 \), d.f. = 15.76, \( p = 0.42 \)); however, average daytime values (ranging from 0.37 to 1.30 m d\(^{-1} \)) were slightly higher than average nighttime values (ranging from 0.07 to 1.03 m d\(^{-1} \)) in CH, RH, and Westford, but not Brookside (Table 2). When measured across each 2 to 3 h period for daytime measurements only, the average \( k_{600} \) ranged between 0.33 and 1.83 m d\(^{-1} \) and was also variable within and among ponds (Table 2). For instance, during the 3 day study, daytime 2 to 3 h estimates of \( k_{600} \) differed by as much as 3.52 m d\(^{-1} \) in Brookside. Among ponds, there was a maximum variability of 3.94 m d\(^{-1} \), with a minimum of 0.01 m d\(^{-1} \) in RH and a maximum of 3.95 m d\(^{-1} \) in Brookside. 3.3.
