The Jassby-Platt model (Eq. 3) fitted to daily GPP rates and normalized to 20°C showed a positive relationship to daily incident irradiance with a tendency towards saturation on days of high irradiance (Fig. 4). The charophyte dominated lakes obtained high metabolic rates during early summer. Metabolic rates were highest in Lake 1 and 2, slightly lower in Lake 4 and 5 and lowest in Lake 3 (Figs. 3, 5). Compared to deeper and larger lakes (Hanson et al. 2003; Solomon et al. 2013), volumetric rates of GPP and R were very high (Table 2; Fig. 6). Despite the shallow water in the charophyte lakes, areal rates were also relatively high compared to other types of aquatic ecosystems (Fig. 7). The high volumetric rates gave rise to extreme diel fluctuations in surface water oxygen saturation. This variability was particularly pronounced in Lake 2 (mean 120% saturation; range 6–279%), where low nighttime oxygen minima (mean 19% saturation, range 6–59%) were frequent during summer 2016. Positive NEP rates are in agreement with the average oxygen supersaturation measured in surface waters of the studied lakes. During summer 2016, NEP was positive in all lakes and of the same level in Lake 1, 2 and 4. However, NEP in Lake 3 was close to zero (Table 2; Fig. 5). Day-to-day variation During spring 2015, day-to-day variations of GPP and R were low in Lake 4 and 5 (Fig. 3). Changes were gradual and sudden day-to-day changes were rare and small. Day-to-day variations were more common for R than for GPP. In the different locations in Lake 4, significant day-to-day differences in metabolism (characterized by non-overlapping 95% CI) occurred on 22–25% occasions for R and only 3–12% occasions for GPP. In Lake 5 loc. A, the significant day-to-day variability was 27% for R and 8% for GPP. A–C and Lake 5 loc. A. Slopes for R (y) vs. GPP (x) ranged from 0.88 to 0.93 for most locations with deeper water and high charophyte biomass to only 0.62 for the shallow location with low charophyte cover (Fig. 6, S2). While the slope differed, the 95% CI of the intercepts (R_{base}) were not significantly different from zero in Lake 4 loc. A–C, which implies that background respiration was negligible. Despite being significantly positive, background respiration was very low in Lake 5 loc. A. Analysis of all four lakes during 9–10 days in June 2016 confirmed the close coupling between R and GPP with a common slope of 0.90 and a low intercept (−1.48 g O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹), which was not significantly different from zero (Fig. 6). This finding is in agreement with the analysis for individual lakes. Thus, in these shallow charophyte lakes, respiration is closely coupled to lake production on the same day and background respiration is low or negligible. Discussion Submerged macrophytes and temperature gradients The present analysis confirmed that small, shallow lakes with dense macrophyte vegetation undergo extreme diel temperature cycles (Andersen et al. 2016). Large diel variations in surface water temperatures at about 15 °C are possible due to a shallow mixed surface layer and high light attenuation. The observed high diel temperature range is not uncommon among small lakes (Woolway et al. 2016). Steep vertical stratification also developed during the day as a result of high light absorption in the dense charophyte canopy, while cooling of surface waters during the evening and night induced convective mixing (Andersen et al. 2016). Although it has previously been shown that submerged macrophyte stands can induce large temperature gradients (Dale and Gillespie 1977), the magnitude of temperature gradients demonstrated here for such shallow water columns is much greater than anticipated and unprecedented in previous studies. Because of the high submerged macrophyte biomass, the stratification-mixing cycle is a recurring daily phenomenon. Only modest surface heating is required for daytime stratification to develop as wind induced turbulence is rapidly dissipated by the charophyte canopy (Andersen et al. 2016). Daytime stratification was only absent on very cold, windy or rainy days during spring–summer. Modeling ecosystem metabolism A consequence of diel stratification is that the oxygen signal recorded from surface waters only reflects processes in the mixed surface layer during the day, but the entire water column at night. This should not affect our estimate of GPP because light only penetrates few centimeters into the Fig. 6 Linear relationship of daily rates of R (g O$_2$ m$^{-3}$ day$^{-1}$) versus GPP (g O$_2$ m$^{-3}$ day$^{-1}$) in Lakes 4, 5 (2015) along with the four lakes studied during 2016 (*solid line*, standard major axis regression). Oxygen produced by photosynthesis is released to the mixed surface layer, and production below the thermocline is negligible. Respiration is estimated at night when photosynthesis is zero and the water column is well mixed and thus should encompass all ecosystem components, seeing that the nocturnal convective mixing is quite efficient (Andersen et al. 2016). Overestimation of NEP could occur when respiratory processes in bottom waters do not influence the oxygen signal recorded in surface waters during stratification. In Lake 4 during 2016, water volume below the thermocline constituted only 8–14% of the total volume. Therefore, estimates of lake metabolism by the described procedure include the relevant major components and processes. This conclusion is supported by the close agreement between observed and modeled diel oxygen signals, with generally narrow 95% CI’s. The observed oxygen signal in surface waters was well predicted by using the applied model (Eqs. 2–7). On most days, uncertainty of metabolism estimates was well constrained by the bootstrap analysis. Variation between observed and modeled oxygen signals may arise from processes not included in the model (Eq. 2), such as advective mixing or respiratory substrate limitation (McNair et al. 2013). Modeling the gas transfer velocity as a function of wind may also introduce error due to the fact that near-surface turbulence in small lakes is influenced by convective mixing (Read et al. 2012). Convective mixing is driven by heat loss from surface waters and, with the high diel temperature range observed in the investigated lakes, convective mixing could contribute to near-surface turbulence (Holgerson et al. 2016; MacIntyre et al. 2010). However, the applied empirical model was the best available for use in small lakes within the size range investigated here; it was derived from previous measurements in Lake 4 (Andersen 2015). High rates of ecosystem metabolism The summer metabolic rates reported here are probably close to annual maximum rates because temperature and irradiance were both high. Volumetric metabolic rates estimated in this study are very high compared to values from other aquatic systems (Duarte and Agustí 1998; Solomon et al. 2013). The high volumetric metabolic rates are attributed to the high charophyte biomass, shallow photic zone and high light availability in the upper canopy. Fig. 7 Aquatic ecosystem metabolism showing GPP versus R during summer for a data compilation from different aquatic ecosystems (Hoellein et al. 2013). Filled circles are daily rates of metabolism from measurements on shallow charophyte lakes during May and June in the present study (n = 111). The data ranges in the different ecosystems are enclosed within the covered areas Metabolic rates normalized to area are also high compared to other aquatic ecosystems (Fig. 7), because of the high proportion of incident irradiance absorbed by photosynthetic pigments. Absorption in these clear lakes not owing to photosynthetic pigments is likely to stem from precipitated CaCO₃ as well as associated colored components on the surfaces of charophytes. The high volumetric rates of production result in high demands for dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) in surface waters. The charophyte lakes are located on calcareous rock and have average DIC concentrations of 0.7–2.7 mM mainly available for photosynthesis in the form of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Free CO₂ has been shown to be used five to six times more readily than HCO₃⁻ by the dominant charophyte species (Chara aspera) in the lakes (Van den Berg et al. 2002), which requires active ion-transport (Lucas and Berry 1985). Bicarbonate is present typically in 10- to 100-fold higher concentrations in the charophyte lakes, and is the most important and stable source of inorganic carbon to charophyte photosynthesis (Madsen and Sand-Jensen 1991). The continuously high GPP rates in the charophyte lakes are unlike those of deep lakes with seasonal stratification in which gradual epilimnetic depletion of nutrients and DIC increasingly limits primary production during summer (Brighenti et al. 2015; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). In the charophyte lakes, photosynthesis can be constrained by reduced DIC in the afternoon (Andersen 2015), but the DIC pool is re-established by nocturnal mixing because CaCO₃ is dissolved and organic matter is degraded in the bottom waters during the stratification period. Thus, regeneration of DIC and nutrients, mixing and reinjection of resources into surface waters are daily recurring phenomena, which can sustain high GPP rates. During the summer 2016, volumetric rates of GPP and R in Lake 2 averaged at 74 (range 50–92) and 65 (range 39–90) g O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹, respectively (Table 2). These values correspond to oxygen pool turnover times of only 3.4–3.8 h. Despite a shorter turnover time of the oxygen pool than the duration of the night (5.5–6 h summer 2016), Lake 2 did not turn anoxic, though nocturnal oxygen minima were low. The lack of anoxia was probably due to enhanced gas exchange as surface water oxygen decreased and respiratory substrate limitation as previously demonstrated by large nocturnal decline of ecosystem respiration in free-water measurements in Lake 4, and confirmed by charophyte respiration in bottle incubations (Andersen 2015). Net ecosystem production Positive NEP values imply that ecosystems are net autotrophic and have a production surplus which can be incorporated into additional charophyte biomass, or accumulated in the sediment as organic matter (Staehr et al. 2012). Solomon et al. (2013) found that mean summer NEP values in 25 globally distributed lakes ranged between −7.3 and 9.9 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹ [−7.0 and 1.5 for lakes with total-P < 20 L⁻¹, Hoellein et al. (2013)]. The charophyte lakes studied here have oligotrophic waters and most nutrients are incorporated into charophyte biomass and buried in the sediments (Christensen et al. 2013). From this analysis, it cannot be concluded whether these charophyte lakes are net autotrophic or net heterotrophic on an annual scale, but they are probably close to zero or slightly net autotrophic as shown previously for Lake 4 (Christensen et al. 2013). Only thin sediments have built up in the deeper parts during the lakes’ 30 years of existence, and it shows that storage of organic carbon and dead charophyte fragments within the systems are low. Allochthonous organic carbon would contribute to this storage, but is low due to the sparse terrestrial vegetation and the restricted water input. An earlier study of a charophyte lake on Räpplinge alvar also found that NEP was slightly positive during spring and early summer (0.2–1.4 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹), but negative during desiccation in mid-summer and positive again in August in the time of refilling (Christensen et al. 2013). For the period studied here, the water depth did not reach the critical threshold in the deeper charophyte lakes. NEP ranged between −0.8 and 4.8 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹, but was predominantly positive. However, as a result of desiccation, periods of negative NEP were observed in the shallow Lake 3 and the shallow location Lake 5 loc. B during summer 2015. Measurements show that sediment respiration is low in the charophyte lakes (Andersen 2015). The positive NEP is mainly utilized by the charophytes for growth. Converting previously measured sediment respiration from Lake 4 (Andersen 2015) at 15°C to diel mean temperature, applying a Q_{10} value of 2.0 for the summer 2016, revealed that sediment respiration (R_{sed}) constituted, on average, 12% of total ecosystem respiration during the period in Lake 4 (Fig. 5). Respiration in free water is negligible and the main driver of both GPP and R is the large charophyte biomass (Andersen 2015). Assuming that respiration is only a result of charophytes (R_{Chara}) and sediments (R_{sed}), the net charophyte production (NP_{Chara}) can be estimated as NP_{Chara} = NEP + R_{sed}. For the 2016 summer period, this yields mean NEP values of 1.8 and NP_{Chara} of 2.6 g O_2 m^{-2} day^{-1}. This surplus is at the same level as the possible daily increase of charophyte biomass in g organic dry matter m^{-2}, which is equivalent to a biomass accumulation of about 200–300 g organic dry matter m^{-2} over 4 months in agreement with the measured level of charophyte biomass. Similar levels were reported by Christensen et al. (2013). R-GPP coupling and baseline respiration By applying regression analysis, a close coupling of R and GPP daily estimates was found. This finding was supported by data from Lake 4 and 5 in spring 2015 as well as Lake 1, 2, 3 and 4 in summer 2016. The very low or zero background respiration implies that terrestrial contribution to ecosystem metabolism is low or negligible during the spring–summer periods in the five charophyte lakes. The pool of more recalcitrant organic matter would likely consist of particulate matter from the sparse terrestrial vegetation, but otherwise be dominated by detritus from dead charophytes. Tight R-GPP coupling has previously been shown in nutrient-poor lakes (Richardson et al. 2016; Sadro et al. 2011; Solomon et al. 2013), as well as in Spanish shallow lakes with high metabolic rates (Geertz-Hansen et al. 2011). As a result of the small lake sizes, low horizontal heterogeneity of metabolism estimates was expected. Previous studies in larger lakes have found substantial spatial variation of metabolism within lakes (Lauster et al. 2006; Van de Bogert et al. 2012), which suggests that the mixed surface layer is not necessarily well mixed horizontally, or that the rates of turbulence are low compared to the local differences of metabolism. The shallow location C in Lake 4 is different from location A, B and D by being susceptible to desiccation resulting in a less dense and shorter charophyte canopy. This difference could explain the high GPP relative to R at this location. When self-shading is low in the canopy it will require less respiration in order to sustain the lower biomass. Comparison of ecosystem metabolism across aquatic systems A recent comprehensive study compiled estimates of ecosystem metabolism in different aquatic systems (Hoellein et al. 2013), for which we have added metabolic rates from the present study of shallow vegetated lakes (Fig. 7). The small oligotrophic vegetated lakes studied here do not fit the expectation that GPP should increase along a gradient of total P concentration as observed in larger lakes (Hanson et al. 2008; Solomon et al. 2013). The very low phosphate levels measured in Lake 3 and 4 are likely characteristic for all the investigated lakes located within short distances on the nutrient-poor alvar. The pattern can be explained by the dominance of benthic primary producers in the small lakes in contrast to the dominance of pelagic production by phytoplankton in larger, deeper lakes (Kalff 2002). Daily GPP is positively related to daily incident light utilized by a high density of photosynthetic pigments. The biomass of phytoplankton communities is often nutrient limited and is much higher in eutrophic than oligotrophic lakes (Kalff 2002). Maximum rates of photosynthesis relative to absorbed light are, however, comparable for phytoplankton- and submerged macrophyte communities (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998). As a result, the same high areal rates of GPP can be reached in dense charophyte stands in shallow, oligotrophic lakes as in deeper phytoplankton-rich water columns of eutrophic lakes (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998). Previous studies have shown that small lakes are active sites of carbon processing and atmospheric carbon emission compared to medium-sized and large lakes (Holgerson and Raymond 2016; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Their role in global carbon budgets is open to debate because of the uncertainties associated with the estimation of the number and surface area of small lakes (Downing et al. 2006; Verpoorter et al. 2014). Using the areas for small lakes (<0.01 km^2) and larger lakes (>0.01 km^2) reported by Downing et al. (2006), and the median areal GPP and R reported in this study and the lakes compiled in Hoellein et al. (2013), show that 30 and 21% of the global lake GPP and R may take place in small lakes. The values of GPP in the small, shallow lakes dominated by submerged macrophytes are probably higher than for many small lakes devoid of macrophytes. Nonetheless, the evaluation supports the notion that small aquatic systems are very important components of global carbon processing. Identification of total phosphate, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size thresholds for success of biomanipulation in peri-urban eutrophic ponds Sylvia De Backer · Samuel Teissier · Ludwig Triest Received: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 27 October 2013 / Published online: 8 November 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract In small shallow lakes and ponds, the clear-water state can generally be maintained at higher nutrient concentrations compared to larger shallow lakes. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for total phosphorus (TP), submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size that determine biomanipulation success in peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationship between transparency and TP is discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Using classification trees, a threshold TP concentration of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was determined below which a clear-water state was generally maintained after biomanipulation. When the average TP concentration was >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of the clear-water state largely depended on the presence of sufficiently large zooplankton (>0.87 mm) or a submerged vegetation cover of >82% at some point during the year. This threshold TP concentration is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) which is generally suggested for longer-term success of biomanipulation in shallow lakes. Such threshold nutrient concentration is important when restoring ecological quality in eutrophic small lakes and ponds. Extended follow-up of biomanipulation success in eutrophic ponds could provide more insight into the feasibility of these thresholds on the longer term. Keywords Ponds · Shallow lakes · Eutrophic · Clear-water state · Restoration · Turbid Introduction During the past decades, ecological quality of shallow lakes and ponds has often been degraded as a result of eutrophication due to human activities, causing a transition to a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state, often associated with severe blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (Willame et al., 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Nutrient reduction alone as a method to restore such lakes and ponds is often expensive and inefficient, as recovery is often delayed by internal phosphorus loading or biological resistances (Søndergaard et al., 2005a; Jeppesen et al., 2007). Internal loading was found to be a significant part of total P loading during the productive summer period in eutrophic Danish lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2013). Next to nutrient reduction measures, biomanipulation, through complete or partial fish removal, is often performed to improve ecological quality of shallow lakes (Meijer et al., 1994; Lammens, 1999; Jyväsjärvi et al., 2013). In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012). Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes. When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected. Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus rutilus L.) and tench (Tinca tinca L.) (De Backer et al., 2010). More detailed characteristics of the studied ponds, including an overview of the applied restoration measures for each pond, are given in Table 1. Restoration measures Biomanipulation was performed in 13 ponds during 2005–2009 by water drawdown and complete fish removal (Table 1). This was generally done in winter or early spring to avoid the presence of numerous juvenile fish which could easily escape or survive in the mud for some time. In most ponds, the water level could be lowered manually, due to their artificial nature. During water drawdown, fishermen removed all or as much fish as possible using fishing nets. More than 500 kg of fish per ha was removed in each pond, confirming that all ponds were overstocked with fish before biomanipulation. A few weeks to several months after fish removal, the ponds were slowly refilled through overflow of neighbouring ponds, groundwater seepage or inflow of small rivulets. In a second phase, northern pike (Esox lucius L.) were added in an attempt to stabilize the clear-water state. Addition of piscivores is often performed in an attempt to control planktivorous fish after biomanipulation, allowing large zooplankton to increase grazing pressure on phytoplankton and, as such, further stabilizes the clear-water state (Lammens, 1999; Ha et al., 2013). The individuals that were added in the studied ponds were larger than the 0+ pike that are generally used for this purpose, as the result of 0+ pike additions is often not just temporary (Søndergaard et al., 1997) or the added pike lack piscivory (Skov et al., 2003). In February 2008, only 1+ pikes were added to 10 biomanipulated ponds (Table 1). In February 2010, various densities of 1+, 2+ and 3+ pike (with a size of 20, 30 and 45 cm, respectively) were added into 7 biomanipulated ponds. Sampling and sample processing Samples were taken 1 year before and 1–5 years after biomanipulation during the warm season (May–September) on 3–5 occasions per year. A detailed overview of all sampling occasions is given in Table 2. Except for very small ponds, all samples were taken from a boat. Secchi depth was measured using a 30-cm-diameter disc. In case the Secchi disc was still visible when reaching the pond bottom, Secchi depth was estimated as the actual pond depth plus 1 m in case the disc was still clearly visible or plus 0.1 m in case it was only partially visible. This approach is similar to the method of Cottenie et al. (2001) and was used to obtain a more realistic Secchi depth when the disc was still visible at the pond bottom. Quantitative phytoplankton, Chl \( a \), main nutrient (TP, soluble reactive phosphorus—SRP, and dissolved inorganic nitrogen i.e. \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) and \( \mathrm{NO}_x \) (NO\(_2^-\) and NO\(_3^-\))) and zooplankton samples were collected on each occasion. Mixed water samples based on 10 random subsamples were taken from each pond (including vegetated parts) with a plastic tube sampler of 4.5 cm diameter and 70 cm length that closes in the lower part. An extension was fixed to the sampler to reach the deeper parts of the ponds when appropriate. In case of deeper ponds (depth >1 m), subsamples were taken alternately from shallower and deeper parts of the pond in order to obtain a sample representative of the whole water column. After stirring the collected water, 500 ml was taken for phytoplankton identification and quantification, 1 l for chemical analyses and 1 l for Chl \( a \) determination. Samples for Chl \( a \) analysis were filtered onto Whatman GF/C filters and stored at −18 °C for a maximum of 7 days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark for 8 h. Pigment concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically. Nutrient concentrations were measured according to standard methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). Phytoplankton samples were fixed in the field with alkaline lugol, sodium thiosulphate and buffered formalin (Sherr & Sherr, 1993) and stored in the dark before identification and enumeration to genus level using inverted microscopy. Biovolumes were calculated using the approximations of cell shapes to simple geometrical forms (Wetzel & Likens, 2000). Total phytoplankton biovolume was mainly used as a proxy for turbidity of the water column. Eight phytoplankton groups were differentiated: Cyanobacteria, Bacillariophyta, Euglenophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Dinophyta, Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta. In order to assess the zooplankton community structure, 10 subsamples of 1 l were collected with the same sampler used for phytoplankton and nutrients. Statistical data analyses To identify the factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. ‘failure’ or ‘success’), it is essential to define exactly what ‘failure’ is or what can be considered as ‘success’. In terms of phyto- plankton biovolume and composition, ‘failure’ of biomanipulation is essentially a return to a situation that is comparable to the phytoplankton composition and biomass before biomanipulation. Therefore, a hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on aver- aged per year phytoplankton data (division level). All data were log-transformed to obtain normality if needed. By arranging the data into different clusters, we could study how the situation before biomanipu- lation was related to the situation after biomanipula- tion for each pond, in each year. The cluster analysis was performed using PC-ORD (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Sørensen distance was used as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. One-way clustering was carried out on both samples and phytoplankton groups. For the latter, data were relativised (i.e. each value divided by the maximum value observed per phytoplankton group). This is generally done to avoid separation of more common species into separate groups from rare species (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Based on previous field observations and the nature of the data, we expect a clustering into two main groups, corresponding to clear with low phytoplank- ton biomass and to turbid with high phytoplankton biomass conditions. Based on the position of each data point within the cluster, successfully biomanipulated ponds (situation 1), situated inside a low phytoplank- ton biomass group, could be further subdivided into two categories: before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation. Ponds where biomanipulation failed (situation 2) were defined as ponds where data of at least 1 year after biomanipulation were situated inside a high phytoplankton biomass group within the cluster. Situation 2 could be further subdivided into three categories: before biomanipulation (2b), after biomanipulation but before failure (2a, situated in the low phytoplankton subcluster) and after biomanipulation when it failed (2f, data with high phytoplankton biovolume). Essentially, the cluster analysis based on phytoplankton data was performed to assign each data point to one of the 5 predefined categories (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a or 2f). Differences between these 5 categories were analyzed further using One-way ANOVA. A Tukey HSD test, modified for unequal sample size, was used as a post hoc comparison test to compare mean values between individual groups. The one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to investigate the data for normality and the Brown–Forsythe test was used to check for homogeneity of variance. When one of both assumptions was not met (as was the case for SRP and submerged vegetation cover), a non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to investigate differences between the groups. For all analyses, averaged per year per pond data were used. Three repeated-measures ANOVA were carried out on the considered variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, length of large Cladocera and %SVmax) with time (year) as factor because biomanipulations were not carried out in the same year for every pond. ANOVA was done for the years ‘before biomanipulation’, for the first year following biomanipulation and for all follow-up years after biomanipulation. An additional repeated measure ANOVA was done for the same variables for all ponds in 2010 but using pike addition as a factor in three classes, namely no addition, pikes added in 2008 and pikes added in 2010. Previous research indicated that the impact of total phosphorus concentration (TP), large Cladocera length (LCL) and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) on phytoplankton biovolume in these ponds did not show a linear but a threshold relationship (De Backer, 2011). Therefore, classification trees (Breiman et al., 1984) were used to estimate the thresholds of different environmental factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. phytoplankton biovolume). This type of analysis could allow us to identify threshold values for each predictor (TP, LCL and SV_{max}), below or above which biomanipulation will most likely fail or be successful. All classification tree analyses were performed with Statistica version 8 (Statsoft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA). The goodness of fit of each split was estimated by the Chi square statistic. Only the best fitting option was shown in the resulting graph. The ‘prune on deviance’ option was used as a stopping rule with a minimum of 10% of the total number of cases needed to allow a subsequent split. For all classification tree analyses, averaged per year per pond values of post-biomanipulation data were used. A series of classification trees was performed to explore the relationships between phytoplankton biovolume and the three predictors (all together or each predictor individually). Since submerged vegetation can affect phytoplankton, phytoplankton can also affect submerged vegetation cover, using average submerged vegetation cover (SV_{av}) as a predictor of phytoplankton biovolume seems irrelevant, as the percentage of cover might be negatively influenced by phytoplankton itself. Use of SV_{max} as a predictor variable of phytoplankton biovolume, rather than SV_{av}, allows us to identify the threshold cover of submerged vegetation above which an increased phytoplankton growth is prevented. Finally, the relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}), LCL and TP concentration was studied using Pearson product-moment correlations. Results Classification of biomanipulated ponds Hierarchical cluster analysis of averaged per year phytoplankton biovolume (per division) of biomanipulated ponds constructed two main groups (Fig. 1). In Group A, as indicated by relative abundances and percentiles of each phytoplankton group, phytoplankton biovolume was generally lower when compared to Group B. For all phytoplankton groups (with the exception of Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta that clustered separately from all other groups), the highest phytoplankton biovolume values were found in pond samples of Group B. All pre-biomanipulation samples aggregated into Group B, except for two cases (VKn1 and WtMl). For the remaining five ponds, several (for Leyb-a, Leyb-b and MIKI) or all (for NrPd1 and PRB2) post-biomanipulation samples remained situated in Group B, indicating that phytoplankton composition in these ponds during some years after biomanipulation was more similar to the situation before biomanipulation when compared to other succeeded post-biomanipulation situations. These five ponds were considered as ponds where biomanipulation failed (named ‘situation 2’). Based on this cluster analysis, we split up ‘situation 1’ for the successfully biomanipulated ponds (i.e. ponds of which all post-biomanipulation samples were a part of Group A) into their before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation conditions. For ponds where biomanipulation failed (i.e. ponds of which some or all post-biomanipulation samples were classified under Group B), this ‘situation 2’ was split up into three conditions, namely pond samples before biomanipulation (2b), samples of those ponds that temporarily turned into clear water during at least 1 year (2a) and finally samples of these ponds after failure i.e. in turbid conditions (2f). There was only a marginal effect of time on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) when considering the year before biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 2.32, P = 0.058 \)) due to a higher TP and phytoplankton biovolume in 1 out of 13 ponds (PRB1 in 2008). There was no effect of time when considering all ponds just 1 year following biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.22, P = 0.319 \)) or all years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 0.59, P = 0.910 \)). There was no effect of pike addition on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) in the years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.23, P = 0.348 \)). Features of ponds before and after biomanipulation All the ponds studied were rich in nutrients with a mean TP >0.1 mg, before and after biomanipulation. Nutrient levels were generally higher in situations where biomanipulation failed, as TP concentrations were significantly lower in clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a) when compared to turbid ponds following a failure (2f) (Fig. 2; Table 3). All other TP concentrations were intermediate between those of 1a and 2f. SRP concentrations did not differ significantly between before and after biomanipulation but this is only in cases where biomanipulation was successful (1b and 1a). On the other hand, dissolved nutrients (SRP, NH_4^+ and NO_x) often attained more elevated concentrations after biomanipulation (Fig. 2) and this was significantly higher for SRP in ponds where biomanipulation failed (2f). The five status groups (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a and 2f) showed significant differences in total phytoplankton biovolume, relative cyanobacterial biovolume, Secchi depth, large Cladocera length, %SV_{max} cover and SRP, whereas large Cladocera density was only marginally significant (Table 3, Fig. 2). For NH_4^+ and NO_x concentrations, no significant differences were obtained (Table 3; Fig. 2). The three proxies for phytoplankton biomass (averaged total phytoplankton biovolume, Chl a concentrations and Secchi depth) showed a very similar pattern for the distinguishable situations (Fig. 2; Table 3). Phytoplankton biomass was high in all starting conditions prior to biomanipulation and was comparably high for failed situations of subsequent years (1b, 2b and 2f). Significantly low phytoplankton biomass was measured in situations where biomanipulation was immediately (1a) or temporarily successful (2a). In those situations where biomanipulation temporarily kept a clear-water condition before returning to a turbid state (2a), phytoplankton biovolume also did decrease significantly; however, returned in the following year(s) again to failure (2f) up to a level that was comparable to their origin situation before biomanipulation. Although average relative cyanobacterial biovolume did not differ significantly between most of the situations, it varied considerably in those ponds where biomanipulation failed, namely reaching up to 40% prior to biomanipulation (2b) or when the water shifted to a turbid state again (2f). In temporarily successful conditions (2a), the average relative cyanobacterial biovolume (Fig. 2) could reach up to 20% before turning into failure with higher abundances. In ponds where biomanipulation was successful in maintaining clear-water conditions (1a), the relative cyanobacterial biovolume also was <10% in the period prior to biomanipulation (1b). Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. An almost ‘pure’ split was obtained at 10.8 mm3 L−1 of phytoplankton biovolume, separating all clear-water situations (\( N = 38 \) i.e. ‘1a’: after successful biomanipulation and ‘2a’: before failure) with an average phytoplankton biovolume ≤10.8 mm3 L−1 from all failure situations (2f with \( N = 11 \)) with an average phytoplankton biovolume of >10.8 mm3 L−1 (except Springer Fig. 3 Classification tree for three categories of after biomanipulation situations: 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation; 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation: before and after failure, for one case of 2f with a low phytoplankton biovolume). The obtained threshold of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) of phytoplankton biovolume was then used in further analyses to differentiate between clear-water and turbid situations. The likelihood of obtaining such a clear-water state depends mostly on the development of sufficiently large cladocerans after biomanipulation, irrespective of the nutrient levels present (Peretyatko et al., 2009). On the longer term, nutrients will play a more important role in determining biomanipulation success. Biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below 0.300 mg P L$^{-1}$ resided in a clear-water state with low phytoplankton biomass, relatively independent of large cladoceran size or the extent of submerged vegetation cover (except for one case without submerged vegetation Springer Fig. 5 Relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) when TP \leq 0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (left) or >0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (right) in ponds after biomanipulation. Significant Pearson correlations (\( P < 0.05 \)) are indicated by a line; for the lower two graphs, a dotted line corresponds to all cases with LCL \leq 0.87; a full line corresponds to all cases with LCL >0.87. More details concerning the Pearson correlations are given in Table 4 and where large cladoceran length is <0.83 mm). Above 0.300 mg P L^{-1}, the maintenance of the clear-water state mainly depended on large Cladocera size. As long as sufficiently large cladocerans were present (average length >0.87 mm), phytoplankton biomass remained low, even at high TP concentrations. If, however, in such case, large Cladocera size decreased due to predation by recolonizing fish (De Backer et al., 2012), a shift to the turbid state was unavoidable, except for a few cases in which submerged vegetation cover reached >82% and where a clear-water state was maintained despite the lack of sufficiently large cladocerans. Despite the often high cover of submerged vegetation that was often observed in spring, several ponds still developed a high phytoplankton biomass in summer and, nevertheless, returned to a turbid state. Long-term follow-up of these ponds could clarify if this is only a transitional stage to a permanent turbid state where macrophyte cover will eventually be absent, even in spring. Failure of biomanipulation thus appears to be related mainly to a combination of both elevated nutrient concentrations and the lack of large Cladocera grazing, independently of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. After biomanipulation, all ponds remained in a clear-water state below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP, independent of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. It should, however, be noted that in biomanipulated ponds, in most of the ponds with an average TP concentration <0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\), LCL was >0.87 mm, which could have been the main reason for low phytoplankton biomass below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP. Although the positive effect of large zooplankton grazing and the presence of submerged vegetation is generally well recognized (Van den Berg et al., 1997; Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002), few studies have shown the direct impact of these factors on Chl \(a\)--TP relationships in shallow lakes or ponds. Chl \(a\)--TP relationships were studied in the same 13 biomanipulated ponds, showing that after biomanipulation, for a given TP concentration, the yield of Chl \(a\) was lower in ponds with an extensive submerged vegetation cover and high grazing pressure, compared to the same ponds before biomanipulation (Teissier et al., 2012). This directly shows that other factors than nutrients, such as submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing, can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. An additional difference between the situation before biomanipulation and during the first years after biomanipulation is the presence of large benthivorous fish in the former. Benthivorous fish that resuspend the sediment, thereby increasing suspended solids, nutrients and phytoplankton abundance in the water column, can cause a reduction of transparency and prevent macrophyte recolonization (Roozen et al., 2007). Next to the effect of planktivorous fish removal on zooplankton grazing, removal of benthivorous fish also contributes to an increased sedimentation and an improved transparency after biomanipulation (Meijer et al., 1990). This aspect could also have contributed to the lower Chl \(a\)--TP yield in biomanipulated ponds. As in several ponds, fish recolonized after biomanipulation, large benthivorous fish might eventually be present again in these ponds. We did not observe any significant improvement on large zooplankton density or length in 2010 in any of the ponds in which pike were added. Therefore, it is unlikely that the numbers of pike that survived were sufficient to reduce predation pressure on zooplankton in any pond in 2010. In a similar study on non-biomanipulated ponds (De Backer, 2011), no clear-water state is found when TP is >0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\). Therefore, it also is unlikely that biomanipulated ponds with an average TP concentration above this threshold will remain clear in the future (if biomanipulation did not already fail). Consequently, nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation when average TP concentrations exceed the threshold concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg L\(^{-1}\). It is often suggested that in smaller lakes and ponds, phytoplankton is less influenced by nutrients (Jeppesen et al., 1990) and that factors other than nutrients are more important for phytoplankton control (Søndergaard et al., 2005b; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Our results confirm this, although the threshold levels obtained should be interpreted carefully due to limited number of data and additionally need to be validated with an additional training set using non-biomanipulated ponds. The threshold TP concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg P L\(^{-1}\) below which a clear-water state can be maintained is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1–0.125 mg P L\(^{-1}\) that is often suggested for shallow lakes (Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990). As already mentioned, high submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. Possibly, the strong effect of both factors can be the reason for the lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass on nutrients in ponds, compared to shallow lakes. Similar studies on shallow lakes could demonstrate whether the effect of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship would be as strong as it is in the case of the pond systems studied here. Conclusions For biomanipulation of eutrophic ponds, our results suggest that, although a clear-water state can be obtained even when TP concentrations are >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of this clear-water state is insufficient and largely depends on the presence of sufficiently large-sized zooplankton or of a nearly full cover of submerged vegetation. Once they disappear, generally through predation or disturbance by recolonizing fish, a shift to the turbid state is very likely. As fish recolonization is almost inevitable at some point in these peri-urban ponds (or at least difficult to avoid in the near proximity of recreational fishing areas), we suggest that nutrient reduction measures should be undertaken before biomanipulation, in case the average TP concentration is >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\). After 2–4 years following biomanipulation, all biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below this threshold showed promising results, as they remained in a clear-water state during the whole study period. Longer term studies on biomanipulated ponds are necessary to see how the situation in these ponds will evolve. The threshold concentration of 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP above which biomanipulation is likely to fail is considerably higher than similar thresholds known for shallow lakes. Such lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass in the studied biomanipulated ponds could be caused by the strong effect of large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation cover on phytoplankton biomass in eutrophic ponds. In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012).

Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes.

When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected.

We hypothesize that, taking into account that phytoplankton biomass is less affected by nutrients in small lakes and ponds compared to larger shallow lakes, the threshold nutrient level at which both alternative states can exist is higher for ponds than for

Lake metabolism scales with lake morphometry and catchment conditions Peter A. Staehr · Lars Baastrup-Spohr · Kaj Sand-Jensen · Colin Stedmon Received: 21 January 2011 / Accepted: 2 May 2011 / Published online: 17 May 2011 © Springer Basel AG 2011 Abstract We used a comparative data set for 25 lakes in Denmark sampled during summer to explore the influence of lake morphometry, catchment conditions, light availability and nutrient input on lake metabolism. We found that (1) gross primary production (GPP) and community respiration (R) decline with lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, and increase with algal biomass (Chl), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and total phosphorus (TP); (2) all lakes, especially small with less incident light, and forest lakes with high DOC, have negative net ecosystem production (NEP < 0); (3) daily variability of GPP decreases with lake area and water depth as a consequence of lower input of nutrients and organic matter per unit water volume; (4) the influence of benthic processes on free water metabolic measures declines with increasing lake size; and (5) with increasing lake size, lake metabolism decreases significantly per unit water volume, while depth integrated areal rates remain more constant due to a combination of increased light and nutrient limitation. Overall, these meta-parameters have as many significant but usually weaker relationships to whole-lake and benthic metabolism as have TP, Chl and DOC that are directly linked to photosynthesis and respiration. Combining water depth and Chl to predict GPP, and water depth and DOC to predict R, lead to stronger multiple regression models accounting for 57–63% of the variability of metabolism among the 25 lakes. It is therefore important to consider differences in lake morphometry and catchment conditions when comparing metabolic responses of lakes to human impacts. Keywords Lake metabolism · Lake morphometry · Catchment conditions · Intrinsic drivers · Temporal variability Introduction Research on lake metabolism has shown that gross primary production (GPP), respiration (R) and net ecosystem production (NEP = GPP – R) vary considerably among lakes and over time within lakes (Cole et al. 2000; Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007; Staehr et al. 2010a). Many lakes have a negative NEP and most release CO₂ to the atmosphere. This is due to the considerable supply and substantial degradation of allochthonous organic material from the surrounding landscape (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). While day-to-day differences in metabolism within a lake are primarily driven by changes in light, temperature and vertical mixing (Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007), long-term differences in metabolism between lakes are strongly related to changes in concentrations of total phosphorus (TP), phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, autotrophic lakes (NEP > 0) typically have high TP, high Chl and low DOC concentrations, whereas the most heterotrophic lakes have low TP, low Chl and high DOC (Hanson et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Lake morphometry (surface area and depth), catchment properties (geology, size and land use) and hydrology have a strong influence on lake temperature, physical mixing, nutrient concentrations, DOC, Chl and transparency (Fee et al. 1996; Hanson et al. 2007; Nõges 2009), suggesting that these conditions operate as meta-parameters with an indirect but potentially strong effect on lake metabolism. Implicit scaling of lake productivity to lake size has been considered for decades (Thienemann 1927; Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Fee et al. 1992), and location in forests or open landscapes is also known to affect metabolism (Tranvik 1992; del Giorgio and Peters 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, lake area is statistically positively related to wind exposure, water depth and mixing depth and inversely related to external input of nutrients and DOC per water volume and surface area (e.g., Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Duarte and Kalff 1989; Fee et al. 1996). Drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) is positively related to external input of nutrients, CO\(_2\) and DOC (Gergel et al. 1999). Forest cover is negatively correlated with nutrient input and incoming irradiance for small lakes and positively correlated with DOC input and light attenuation by coloured DOC (Xenopoulos et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). In contrast to the substantial literature on the importance of meta-parameters for lake chemistry and physics, there are few comparative measurements of whole-lake metabolism, for a sufficiently large number of lakes, to evaluate the importance of lake size and catchment conditions on whole-lake metabolism and atmospheric CO\(_2\) exchange. This study investigates the effect of these meta-parameters on GPP, R and NEP, and compares their role with that of traditional direct drivers of metabolism (i.e., Chl, DOC, light and temperature). Our general expectation is that meta-parameters are significant though probably not as strong predictors of GPP, R and NEP as the intrinsic variables directly involved in metabolic processes. If so, more general predictive models can be derived and new understanding of control mechanisms can be obtained. Our first specific prediction is that both volumetric GPP and R should decline with increasing lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, as the concentrations and input of nutrients and DOC decrease (Nõges 2009). Although light availability decreases with increasing depth of the photic zone, light availability, is, however, expected to be similar across lake sizes as lower inputs of light absorbing material and greater mixing depth in larger lakes should cause mean light availability to remain similar among lakes of different sizes. Areal rates of GPP integrated over the entire water column is therefore expected to vary little with lake size, and the influence of lake size for GPP expected to be higher for volume specific rates. Our second specific prediction is that small lakes should have higher DOC input and concentrations and be more net heterotrophic (NEP < 0) than large lakes and that forest lakes should be more net heterotrophic than lakes in open landscapes. Small lakes have a greater contact and possibility of exchange of organic material with the terrestrial landscape along its periphery relative to lake surface area than large lakes. Forest lakes have a direct transfer of litter from the surrounding tree vegetation, receive less light for photosynthesis on the lake surface and have higher DOC concentrations in the water column competing with photosynthetic pigments for available photons causing mean light availability to remain low despite of a shallow mixed depth (Staehr et al. 2010a). Conversely, reduced input of DOC in larger lakes should favour positive NEP as mean light availability for primary production is the same but less allochthonous material is supplied for bacterial oxygen consumption. A final mechanism may restrict benthic photosynthesis relative to respiration in small forest lakes, namely the typical organic-rich sediments of flocculated humic material of low mass density that is physically instable for microalgae and unfavourable for growth of rooted plants (Barko and Smart 1986; Sand-Jensen et al. 2005). Our third specific prediction is that the contribution of benthic processes to whole-lake metabolism declines with increasing water depth. Because light penetration to sediments decreases with water depth, the benthic primary production should be more constrained by water depth than respiration and this should be particularly so in forest lakes with high DOC concentrations and poor light conditions. To the extent that lake depth and lake area are correlated, the role of benthic processes should also decline with increasing lake area, while surrounding forest vegetation may stimulate benthic R but impede GPP and NEP. Our fourth specific prediction is that the day-to-day variability of lake metabolism should decline with increasing lake area and depth. Measurements of whole-lake metabolism were performed over 1 week in each lake for subsequent comparison among all 25 lakes. This duration permits reliable calculations of mean daily metabolism and mean values for other physical, chemical and biological properties (Hanson et al. 2003; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). Moreover, 1 week measurements permit calculation of daily variability of metabolic parameters and their relationship to meta-parameters and within-lake parameters. With increasing lake area and water depth, temporal variations in the magnitude of physical mixing affecting different pelagic populations are likely to decline. Reduced external input of nutrients and DOC per unit water volume with increasing lake size should also reduce the carrying capacity for phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacteria and fish per unit volume and, thereby, dampen population changes and blooms. Materials and methods Study sites We studied lake metabolism in relation to physical, chemical and biological characteristics for about 1 week (6–8 days) in 25 medium to high alkaline lakes during May and June 2007. Systems ranged from ponds (0.1 ha) to midsized (1,729 ha) lakes, and were all located in calcareous moraines in Denmark (Table 1). Lakes were sampled in a random order to avoid bias from changing meteorological conditions during the study. Throughout the study, meteorological conditions were measured from a buoy placed on Lake Slotssø. Daily average wind speed (0.3–5.4 m s\(^{-1}\), min–max) and solar irradiance (5–55 mol photons m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) showed large daily variability, but did not change significantly during the course of the study. Lakes were chosen to cover large ranges in lake size, forest cover, TP, Chl and DOC concentrations. Lake area, catchment area, %forest cover in the catchment and drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) were obtained for each lake using the digital Areal Information System (Nielsen et al. 2000). To evaluate effects of forest cover on local wind and light conditions, we also determined the proportion of forest in the 200 m wide riparian zone around the lakes from aerial photographs. Limnological variables Triplicate water samples were collected once from each lake as a depth integrated sample from the upper mixed layer at the center between 10 and 12 o’clock. Samples were analyzed for chlorophyll a, DOC, nutrients, alkalinity and pH. Samples for Chl and phaeopigments were filtered through Advantec\textregistered{} GC-50 filters, extracted in 96% ethanol for 24 h and measured according to Jespersen and Christoffersen (1987) using a Shimadzu UV-160A spectrophotometer. Absorbance of colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) was measured in a GF/F filtrate (0.7 µm) at 300, 340, 360 and 400 nm in a 5 cm cuvette. DOC concentrations (mg C L\(^{-1}\)) were estimated from the linear relationship to CDOM absorption at 360 nm (m\(^{-1}\)): \( \text{DOC} = 0.454 \text{CDOM}_{360} + 1.9 \) (\( r^2 = 0.80 \)) found in a study of 399 water samples from Danish lakes and streams (C. Stedmon, unpubl. data). Total phosphorus (TP) was determined for unfiltered samples by persulfate digestion according to Eaton et al. (1995) and assayed according to Kragh and Sondergaard (2004). Water for determination of pH, alkalinity and CO\(_2\) was transferred to closed, dark glass bottles to avoid CO\(_2\) exchange with the air and prevent photosynthesis before measurement in the laboratory within 2 h. The pH was measured with Radiometer equipment (accuracy 0.01 pH unit). Acidimetric titration of alkalinity (acid neutralizing capacity, ANC), ionic strength, pH and temperature were used to calculate concentrations of free CO\(_2\) according to Rebsdorf (1972). The calculated CO\(_2\) concentrations have previously been shown to be in close agreement with direct CO\(_2\) measurements on an IRGA using a headspace equilibration technique (Sand-Jensen and Frost-Christensen 1998). Fluorescence of DOC was measured on a Varian Eclipse fluorescence spectrophotometer. An emission spectrum was measured every 2 nm between 300 and 600 nm, whilst exciting at 370 nm. The fluorescence index (FI; McKnight et al. 2001) was derived by taking the ratio of the fluorescence at 450 to that at 500 nm. This index can be used to characterize the chemical composition of DOC and indicate the relative contribution of terrestrial and aquatic organic matter. Index values typically range between 1 and 2, with terrestrial plant material resulting in low values. Depth profiles of oxygen and temperature were recorded in situ by an YSI 600XL multisonde. The vertical light attenuation coefficient (K\(_D\), 400–700 nm) was determined from the depth profile of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) using a LiCor 4π sensor. K\(_D\) was calculated as the slope of a linear regression model of irradiance (E\(_z\)) versus depth (z): \( \ln(E_z) = b + K_D \ z \). Physics and metabolism from sonde measurements We deployed a buoy at the centre of each lake to measure surface PAR, wind speed, water temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration (DO) for about 1 week. Three sets of this equipment were moved between lakes in a random order. Surface PAR was measured 1 m above the surface using a HOBO 2π quantum sensor. Wind speed was measured 1.2 m above the lake using a HOBO anemometer. Surface PAR and wind speed at the centre of each lake were normalized to measurements made throughout the summer in medium-sized Lake Slotssø (22 ha, 15% forest cover; Table 1). Normalization was simply the ratio of the wind speed at a lake to that of Lake Slotssø. This permitted comparison among the 25 lakes despite changes in mean weekly wind velocity and surface PAR during the summer. Water temperature was measured every 10 min during buoy deployment at several water depths, using a string of Stow Away Tidbit loggers. These data permitted calculation of mixing depth (Z\(_\text{mix}\)) at high frequency according to an empirical curve-fitting procedure (Staehr et al. 2010a). Dissolved oxygen was measured at 0.5 m either with an Oxyguard DO sensor or a YSI 600XL multisonde. Oxygen sensors were cleaned and calibrated prior and after each application. Electrode drift was small and was corrected for assuming it is linear over time. Oxygen concentrations recorded every 10 min were used to calculate NEP for 30 min intervals, according to the guidelines presented in Staehr et al.
