Atmospheric exchange was calculated as \( D = k(O_2 - O_{2sat}) \), where \( O_2 \) is actual oxygen concentration, \( O_{2sat} \) is oxygen concentration in water in equilibrium with the atmosphere at ambient temperature, and \( k \) is oxygen exchange calculated for each time step from the estimate of \( k_{600} \) and the ratio of Schmidt numbers as \( k = k_{600} ((Sc/600)^{-0.5}) \) according to Jähne et al. (1987). \( k_{600} \) [k for a Schmidt number (Sc) of 600] was estimated as a function of wind speed at 10 m above the lake surface as: \( k_{600} \) (cm h⁻¹) = 2.07 + 0.215 U¹.⁷ according to Cole and Caraco (1998). Assuming a neutrally stable boundary layer, wind speed (U) at 10 m was calculated from our measurements at 1.2 m using the relationship in Smith (1985). Because there is no photosynthesis at night, we assume nighttime R equals nighttime NEP measured from 1 h past sunset until 1 h before sunrise. Assuming that the daytime rate of R is equal to the nighttime rate (Hanson et al. 2003; Lauster et al. 2006) we calculated daily respiration rates as hourly R during nighttime × 24 h. GPP was determined as the sum of daytime NEP and R, and daily NEP was finally calculated as GPP – R (where R is in positive numbers). For ease of comparison, we present GPP values as positive and R values as negative. Volumetric metabolic rates (mmol O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were turned into areal rates (mol O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹) by multiplying with daily estimates of \( Z_{mix} \) for stratified lakes and mean water depth for fully mixed lakes. Pelagic metabolism from bottle measurements While calculation of whole-lake metabolism from sonde measurements are relatively common, measurements of benthic metabolism are rare because they require special sediment chambers and Scuba diving to set up and many replicates are needed because of great spatial heterogeneity. Because we wanted to make a comparative analysis among many lakes, direct sediment measurements were not an option. Instead, we evaluated the influence of benthic processes on free water measures of metabolism as the difference between measured whole-lake metabolism by oxygen sondes in open waters and simultaneous measurements of pelagic metabolism in bottle incubations. Replicate water samples from 0.5 m depth were used to determine net photosynthesis and respiration as the rate of oxygen change in closed 10 ml bottles during incubation for 13.5–23.4 h at ambient temperature. Bottles were placed on a rotating wheel (12 rpm) in a temperature-constant incubator and illuminated by cool-white fluorescence tubes from one side. Oxygen concentrations in the samples before and after incubation were measured using an oxygen electrode (OX500, Unisense with a picoammeter, PA2000, connected to a laptop computer). The electrode was calibrated at the incubation temperature in water at 100 and 0% air saturation. The irradiance was measured inside the incubation bottles with a minute 4π LiCor underwater light sensor. Samples were exposed to seven different irradiances ranging from 36 to 714 μmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ by using a set of neutral filters in front of the bottles. Samples for dark respiration measurements were wrapped in aluminum foil. From the obtained rates of net oxygen production (NP) at different irradiances (I), NP-I curves were constructed using the nonlinear model of Webb et al. (1974) in SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute Inc., 1994): \[ NP = GP_{max} \times \left[ 1 - \exp \left( \frac{(-\alpha \times E_{mean})}{GP_{max}} \right) \right] + Int \] where \( NP \) is net and \( GP_{max} \) is maximum gross photosynthesis (mg O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹), \( \alpha \) is the initial slope of photosynthesis versus irradiance, \( Int \) is the intersection with the y-axis corresponding to dark respiration and \( E_{mean} \) is the mean available irradiance in the mixed zone. Daily light availability (\( E_{mean} \); mol photons m⁻² day⁻¹) was calculated as an average for the mixed surface zone. Using data for surface irradiance (\( E_0 \); μmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹), mixing depth (m), and light attenuation (\( K_D \); m⁻¹), with a constant of 0.1 for back-scattering and surface reflection, \( \beta \) (Kirk 1994), \( E_{mean} \) was calculated from the equation: \( E_{mean} = E_0 (1 - \beta) (1 - e^{-K_D Z_{mix}})/(K_D Z_{mix}) \), modified from Riley (1957). Each NP-I curve was examined visually and obvious outliers were excluded to obtain reasonable models. NP-I models that did not saturate at high irradiance were also excluded. The calculated models yielded maximal net photosynthesis (\( NP_{max} \)), dark respiration (R), light utilization efficiency (\( \alpha \)), light compensation point (E_C) (the irradiance of which NP = 0) and light saturation point (\( E_K = NP_{max}/\alpha \)) (the irradiance at which photosynthesis starts to saturate). Using the derived NP models and measurements of ambient irradiance, we calculated net primary production in daylight (NPP_bottle; mg O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) by integrating hourly NP rates from sunrise to sunset as: NPP = mean NP × h of daylight. Daily respiration (R_bottle; O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were calculated by multiplying hourly rates by 24. Daily rates of gross primary production (GPP_bottle; mg O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were calculated as the sum of NPP and R_bottle. Daily values of GPP_bottle and R_bottle were calculated for the duration of the buoy deployment and average values were finally calculated for each lake to compare with averages of sonde-based metabolic rates. Statistical analysis Simple relationships between metabolic rates and physical and chemical variables were evaluated using a two-tailed Pearsons correlation analysis. All variables were log transformed to normalize distributions, ensure variance homogeneity and linearize relationships. To avoid negative NEP values in the analyses we added +1,000 to turn all NEP values positive. In our analysis, we applied p < 0.05 as a criteria for significant correlations. Empirical models of the variation in GPP, R and NEP as a function of lake size, forest cover were analysed by stepwise regression analysis. Only parameters which contributed significantly (p < 0.05) were included in the final regression models performed in SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute Inc., 1994). Results Lake characteristics The 25 lakes varied substantially in surface area (0.1–1,729 ha), mean depth (0.5–13.5 m), mixing depth (0.7–10.3 m; 12 out of 25 lakes were stratified) and forest cover in the catchment (1–91%; Table 1). Lake trophy ranged from mesotrophy to hypereutrophy and dystrophy according to the levels of TP (17–249 mg m^{-3}), Chl (4–402 mg m^{-3}), K_D (0.5–5.7 m^{-1}) and DOC (2.6–45.6 mg L^{-1}; Table 1). Lakes were medium to high alkaline (ANC; 2.3 ± 0.1 mq L^{-1} mean ± SE) and usually supersaturated (22 lakes) with CO_2 (Table 1). With increasing lake surface area, lakes became deeper, had deeper mixing depth (Table 2), were more wind exposed and received more incident light (Fig. 1; Table 2). Forest cover was not related to lake surface area and mean water depth (Table 2), but wind exposure and surface irradiance declined significantly with forest cover (Fig. 1b, d; Table 2). With increasing surface area, deeper water and lower drainage ratio, lakes contained less phosphorus, were more transparent and had significantly less phytoplankton (Chl), while none of these variables were significantly correlated to forest cover (Fig. 2; Table 2). Lake metabolism Volumetric rates of GPP and R declined more than fivefold with increasing lake area, while correlations with forest cover were not significant (Fig. 4a–d; Table 2). NEP was negative in 14 lakes, positive in only two lakes and close to zero in the remaining 8 lakes (Fig. 4e, f). For one lake, sonde data were lost, and metabolic rates not calculated. NEP correlated with CO₂ saturation (r = −0.48, p = 0.02), and NEP became significantly more negative as lake area declined and forest cover and DOC increased (Table 2). Consequently, the most negative NEP rates were observed in DOC and CO₂ rich lakes smaller than 1 ha located in catchments dominated (>60%) by forest. Volumetric rates of GPP and R were significantly correlated with each other (r = 0.91, p = 0.006) and positively correlated with TP, Chl and DOC (Table 2). R increased significantly more than GPP with higher DOC concentrations, causing NEP to become significantly more negative and CO₂ super saturation to increase (Table 2). Correlations of GPP, R and NEP with lake surface area, water depth, drainage ratio and forest cover (only NEP) were often not as strong as correlations with intrinsic variables (e.g., TP, Chl and DOC) closely coupled to metabolic processes (Table 2). Day-to-day variability of GPP, R and NEP, can be described by the standard deviation (SD) of metabolism over the period of measurement and by the coefficient of variation being the standard deviation normalized to the mean (CV = SD/X_{mean}). Both in absolute (SD; r = -0.46, p = 0.02) and relative terms (CV; r = -0.44, p = 0.03; Fig. 5), the daily variability of GPP declined with lake area as we had anticipated and it was highest in small lakes receiving high inputs of exogenous nutrients and DOC. The influence of benthic processes on rates of whole-lake metabolism was evaluated by subtracting measured pelagic rates (bottle incubations) from sonde based rates using the diel open water technique. According to the sonde-bottle estimates of GPP and R, the influence of benthic processes declined significantly with increasing lake area, water depth and drainage ratio (only R, but almost GPP), but showed no significant relationship to forest cover (Fig. 6a, b; Table 2). Since sonde estimates of whole-lake NEP were generally more negative than bottle estimates of pelagic NEP, the NEP_{sonde-bottle} estimates were mostly negative (Fig. 6c; 19 lakes in total). This result suggests that benthic processes become less important for the net metabolic balance as lake area and water depth increased (Fig. 6; Table 2). The relative importance of lake meta-parameters and intrinsic biological and physical drivers for weekly averages of volumetric rates of GPP, R, and NEP was evaluated by multiple regression analysis. Among meta-parameters, mean lake depth was the best predictor of GPP and R, and both decreased with increasing water depth. A combination of lake area and %forest cover was the best predictor of NEP (Table 3A). Light and temperature did not contribute significantly to explain between lake variability in GPP, R or NEP, suggesting that differences in these drivers were small and unimportant across the studied lakes during the study period (Table 3B). Algal biomass (Chl) was, as expected, the best predictor of GPP, while high rates of respiration and strong net heterotrophy (NEP < 0) were both related to high DOC (Table 3B). Evaluating the combined effect of meta-parameters and biological and physical conditions on weekly rates of whole lake metabolism, showed that GPP increased with higher algal biomass and lower water depth (Table 3C). Similarly, respiration increased with DOC and decreased with water depth. Variations in NEP were best explained by DOC, with no significant contributions from either lake size or forest cover. Thus, except for NEP, combining meta-parameters with internal biological drivers raised the overall explanatory power (r²) of variations in lake metabolism by 14–15% to 57–63% (Table 3C). Discussion Overall, this study revealed strong broad-scale scaling patterns of lake metabolism and limnological properties to lake meta-parameters. With increasing lake area and depth, lakes received more light, were less wind exposed, had clearer water, deeper mixing depth and contained less nutrients and DOC, causing lakes to be less net heterotrophic and with less importance of benthic metabolism and less day-to-day variability in GPP. Also, with increasing forest cover lakes become shaded and less wind exposed, more humic and CO₂ rich, and more net heterotrophic. Meta-parameters were found to have as many significant, but usually weaker relationships, to whole-lake and benthic metabolism as the intrinsic drivers (TP, Chl and DOC) that are directly linked to photosynthesis and respiration. Combining water depth and Chl to predict GPP, and water depth and DOC to predict R, lead to stronger models of the variability of metabolism among the studied 25 lakes, stressing the importance of physical boundary conditions for lake performance. Influence of lake size and forest cover on limnological properties Physico-chemical features in 25 medium to high alkaline Danish lakes varied significantly with lake size and differences in forest cover of the catchments (Table 1). Only parameters that fulfilled the required significance of p < 0.05 are shown, n = 25 forest surrounding the lakes (Fee et al. 1996; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Also, small surface areas were, as expected, statistically linked to shallow water and shallow mixing depth (Strasbaska 1980; Duarte and Kalff 1989; Fee et al. 1996). Our findings that small lakes are generally richer in nutrients, algal biomass, dissolved organic matter and CO$_2$ than large lakes located in the same surroundings, likewise agree well with previous broad-scale comparisons (Søndergaard et al. 2005; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007; Hanson et al. 2007; Nøges 2009). Loading of DOC to lakes has previously been associated with the amount of wetlands in the watershed (Gergel et al. 1999), in particular wetlands with coniferous vegetation (Xenopoulos et al. 2003). The catchments of our study lakes had a small share of wetlands (0–7%), and DOC concentration was better related to the proportion of forest in the catchments, suggesting that regional models have limited applicability in predicting DOC in other geographical areas of the world (Xenopoulos et al. 2003). The strong influence of lake area and forest cover on lake DOC (Fig. 3a, b) supports two explanations. Firstly, hydrological input of DOC and nutrients across the terrestrial-aquatic boundary increases when the drainage ratio (catchment area to lake surface area) is high. Secondly, small lakes possess a long shoreline for input of air-born terrestrial organic matter relative to lake surface area and volume and receive significant amounts of organic matter from litter fall (Gasith and Hasler 1976). The implications of higher DOC for physical and biological processes were firstly, shallower surface mixed layers and reduced light penetration (Snucins and Gunn 2000; Houser 2006) secondly, reduced planktonic production and increased planktonic respiration (Del Giorgio and Peters 1994), and finally, increased ecosystem respiration through mineralization of allochthonous organic carbon (Hanson et al. 2003; Staehr et al. 2010a). The fluorescence index (FI) as derived by McKnight et al. (2001) suggested that not only does the amount of DOC vary notably across the studied lakes, but the quality (or origin) of the DOC varies as well (Fig. 3e, f). In agreement with expectations, we found that small lakes tend to contain more terrestrial material, whereas autochthonous production was a more important DOC source in larger lakes. The low FI in algal rich small lakes (Table 2) show that the terrestrial input of DOC is much higher than the input of DOC from degrading or leaking phytoplankton. Although large lakes do receive allochthonous DOC, its signal is overwhelmed by the production of autochthonous DOC and the greater exposure to photochemical and microbial degradation as a result of longer residence times (Lindell et al. 2000). Regulation of ecosystem metabolism by meta-parameters Previous investigations on the influence of lake morphometry and catchment conditions on pelagic productivity of lakes has provided deviating conclusions. A global comparison of 55 shallow to deep lakes (1–730 m) showed that volumetric estimates of primary production decreased with increasing lake size, but was more strongly influenced by light and nutrient availability (Brylinsky and Mann 1973). In agreement with our findings (Fig. 2), studies in small to large lakes (1–3 × 10^6 ha) by Duarte and Kalff (1989) found declining trophy and phytoplankton biomass with increasing area and mean depth. Work by Fee and co-workers on seven mid-sized to very large pristine lakes (30–10^7 ha), however, showed that lake size was a poor predictor of lake trophy and phytoplankton photosynthesis (Fee et al. 1992, 1996; Guildford et al. 1994). This response was explained by a greater turbulence and probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer in very large lakes and greater upward nutrient flux (N and Si, but not P) across the thermocline. Also, in more recent studies of small lakes (0.02–20 ha), nutrients, algal biomass and CO_2 super saturation decreased with lake size, but no apparent scaling was found for pelagic metabolism (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, previous studies on the importance of lake morphometry for primary productivity generally support our findings in small to mid-sized lakes (0.1–1,700 ha). However, relationships were weaker or inconsistent for the full range of lake sizes and relationships also depended on methodology. Earlier conclusions on lake metabolism were all based on bottle incubations, which only provide estimates of pelagic productivity. We used open water diel changes in DO to estimate whole-lake metabolism, which offer more reliable results and integrate pelagic and benthic processes under conditions of full vertical mixing (see more in Staehr et al. 2010b). Forest lakes received less light and were expected to receive less easily accessible dissolved nutrients for phytoplankton production compared to lakes in fertilized agricultural landscapes (Larsen et al. 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2009). We therefore expected high forest cover to be associated with lower nutrient status, phytoplankton biomass and GPP in the lakes (Jackson and Hecky 1980). Nutrient levels were, however, similar for our open and forested lakes, and little differences in GPP were found between lakes of the same size but different forest cover. High inputs of organic material in forest lakes, on the other hand, stimulate growth and metabolism of bacteria and zooplankton and enhance community respiration and constrain phytoplankton production due to greater background shading from colored DOC (Christensen et al. 1996; Jonsson et al. 2001; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Brown-colored small lakes in forest catchments were therefore significantly more net heterotrophic, in agreement with previous studies (Del Giorgio et al. 1999; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). The high perimeter to area ratio for small lakes, coupled with high DOC flux and retention (Curtis and Schindler 1997) elevated carbon mineralization and net efflux of CO_2 to the atmosphere. Influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism With increasing lake area, water depth tends to increase and the relative influence of benthic primary production can be expected to decrease as light becomes more limiting (Kemp et al. 1992). Although the importance of benthic primary producers is expected to be higher in shallow systems, poor light conditions associated with eutrophication may switch the dominance from benthic to pelagic processes (Vadeboncoeur et al. 2003). Our lakes were all placed in medium to high alkaline, nutrient-rich catchments, with relatively poor light conditions for benthic plant growth even in shallow lakes (See Table 1). Except for a few shallow lakes, most of our lakes had little submerged vegetation, and the benthic zone was accordingly dominated by carbon-rich and oxygen demanding sediments (author, pers obs), suggesting dominance of heterotrophic processes in the benthic environment. In support of this, we generally found higher sonde based (~ whole-lake) than bottle based (~ pelagic) respiration rates, especially so in small and shallow lakes (Table 2; Fig. 6b). Also the difference between sonde and bottle based NEP declined with increasing lake depth (Table 2) and area (Fig. 6c), indicating the influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism to decrease with increasing lake size. As shown in Coloso et al. (2011), diel changes in mixing depth and microstratification occurred in all of the lakes that were deep enough to stratify (12 out of 25). For these lakes, metabolic rates based on sonde measurements at shallow depth do not represent whole-lake estimates but rather the upper mixed layer (Coloso et al. 2008). The influence of benthic processes is therefore likely underestimated for our stratified lakes by a degree which depends on the volume of water below the mixed layer depth and the proportion of the lake bottom not being exposed to the upper mixed layer (Staehr et al. 2011), which in turn depends on lake morphometry and variability in mixing depth (Coloso et al. 2011). Applying hypsographic tables for the stratified lakes, we find that 40–90% (mean 57%) of the lake volume and 20–70% (mean 53%) of the lake bottom is represented within the upper mixed layers of our stratified lakes. This suggests that a variable but likely substantial benthic signal is in fact included in our sonde-based estimates of metabolism in these lakes. Removing data from stratified lakes in our analysis (open circles in Fig. 6) would furthermore only weaken and not change relationships between the influence of benthic processes on lake metabolism and lake size. Areal versus volumetric rates In agreement with expectations, the implicit scaling was much weaker for areal than volumetric rates, and only GPP was significantly related to lake area (Table 2). Weak or absent relations to areal rates may derive from the confounding effect of co-variation of lake surface area and water depth. However, light utilization for photosynthesis per unit area is also known to be relatively similar among different plant communities and among systems of different depth (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998), and shallow lakes can accordingly be viewed as a compressed version of deeper lakes (Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998) with little differences in areal rates of productivity. Comparison of lake productivity amongst contrasting lakes can also be obtained by normalizing GPP to phytoplankton biomass, which serves as an index of the growth potential of algae (Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). For the lakes in this study, chlorophyll specific GPP decreased significantly with increasing TP concentration (r = −0.42, p < 0.05), while it increased with increasing mean light availability (r = 0.47, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that the efficiency of nutrient use of the autotrophic community increases with the degree of nutrient limitation, and that light availability is more important than nutrient availability for variation of primary production. Considering that the mean available irradiance (a function of surface irradiance, light attenuation and mixing depth) was unrelated to lake area and depth (Table 2), it is not surprising that areal rates of GPP, R and NEP show weak dependencies of lake morphometry. Drivers of daily variability in metabolism According to general scaling theory, the chemical and biological components of small aquatic systems are more variable as they are more sensitive to initial conditions, have limited external exchange of material and organisms with surroundings, and low buffering capacity (Kemp et al. 2001). Studies of scaling rules in aquatic ecosystems have furthermore shown that food chain length decreases with reduced lake volume (Post et al. 2000) and these smaller lakes are less species rich, have less interspecies competition, and higher chance of rise and fall of populations. In this study, daily variability of GPP declined with lake area and was highest in small nutrient rich and productive lakes. High productivity in nutrient-rich lakes is known to be associated with high day-to-day variability in GPP, R and NEP, and this is suggested to reflect the dynamic behavior of the lake ecosystem in response to changes in incident irradiance and available irradiance in the mixed surface layers (Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). High day-to-day variability in GPP in small lakes may also be impacted by changes of physical processes such as advection and inflow, and a greater influence from littoral metabolism (Vadeboncoeur et al. 2001). High variability of GPP also occurred in the small DOC rich lakes, which is somewhat counter intuitive. High input of DOC may restrict photosynthesis through greater competition for available light (Staehr et al. 2010a) and greater competition for nutrients among autotrophs and heterotrophs (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998) tend to reduce the temporal variability of metabolism. This stabilizing effect of DOC in forested lakes may also be due to the fact that DOC is a relatively time-stable energy source to bacteria and zooplankton (Cole et al. 2002). Thus, our results suggest that the stabilizing effect of DOC on GPP to be less influential than the destabilizing effects of high levels of nutrient, short food-chain length and stronger physical disturbance found in smaller sized lakes. Our findings support the use of metabolic responses in lakes as a common metric that integrates terrestrial impacts on lake ecosystems (Williamson et al. 2008). The strong influence of lake morphometry and catchment conditions suggest that broad-scale comparisons among lakes and evaluation of their responses to human impacts (e.g., eutrophication, deforestation and climate change) need to take into account the strong implicit scaling with the physical boundary conditions. These operate directly through differences in shading, sheltering, physical mixing and indirectly through input of nutrients and organic matter. Regulation of ecosystem metabolism by meta-parameters

Previous investigations on the influence of lake morphometry and catchment conditions on pelagic productivity of lakes has provided deviating conclusions. A global comparison of 55 shallow to deep lakes (1–730 m) showed that volumetric estimates of primary production decreased with increasing lake size, but was more strongly influenced by light and nutrient availability (Brylinsky and Mann 1973). In agreement with our findings (Fig. 2), studies in small to large lakes (1–3 × 10^6 ha) by Duarte and Kalff (1989) found declining trophy and phytoplankton biomass with increasing area and mean depth. Work by Fee and co-workers on seven mid-sized to very large pristine lakes (30–10^7 ha), however, showed that lake size was a poor predictor of lake trophy and phytoplankton photosynthesis (Fee et al. 1992, 1996; Guildford et al. 1994). This response was explained by a greater turbulence and probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer in very large lakes and greater upward nutrient flux (N and Si, but not P) across the thermocline. Also, in more recent studies of small lakes (0.02–20 ha), nutrients, algal biomass and CO_2 super saturation decreased with lake size, but no apparent scaling was found for pelagic metabolism (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, previous studies on the importance of lake morphometry for primary productivity generally support our findings in small to mid-sized lakes (0.1–1,700 ha). However, relationships were weaker or inconsistent for the full range of lake sizes and relationships also depended on methodology. Earlier conclusions on lake metabolism were all based on bottle incubations, which only provide estimates of pelagic productivity. We used open water diel changes in DO to estimate whole-lake metabolism, which offer more reliable results and integrate pelagic and benthic processes under conditions of full vertical mixing (see more in Staehr et al. 2010b).

Forest lakes received less light and were expected to receive less easily accessible dissolved nutrients for phytoplankton production compared to lakes in fertilized agricultural landscapes (Larsen et al. 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2009). We therefore expected high forest cover to be associated with lower nutrient status, phytoplankton biomass and GPP in the lakes (Jackson and Hecky 1980). Nutrient levels were, however, similar for our open and forested lakes, and little differences in GPP were found between lakes of the same size but different forest cover. High inputs of organic material in forest lakes, on the other hand, stimulate growth and metabolism of bacteria and zooplankton and enhance community respiration and constrain phytoplankton production due to greater background shading from colored DOC (Christensen et al. 1996; Jonsson et al. 2001; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Brown-colored small lakes in forest catchments were therefore significantly more net heterotrophic, in agreement with previous studies (Del Giorgio et al. 1999; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). The high perimeter to area ratio for small lakes, coupled with high DOC flux and retention (Curtis and Schindler 1997) elevated carbon mineralization and net efflux of CO_2 to the atmosphere.

Influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism

With increasing lake area, water depth tends to increase and the relative influence of benthic primary production can be expected to decrease as light becomes more limiting (Kemp et al. 1992). Although the importance of benthic primary producers is expected to be higher in shallow systems, poor light conditions associated with eutrophication may switch the dominance from benthic to pelagic processes (Vadeboncoeur et al. 2003). Our lakes were all placed in medium to high alkaline, nutrient-rich catchments, with relatively poor light conditions for benthic plant growth even in shallow lakes (See Table 1). Except for a few shallow lakes, most of our lakes had little submerged vegetation, and the benthic zone was accordingly dominated by carbon-rich and oxygen demanding sediments (author, pers obs), suggesting dominance of heterotrophic processes in the benthic environment. In support of this, we generally found higher sonde based (~ whole-lake) than bottle based (~ pelagic) respiration rates, especially so in small and shallow lakes (Table 2; Fig. 6b). Also the difference between sonde and bottle based NEP declined with increasing lake depth (Table 2) and area (Fig. 6c), indicating the influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism to decrease with increasing lake size.

As shown in Coloso et al. (2011), diel changes in mixing depth and microstratification occurred in all of the lakes that were deep enough to stratify (12 out of 25). For these lakes, metabolic rates based on sonde measurements at shallow depth do not represent whole-lake estimates but rather the upper mixed layer (Coloso et al. 2008). The influence of benthic processes is therefore likely underestimated for our stratified lakes by a degree which depends on the volume of water below the mixed layer depth and the proportion of the lake bottom not being exposed to the upper mixed layer (Staehr et al. 2011), which in turn depends on lake morphometry and variability in mixing depth (Coloso et al. 2011). Large fractionations of C and H isotopes related to methane oxidation in Arctic lakes Sarah B. Cadieux a,*, Jeffrey R. White b, Peter E. Sauer a, Yongbo Peng a,1, Amy E. Goldman a,b,2, Lisa M. Pratt a a Department of Geological Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA b School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA Received 14 November 2015; accepted in revised form 3 May 2016; available online 9 May 2016 Abstract Microbial oxidation of methane (CH4) plays a central role in carbon cycling in Arctic lakes, reducing potential CH4 emissions associated with warming. Isotopic signatures of CH4 (δ13C and δ2H) are indicators of microbial oxidation, wherein the process strongly enriches 13C and 2H in residual CH4. We present δ13C and δ2H measurements obtained from sampling the water column and sediment for dissolved CH4 from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland under both open-water and ice-covered conditions from 2013 to 2014. Despite substantial variations in aquatic chemistry among the lakes, δ13C and δ2H of CH4 suggested that CH4 was produced predominantly by acetoclastic methanogenesis in the littoral sediments and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. Surprisingly large variations for both δ13C and δ2H of CH4 were observed, with δ13C extending from −72‰ to +7.4‰ and δ2H from −390‰ to +250‰. The CH4 isotopic values reported here were significantly more enriched (p < 0.0001) in both 13C and 2H than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments. As is characteristic of methanotrophy, the enrichment in 13C and 2H was associated with low CH4 concentrations. We suggest that the CH4 most enriched in 13C and 2H may reflect unusually efficient methanotrophic communities in Arctic ice-margin lakes. This study provides the first measurement of δ2H for CH4 in an Arctic freshwater environment at concentrations <10 μM. The extreme enrichment of 13C and 2H of CH4 from Arctic methanotrophy has significant implications for interpreting sources and sinks of CH4. Without knowledge of local geology, stable isotope values of CH4 higher than −30‰ for δ13C and −150‰ for δ2H could be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic origins. Given crystalline bedrock and the strong positive correlation between δ13C and δ2H throughout the water columns in three Arctic lakes confirms that CH4 heavily enriched in 13C and 2H is the result of methanotrophy. Keywords: Methane; Hydrogen isotopes; Carbon isotopes; Arctic; Lakes 1. INTRODUCTION Small lakes (<10 km^2) represent approximately half of the total area of surface water in Arctic environments (Abnizova et al., 2012) and emit more methane (CH4) per unit area than larger lakes (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009; Downing, 2010). Microbial oxidation of CH4 is an important process in freshwater ecosystems, reincorporating CH4 back into the biogeochemical carbon cycle rather than being released as CH4 into the atmosphere. In northern lakes, up to 88% of the CH4 produced by microbes is oxidized by methanotrophs (Kankaala et al., 2006, 2007; Bastviken et al., 2008; López Bellido et al., 2009), leaving low concentrations of CH4 in surface water of lakes. Due to the challenge of reliably measuring stable isotope abundances at very low concentrations, the effect of methanotrophic oxidation on isotopes of CH4 in Arctic lakes has not previously been reported. The combination of concentration and isotopic signature is vital for understanding biogeochemical cycling of CH4 on Earth and for assessing pathways for production and oxidation of CH4 on Mars where episodic plumes of CH4 at low concentrations have been detected remotely and measured by instruments on martian rovers. In anticipation of returning samples from Mars to Earth and with increasing interest in astronauts as explorers on Mars, it is urgent to assess geochemical and/or biological processes influencing rates of CH4 formation and destruction (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Kinetic isotope effects associated with enzymatic processes during methanogenesis and methanotrophy are well established terrestrial biomarkers and are potential martian biomarkers for subsurface life. Measuring CH4 concentrations and CH4 fluxes are useful to assess the magnitude of emissions, but alone are unable to be used to decipher active production and pathways. Stable isotopic analysis of carbon (δ13C) and hydrogen (δ2H) is a well-established method to delineate the origin of CH4 gas, allowing for the differentiation of CH4 produced by microbial and thermal processes as well as microbial production and oxidation (Schoell, 1980; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Despite a wide range of literature using 13C and 2H to interpret origin and thermal maturity of hydrocarbons in petroleum systems (Stahl and Carey, 1975; Schoell, 1980, 1988; Whiticar, 1989; Jackson et al., 2014), there has been limited work on δ13C and δ2H of CH4 in natural environments, most of which has been focused on wetlands (Martens et al., 1992; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Sugimoto and Fujita, 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). Biogenic CH4 in freshwater environments is produced predominantly within anoxic sediments and is exported into the water column by ebullition (bubbling) or diffusion (Strayer and Tiedje, 1978; Bastviken et al., 2008). Microbial CH4 is produced by methanogens, strictly anaerobic Archaea, who are responsible for 10–50% of overall carbon mineralization in freshwater lakes (Bastviken et al., 2008). In freshwater environments, there are two primary metabolic pathways for CH4 production, acetoclastic methanogenesis (AM) and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM), which have been demonstrated to vary spatially in permafrost-influenced ecosystems (Prater et al., 2007). Both AM and HM are associated with a kinetic isotope effect resulting in depletion of 13C in the product CH4 relative to the pre-cursor substrate (Whiticar et al., 1986; Balabane et al., 1987; Valentine et al., 2004a,b). However, the magnitude of the carbon isotope effect is different for the two primary methanogenic pathways, with AM resulting in δ13CCH4 ranging from −60‰ to −40‰, and HM ranging from −110‰ to −60‰ (Whiticar et al., 1986). Hydrogen isotopes of CH4 similarly become depleted in 2H during microbial CH4 production. The δ2H value of CH4 depends on the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is either from cleavage of H2O or acetate (Woltemate et al., 1984; Whiticar, 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Although this remains contentious, it is generally assumed that during HM, all 4 H atoms are supplied by formation water, whereas during AM, the transfer of the methyl group to CH4 supplies 3 H atoms, and the additional H atom is derived from formation water (Whiticar et al., 1986). As a result, the magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect of hydrogen is different for the two pathways, dependent on value of precursor δ2H, with AM resulting in δ2HCH4 ranging from −530‰ to −250‰, and HM ranging from −250‰ to −170‰ (Sugimoto and Wada, 1995). The isotope systematics of hydrogen for homoacetogenesis in competition with methanogenesis under substrate-limiting conditions and low temperatures of natural systems is not well known (Kotsyurbenko et al., 2001), although culture studies suggest that there is rapid hydrogen isotope exchange between H2 and H2O during homoacetogenesis (Valentine et al., 2004a,b). Methane oxidation (MOx) depends on both the availability of CH4 and dissolved oxygen (DO); high CH4 oxidation rates are usually found at the oxic/anoxic interface where both CH4 and DO are abundant (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) can also occur by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors in lieu of dissolved oxygen (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). High affinity methanotrophs are able to oxidize CH4 at or below atmospheric concentrations (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Isotope fractionation associated with microbial CH4 oxidation leads to systematic enrichment in both 13C and 2H of CH4 in the residual un-oxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). The enrichment in both 13C and 2H during oxidation results in values being increased by <1–30‰ for δ13CCH4 and 3–200‰ for δ2HCH4 (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Bastviken et al., 2002). In this study, we report values of δ13C and δ2H for CH4 collected from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland to assess seasonal sources and sinks of CH4. Lakes were sampled during open-water conditions in July 2013 and under ice-cover in April 2014 when the lakes had been ice-covered and isolated from the atmosphere for 7–8 months. The studied lakes show considerable variation in concentration and proportions of major ions despite being located along a 6 km segment of a narrow valley. Therefore, we hypothesize that due to chemical heterogeneity, sources and sinks of CH4 in each lake would vary lake-to-lake as well as seasonally. Hundreds of thousands of Holocene lakes dot the landscape in southwestern Greenland (Anderson et al., 2001; Anderson and Stedmon, 2007) and are underlain by continuous permafrost (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Deglaciation began in the region ~11,000 BP (Van Tatenhove and van der Meer, 1996; Leng et al., 2012), exposing Precambrian metamorphic crystalline bedrock, primarily felsic gneisses (Jensen et al., 2002). As a result, CH4 in these lakes has had little to no influence from buried ancient organic matter, allowing biogenic CH4 cycles to be studied in isolation. To our knowledge, this work provides the first coupled measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 under both open-water and ice-covered conditions in a relatively undisturbed, periglacial, lacustrine setting thereby filling critical knowledge gaps concerning biogeochemical cycles of CH4 within small Arctic lakes and isotope fractionation of CH4 in low concentration environments. 2. STUDY AREA Lakes in this study are located between the village of Kangerlussuaq, Greenland at the head of Søndre Strømfjord and the active terminus of the Russell Glacier (Fig. 1). During the last Glacial Maximum, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) covered the area. Retreat of the GIS likely resulted in formation of the lakes in glacially scoured hollows (Leng et al., 2012). Currently, the margin of the GIS is ~2 km away from the study lakes. The region has continuous permafrost <50 cm below the surface, extending down to 130 m at Kangerlussuaq and 500 m at the edge of the ice sheet (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Bedrock is predominantly garnet-grade, Archean gneisses with Quaternary glacial, fluvial and alluvial deposits present in low-lying areas. Mean annual air temperature at the Kangerlussuaq weather station from 1974 to 2012 was −6 °C. During warm months of late May to early September, mean temperatures often exceed +11 °C and peak to +20 °C in July. The cold season extends from November to late March, with mean daily temperature averaging −21 °C in February. Precipitation in the Kangerlussuaq area is minimal, with annual precipitation <150 mm yr−1, mostly from June to August (Ohmura and Reeh, 1991). Dwarf shrubs (Salix, Vaccinium and Betula), Sphagnum spp., and graminoids (Carex and Calamagrostis) dominate the tundra vegetation in the region. 2.1. Study lakes In this paper three, small adjacent lakes (surface area <3 ha, maximum depth <8 m) with a range of different morphometries and aquatic chemistries (Fig. 1; Table 1) are studied. Lake names used herein are informal names. The study lakes are part of a series of lakes within a narrow valley overlying a structural shear zone extending from the Russell Glacier to the Søndre Strømfjord (Fig. 1). The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 μS cm⁻¹. In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 μS cm⁻¹) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (Zmax), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L⁻¹), pH, and specific conductivity (μS cm⁻¹) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column CH₄ collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved CH₄ in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and CH₄ was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved CH₄ in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved CH₄ in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment CH₄ Profundal sediment samples were taken from Zmax of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Sediment was collected in polycarbonate plastic barrels with an internal diameter of 6.7 cm. Dissolved gas in the sediment was sampled using an equilibrium gas stripping method similar to the water-column CH₄ (Section 3.1.2.1). Sediment cores were subsectioned into 6–10 cm intervals and put into 8 L Nalgene bottles, with lids altered to include two syringe ports connected to Luer-Lock fittings. Once the sediment was put into the bottle and the lid was shut, the bottle was evacuated using a hand pump connected to a lid port. After evacuation, zero-CH₄ water was injected to create a 4 L sediment–water slurry. The bottle was vigorously shaken for 5 min to displace gas from the sediment-slurry into the headspace. 3.1.4. Littoral sediment CH₄ Littoral sediment gas samples were collected during open-water conditions by physically disturbing the sediment in order to release entrained gas bubbles. Each sample was collected from a vegetated region where water depth was <0.5 m. Gas bubbles were collected using an inverted plastic funnel (28 cm diameter) with a gas-tight sampling tube and 3-way Luer-Lock valve attached to the neck. Gas in the funnel was transferred to a Cali-5-Bond bag using a plastic syringe. Note that we were unable to quantify the volume of sediment sampled. Consequently, concentrations of CH₄ in gas collected from littoral sediments cannot be converted into pool size of CH₄ in the littoral sediments. Rather, the samples were used to constrain the isotopic composition of CH₄ present in the littoral sediments (Chanton, 2005). 3.2. Laboratory methods 3.2.1. Concentration of CH₄ Concentration of water-column CH₄ and sediment CH₄ was measured using a Los Gatos Research (LGR) Methane Carbon Isotope Analyzer (MCIA) (LGR, Mountain View CA, USA) at the Kangerlussuaq International Science Support facility (KISS). The LGR MCIA is a portable, off-axis, integrated cavity output spectrometer that measures CH₄ without sample preparation. All samples were processed within 24 h of collection. For each analysis, 400–600 mL of gas sample was required. Calibration was repeated every 10 samples, with Scotty® gas standards of 50 and 100 ppmv CH₄. Samples were diluted with a known volume of zero-air in order to bring them within the range of the calibration gases. The total concentration of CH₄ in each sample was corrected for dilution and calculated from the sum of the measured headspace partial pressure and the dissolved CH₄ remaining after gas stripping, calculated according to Henry’s law using values after Lide and Fredrikse (1995). Instrumental uncertainty of CH₄ from the MCIA was ±0.5 ppmv, which is one standard deviation of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. Previously, concentrations of CH₄ from MCIA were analyzed on a Gas Chromatograph Flame Ionization Detector (GC-FID) to confirm validity (Appendix 2). Aliquots of each sample were transferred to pre-evacuated glass vials and returned to Indiana University, USA for carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄. 3.3. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄ Stable C and H isotopes of CH₄ were analyzed using two approaches. MCIA was used for C isotopic analysis on samples with CH₄ concentrations >50 ppmv, but the MCIA produces unreliable results at lower concentrations (Appendix 3). Therefore, stable isotope ratios of both carbon and hydrogen of CH₄ were measured using continuous-flow gas chromatography-oxidation/pyrolysis isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-ox/pyr-IRMS) with a laboratory-built gas pre-concentrator interfaced with a ThermoFinnigan GCC and Delta Plus XP IRMS at the Stable Isotope Research Facility (SIRF) at Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana. The pre-concentrator design was modeled after principles described by Merritt et al. (1995) and inlet system developed by Miller et al. (2002) for carbon isotope analysis and Brass and Rockmann (2010) for carbon and hydrogen isotopes. The gas sample containing CH₄ is first dried by passing through a cold trap and then passed into a stainless steel sample loop packed with HayeSep D and kept at −130 °C. After the CH₄ is extracted, the trap is warmed to −20 °C and the CH₄ is cryofocused at the head of Varian Porabond Q GC column. Carbon of CH₄ is converted to CO₂ at 950 °C and H is converted to H₂ in an alumina reactor at 1450 °C. Carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios are expressed in standard δ notation (δ¹³C and δ²H): \[ \delta = [(R_{\text{sample}} - R_{\text{standard}})/R_{\text{standard}}] \times 1000 = \%o \] where \( R \) is the molar ratio of heavy to light isotopes (¹³C/¹²C, ²H/¹H) for both sample and standard. Carbon isotope values are referenced to VPDB and hydrogen isotope values are referenced to VSMOW by comparison with pure CH₄ where the isotopic composition has been measured by off-line combustion (http://mypage.iu.edu/~aschimme/compounds.html). Instrumental uncertainty of δ¹³C and δ²H from the GC-C-IRMS was calculated as ±0.4‰ and as ±10‰ respectively, which is one standard deviation for repeated measures of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. 3.4. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were made using IBM SPSS Statistics. Combined concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic compositions for all study lakes during each season were assessed for normal distribution via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and were found to be non-normally distributed. Student’s t tests of unequal variance were used for testing statistically significant differences in concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic values of CH₄ between seasons and between study results and reported isotopic values from other natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude. Systematic changes in δ¹³C and δ²H were analyzed using linear regression, based upon the pathway of oxidation leading to systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of CH₄ in the residual unoxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). 4. RESULTS 4.1. Water-column CH₄ 4.1.1. Concentration of CH₄ Under open-water conditions, concentrations of CH₄ were strongly related to DO dynamics (Fig. 2). Dissolved CH₄ concentrations in the surface waters of the three lakes ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 µM (Fig. 3). Clinograde DO profiles were measured in EVV Upper and Potentilla lakes with DO saturated in surface water (9.5 and 11.0 mg L⁻¹ respectively), and decreasing with depth to anoxia (<0.5 mg L⁻¹; Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column with decreasing DO, with the maximum CH₄ observed in the anoxic water at the sediment–water interface (150 and 67 µM respectively). Teardrop lake was oxic to suboxic (DO > 1 mg L⁻¹) throughout the water column with an oxygen anomaly at 4.0 m, wherein DO drastically shifted from >10 mg L⁻¹ at 3.5 m to 1.8 mg L⁻¹ at 4 m, and then returned to 7 mg L⁻¹ at 4.5 m. Throughout the water column of Teardrop lake, there were low CH₄ concentrations (<8.1 µM; Fig. 3). In all three lakes, concentrations of CH₄ were significantly greater under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (n = 31, p = 0.0002). A downward increase in CH₄ concentration from below ice-cover to the sediment–water interface was measured in all three lakes under ice-covered conditions (Fig. 3). Potentilla lake was the only lake with measurable DO under ice-cover (Fig. 3). Consequently, CH₄ concentrations dynamically followed DO with highest concentrations (220 µM) observed within the anoxic bottom waters and decreasing concentrations tracking increasing dissolved DO upward through the water column until concentrations of CH₄ reached levels <1 µM immediately below the ice (Fig. 3). EVV Upper and Teardrop lakes were entirely anoxic below ice-cover with concentrations of CH₄ >50 µM throughout the water column (Fig. 3). 4.1.2. \( \delta^{13}C \) of water-column CH₄ Under open-water conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the three lakes ranged from −68.7‰ to +7.4‰ (Fig. 3). In both EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ was enriched in \( ^{13}C \) in the surface waters relative to the bottom waters (Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake, CH₄ became depleted in \( ^{13}C \) by 20‰ down the water column, with \( \delta^{13}C \) decreasing from −48.1‰ at the surface to −68.7‰ at 5.0 m depth. The depletion of CH₄ in \( ^{13}C \) in EVV Upper lake down the water column corresponded with an increase in CH₄ concentration (Fig. 3). In Teardrop lake, CH₄ in the surface water was more depleted in \( ^{13}C \) compared to bottom waters (Fig. 3). An overall enrichment of 10‰ was observed down the water column, with \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) increasing from −47.4‰ at the surface to −36.5‰ at 5.0 m. At 4.0 m depth, an anomalously heavy \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) value of +7.4‰ was observed (Fig. 3). In Potentilla lake, with the exception of 2.0 m, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) was stable from the surface down the water column to 6.0 m. From 4.0 m to 7.0 m, \( \delta^{13}C \) of CH₄ became enriched by 28‰, with \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) increasing from −52.6‰ to −24.5‰ (Fig. 3). From 7.0 m to 7.25 m, a depletion of 43‰ was observed, corresponding with a sharp increase in CH₄ concentration (Fig. 3). Under ice-covered conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) values ranged from −72.2‰ to −33.2‰ (Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) was stable throughout the water column, ranging from −72.2‰ to −71.3‰, corresponding with stable CH₄ concentrations. The \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in Teardrop lake was also relatively stable, ranging from −59.1‰ to −56.3‰. However, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column. Isotopic evidence of production pathways for CH4 in Greenlandic lakes Bedrock in the Kangerlussuaq region consists of tightly folded, felsic gneisses exposed to garnet-grade metamorphism and contains no measurable organic C, therefore we assume that all CH4 within the study lakes is biologically produced. To look at differences in microbial production of CH4, we focus our discussion on the sediment CH4 in the study lakes from open-water conditions. In order to distinguish AM and HM CH4 production pathways from each other isotopically, isotopic compositions of H2O, dissolved inorganic matter (DIC), and organic matter (OM) must be constant. If not, the variation in δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 reflect not only different production pathways, but also variation in environmental factors that affect isotopic composition of reactants. In the study lakes, δ2H2O in the water column slightly decreases with distance away from the margin of the GIS, from a median of −91.5‰ in EVV Upper lake to −97.4‰ in Potentilla lake. Despite the spatial variation in δ2H2O among the lakes, there is no significant relationship between δ2H2O from the water column and δ2HCH4 from sediments (Fig. 5), suggesting that δ2HCH4 is not a direct reflection of variation in 2H2O. In addition to differences in δ2H2O among the lakes, there are also variations in δ13CDIC from the water column among the lakes (Stern et al., 2014). However, there is not enough data to confirm or deny if δ13CCH4 is reflecting variation in δ13CDIC. Approximately a 5‰ difference in δ13COM of particulate OM from profundal sediments was observed lake-to-lake, ranging from −29.2‰ in EVV Upper lake to −24.5‰ (Table 1). Data suggest that the ~45‰ difference in δ13CCH4 of profundal sediment may reflect the δ13COM of precursor OM (Fig. 5b). However, the range in δ13COM is narrow compared to the overall range observed in aquatic chemistry and δ13CCH4 among the lakes. In both the profundal and littoral sediments of the study lakes, values of δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 are consistent with microbial CH4 production (Fig. 4) (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Profundal sediment CH4 is more depleted in 13C and enriched in 2H relative to littoral sediment CH4 (Table 2), suggesting different microbial production pathways, partial oxidation of the littoral sediments, or higher precursor δ13COM in the littoral sediments. However, δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 values from both profundal and littoral sediments plot primarily within the AM field (Fig. 4). The HM pathway field in the δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 classification diagram was determined from marine samples where δ2H2O is ~0‰ (Whiticar, 1999; Waldron et al., 1999b). As a result, the HM pathway field may not accurately represent Arctic waters where δ2H2O ≪ 0‰. Using the assumptions from Chanton et al. (2006), we can adjust the measured sediment δ2HCH4 for the δ2H2O of the water in the lake where the CH4 was formed using the following equation: \[ \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-measured}} - \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\text{ water}} = \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-adjusted}} \] In order to use this equation, δ2HCH4 in the sediments must reflect CH4 production without isotopic overprinting from oxidation. If CH4 in the sediments was subjected to oxidation then a positive correlation between δ13CCH4 and δ²HCH₄ would be observed (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). An inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ from sediments, confirming CH₄ in the sediments had not been oxidized (Fig. 4). The adjustment for δ²H₂O shifted δ²HCH₄ of profundal sediments into the HM pathways field, whereas the littoral sediment δ²HCH₄ remains primarily in the AM pathway field (Fig. 6). Without δ¹³COM in the littoral sediments of each lake, we are unable to assess if the variations between the sediments are the result of different microbial pathways, or if there is also variations in precursor OM. However, δ¹³COM and C/N ratios of littoral sediments from EVV Upper lake suggested OM is sourced from in-lake primary production (Thompson, 2015). The difference in CH₄ production pathway between the littoral and profundal sediments likely reflects the supply of labile organic compounds and δ¹³COM, which would influence CH₄ formation (Duc et al., 2010). In the littoral sediments, aquatic macrophytes and phytoplankton supply a source of labile OM, resulting in AM. Correspondingly, the lake with the highest CH₄ concentrations in the littoral sediments (EVV Upper lake) has the highest concentration of aquatic macrophytes, with the shoreline dominated by Hippuris vulgaris. In freshwater environments, CH₄ typically is produced by AM (Whiticar et al., 1986; Conrad, 1999) because plant root exudates and fresh OM provide a ready supply of labile OM to the bacteria. Previous theoretical values predict that HM accounts for ~30% of overall CH₄ production in freshwater lakes (Conrad, 1999). In high-latitude Sphagnum bogs, CH₄ production via HM is dominant because of an inhibition of the AM pathway, whereas AM is dominant in Carex-rich environments (Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Sphagnum spp. was a significant component of littoral communities of lakes in this study. In closed lake basins, OM from these areas may represent important carbon inputs, which could be influencing the HM pathway for CH₄ production in the profundal sediments. We were surprised to discover that despite significant variations in DOC, SO₄²⁻ and conductivity among the lakes, formation pathways of CH₄ in littoral and profundal sediments seem to be identical in all of the lakes. Competition for substrates (particularly acetate and H₂) favors sulfate reduction (SR), inhibiting CH₄ production (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Ward and Winfrey, 1985; Scholten et al., 2002). Methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased because SR can very effectively uptake both H₂ and acetate, maintaining H₂ and acetate concentrations too low for methanogens (Lovely and Klung, 1986). In the study lakes, EVV Upper lake has the highest SO₄²⁻ concentrations and is the only lake with detectable H₂S in the water column during open-water conditions (Table 1). The presence and accumulation of CH₄ in the sediments indicates that there is sufficient carbon to both fuel reduction of the SO₄²⁻ pool and support methanogenesis in EVV Upper lake. Given the current data, there is no way to assess if communities are spatially coexisting or separated by vertical stratification. However, EVV Upper lake does have the lowest concentration of CH₄ in the profundal sediments, which could be due to SR reducing methanogenesis. Isotopic evidence of consumption of CH₄ by methanotrophic oxidation Under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, concentrations of CH₄ are strongly related to dissolved oxygen dynamics, suggesting MOx is reducing water column CH₄. Methane can also be consumed under anoxic conditions, by AOM (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). However, the strong relationship between CH₄ and DO suggests that in the lakes here, aerobic MOx is the dominant pathway consuming CH₄. Oxidation of CH₄ leads to a systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of the residual un-oxidized CH₄ (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). In the profundal and littoral sediments of all of the lakes, an inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄, suggesting the CH₄ has not been fully oxidized. In the water column under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, a strong, positive correlation between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ is observed in all the lakes (\( n = 51, R = 0.93, p < 0.001 \); Fig. 2c), indicating CH₄ has been oxidized. In oxic waters, CH₄ is systematically enriched in both ¹³C and ²H, which is consistent with MOx (Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Happell et al., 1994; Whiticar, 1999; Bastviken et al., 2002; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). The slope of enrichment of ¹³C and 2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly. Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994): \[ f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000) \] where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx. The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014). 5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported. Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed.
