2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly.

Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994):

\[
f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000)
\]

where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx.

The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014).

5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data

In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported.

5.4. Implications for astrobiology

On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes.

6. CONCLUSIONS

In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed.

The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 μS cm⁻¹. In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 μS cm⁻¹) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (Zmax), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L⁻¹), pH, and specific conductivity (μS cm⁻¹) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column CH₄ collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved CH₄ in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and CH₄ was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved CH₄ in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved CH₄ in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment CH₄ Profundal sediment samples were taken from Zmax of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Thomas Keywords: Lentic small water bodies Flufenacet Metazachlor Pesticides Transformation products Input pathways Pond GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT A B S T R A C T Lentic small water bodies have a high ecological potential as they fulfill several ecosystem services such as the retention of water and pollutants. They serve as a hot spot of biodiversity. Due to their location in or adjacent to agricultural fields, they can be influenced by inputs of pesticides and their transformation products. Since small water bodies have rarely been part of monitorings/campaigns up to now, their current exposure and processes guiding the pesticide input are not understood, yet. This study presents results of a sampling campaign of 10 lentic small water bodies from 2015 to 2016. They were sampled once after the spring application for a pesticide target screening, before autumn application and three times after rainfall events following the application. The autumn sampling focused on the herbicides metazachlor, flufenacet and their transformation products - oxalic acid and - sulfonic acid as representatives for common pesticides in the study region. The concentrations were associated with rainfall before and after application, characteristics of the site and the water bodies, physicochemical parameters and the applied amount of pesticides. The key results of the pesticide screening in spring indicate positive detections of pesticides which have not been applied for years to the single fields. The autumn sampling showed frequent occurrences of the transformation products, which are formed in soil, from 39% to 94% of all samples (n = 71). Discharge patterns were observed for metazachlor with highest concentrations in the first sample after application and then decreasing, but not for flufenacet. The concentrations of the U. Introduction The environmental fate of pesticides and their effects on non-target areas and organisms has been investigated for many decades (among others Kreuger, 1998; Leu et al., 2004). Due to the European Water Framework Directive (WFD) (2009/128/EC, 2009), a monitoring of pesticide concentrations in rivers with a catchment > 10 km², in lakes with a surface area >50 ha and groundwater has been obligatory in the European member states since 2000. Surface water bodies below these surface/catchment sizes are not considered within the EU-WFD. These so called small water bodies (SWB) are often located in rural areas with intensive agricultural use and have a considerable potential to be harmed by agrochemicals since they are adjacent and in direct contact with agricultural fields (Schäfer et al., 2007; Liess et al., 2008; Bunzel et al., 2014). Potential input pathways are by air and water. Water related transport pathways are by surface runoff, lateral flow in the unsaturated zone or shallow groundwater in the saturated zone (Du et al., 2016; Fares, 2016). However, SWB should receive more attention since they perform important hydro-ecological functions: they collect storm water directly by tile drainages and surface runoff or indirectly by subsurface flow and can interact with groundwater (EPCN, 2010; Céréghino et al., 2014; Golus and Bajkiewicz-Grabowska, 2016). Furthermore, SWB retain pollutants by sorption/sedimentation processes, support microbiological degradation and plant uptake (Steidl et al., 2008; Das Gupta et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016). Due to the changing physicochemical environment in SWB (Lischeid and Kalettka, 2012), they provide a variety of different habitats which leads to a high biodiversity in these ecosystems (Downing, 2010; Biggs et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2016). Especially for amphibians, lentic SWB are of importance since they enable the change between aquatic and terrestrial habitat according to the current life cycle. If SWB are located in an appropriate setting, they act as step stones for migrating species and support genetic exchange as well as meta-populations in habitats (Roe and Georges, 2007; Jeliazkov et al., 2014). Such a patchy spatial arrangement of SWB allows species to migrate to favored habitats when climate change alters environmental conditions (Rosset and Oertli, 2011). According to their high number at global scale, SWB are assessed to be a relevant part of the carbon cycle and contribute significantly to carbon sequestration (Gilbert et al., 2016; Holgerson and Raymond, 2016). So far, SWB have just been protected by the Council Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (92/43/EEC, 1992). Since authorities/researchers are aware of the importance of SWB, they attract more attention by selected monitoring programs (Brinke et al., 2015; Tamis et al., 2017) or legal instruments such as National Action Plans for the sustainable use of Pesticides (NAP). The mentions of SWB s in NAPs of other European states are listed in (Table 1). Considerable pesticide contaminations have been found in lotic SWB with maximum concentrations up to 130 µg L⁻¹ for prosulfocarb, 129 µg L⁻¹ for ethofumesat and 92 µg L⁻¹ for metamitron and several exceedances of environmental quality standards were reported (Neumann et al., 2003; Brinke et al., 2015; Szöcs et al., 2017). However, these studies demonstrate that the data base for SWB is too small to give a representative status of contamination, especially for lentic SWB (LSWB). The collected data are inconsistent in sampling procedure, strategy, amount and selection of the active compound and solely demonstrate the current status at the date of sampling (Schreiner et al., 2016; Ulrich et al., 2015; Brinke et al., 2015). Besides, driving factors of pesticide transport into LSWB and of their transformation processes have not been investigated and are not understood, yet. To better understand pesticide fate at sites with lentic SWB and to protect valuable functions of these water bodies, the objectives of our study are (i) to improve and enhance the data base for pesticide contamination in lentic SWB, (ii) to observe the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of pesticide input into these water bodies within one catchment, (iii) to record transformation patterns of the mother compounds into their transformation products and (iv) to relate physico-chemical characteristics of the target compounds, hydrological parameters and site characteristics to the findings. Despite of several definitions of SWB in terms of size or water levels, the authors refer to perennial rivers/lotic water bodies with catchments <10 km² and lakes/lentic water bodies with a surface area <50 ha based on the EU Water Framework Directive. 2. Material and methods In our study, 10 LSWB were monitored in autumns 2015 and 2016 after pesticide application. Event-based grab samples were analyzed for the applied herbicides flufenacet and metazachlor as well as their transformation products - oxalic acid (OA) and - sulfonic acid (ESA). 2.1. Description of the study site and sampling points The catchment of the lowland river Kielstau is located in the North of Germany, Federal State Schleswig-Holstein (Fig. 1). Briefly summarized, it is a catchment with an area of 50 km² and the river Kielstau has a length of 17 km. The region with plain topography is intensively used for agriculture (63% of catchment area). Due to the lowland character, hydraulic gradients are low and there is a high potential for water retention in the landscape (Kiesel et al., 2010). The groundwater levels are high and the shallow groundwater is in close interaction with surface water (Pfannerstill et al., 2014). Approximately 38% of the agricultural fields are drained to improve management practices and plant growth (Fohrer et al., 2007). The prevalent soil types are Planosols and Luvisols and Gleysols and Histosols in the depressions. The average annual temperature is 8.9 °C, the annual precipitation is 885 mm and the annual sunshine duration is 1631 h (data from 1990 to 2016; DWD, 2017a). The Kielstau catchment was appointed as Unesco demosite in 2010 (Fohrer and Schmalz, 2012). As selection criteria, the target pesticides had to be applied to the surrounding fields, the owners had to agree to the sampling and provisioning of application data. Since metazachlor and flufenacet are the most common herbicides applied in rape and winter grain in autumn, the LSWB are located in either rape or winter grain fields with sizes of 4–15 ha. The LSWB are closed depression not connected to discharging or supplying drainage pipes. Evaporation and seepage are assumed to be the loss components. The LSWB are mainly surrounded by a furrow/dam. Exemplarily, Fig. 2 shows the variety of the LSWB concerning size and vegetation. The land use changed from 2015 to 2016 due to the crop rotation system (Table 2). The farmers reported about the date of application, product used, amount applied, field size and drainage system. 2.2. Sampling procedure and chemical analyses In both years, samples were collected in each LSWB once before application of the herbicides on 27/08/2015 and 23/08/2016 and at three dates after application. The individual sampling was event based depending on the date of application and the occurrence of rainfall (see chapter 2.4). The samples were collected at 1 to 3 locations of the water body in a depth of approximately 10–20 cm below the surface with a grab sampler and merged to a mixed sample. These locations were marked and used for subsequent sampling. The samples were stored in glass bottles at −18 °C until analysis. The water samples were analyzed for pH, Oxygen content, electrical conductivity, temperature and redox potential (WTW 3540) in the field according to the common guidelines (DIN 384044, 1976; DIN 384046, 1984; ISO 5814, 2012; ISO 7888, 1993; ISO 10523, 2008). The autumn samples were analyzed after 24 h sedimentation using an AB Sciex 5500 Qtrap with a Synergi 4 μm HydroRP 80A (Phenomenex) column in negative modus for flufenacet-ESA, -OA and metazachlor-ESA. The mobile phase consists of 1 mmol L−1 ammonium acetate buffer and acetonitrile/methanol 50:50, both acidificated with 20 μL acidic acid L−1. Flufenacet, metazachlor and -OA were analyzed with an AB Sciex 6500 Qtrap and a Zorbax Eclipse XDB 3.5 μm (Agilent) column in negative modus with mobile phase of 100% ultrapure water and 100% acetonitrile, both acidificated with 1 mL formic acid L−1. The injection volume of both methods accounted for 100 μL. The Limit of Quantification (LOQ) was 0.01 μg L−1 for flufenacet and metazachlor and 0.025 μg L−1 for the other compounds. Results below the LOQ were set to 0.5 LOQ for illustration in figures and further calculations. The recovery rate for all compounds is in the range of 80–120% determined with addition of a 0.25 ng mL−1 standard of each compound in every fifth sample. To estimate the pesticide contamination of the spring applications, all LSWB were sampled as described above on 7th July 2015 and 5th July 2016, and were analyzed for a target screening of 108 pesticides including 7 TPs. The TPs of metazachlor and flufenacet were not part of the target screening. Here, just concentrations above the LOQ are used for further statistical analysis. The samples were first centrifuged for 30 min at 4 °C with 20,000 rotations min−1. The analyses were then carried out with an Agilent 6460 Triple Quadrupole LC/MS and a Hypersil ODS 250 mm, 3 μm (MZ Analysentechnik) column in both, positive and negative modus. The mobile phase consists of 100% acetonitrile and a 11 mmol L−1 ammonium formate buffer. The recovery rate for the compounds is in the range of 80–110% determined with addition of a 0.12 ng mL−1 standard of each compound in every seventh sample. Fig. 2. Hydrological data The effect of pesticide input via drift during the application procedure was estimated with data of wind speed and wind direction from the station “Flensburg Schäferhaus” of the German Weather Service, situated approximately 12 km from the catchment (DWD, 2017b). Water flow into the LSWB during the sampling period may either increase input of pesticides or dilute pesticide concentrations. The changes of the water level in the LSWB were used as indicator for water inflow/outflow since inputs via precipitation were assessed to be negligible due to the small surface area of the LSWB. Simple rods were installed in the water body close to the bank in August 2016. At every sampling date, the distance between water surface and end of rod was measured and relative water level changes were determined. Precipitation data were measured with an automatic rain gauge (Ott Pluvio, Germany) (LLUR, 2017a) as daily sums at Satrup village, in 8 km distance from most LSWB. Additionally, daily sums were measured with a Hellmann rain gauge at a distance of 2–4 km away from the ISWB in Maasbüll to analyze small-scale variation of precipitation (Hansen, 2016). 2.4. Sampling patterns Previous studies within the Kielstau revealed that on average, a rainfall event of approximately 10 mm causes an increase of the main river's discharge (Ulrich, 2011; Ulrich et al., 2012; Fohrer et al., 2014). Hence, the LSWB were sampled after precipitation sums of at least 10 mm. The decision for a sampling was made based on the weather forecast and the rainfall of the last 24 h. The sampling dates varied according to the date of application and the rainfall patterns (Table 3). In 2015, the third sampling took place approximately four weeks after the second sampling to leave time for transformation processes of the studied pesticides. The results from 2015 showed that these processes occur soon after application. Therefore, the third sampling in 2016 was conducted after the third relevant rainfall event. Digital maps and data analysis Landscape parameters in the surrounding of each LSWB were derived from a digital soil type map based on “Reichsbodenschätzung und Bodenübersichtskarte” BUEK25 (LLUR, 2017b), with data of soil type and the humic content classes. A digital elevation grid with a 1 × 1 m (LVermGeo, 2005b) resolution was used to calculate the slopes with spatial analyst of ArcMap 10 (2010). The surface area, the circumference of the LSWB and the shoreline with higher vegetation such as shrubs, bushes and trees, which prevent input via drift, and the width of the buffer strips were quantified with Digital Ortho Photos (GeoBasis-DE, 2012) and field mappings. The analysis of the collected data was carried out with the statistical program R, version 3.3.3 (R Developing Core Team, 2008). The GGally package creates a matrix of plots with a given data set. Here, the following correlations were calculated: • Concentration of target compounds applied with physicochemical data • Concentration of target compounds applied with site characteristics • Mean concentration of target compounds applied at current year with physicochemical data • Mean concentration of target compounds applied at current year with site characteristics • Median concentration of target compounds applied at current year with physicochemical data • Median concentration of target compounds applied at current year with site characteristics 3. 3.2. Physicochemical parameters of water samples The physicochemical parameters determined in the field show common values of surface water bodies (Fig. 3). The oxygen concentration was in the range of 1.86–12.74 mg L⁻¹, the temperature in the range of 0.4–18.4 °C (not displayed), the conductivity in the range of 151–664 μS cm⁻¹, the pH value in the range of 6.66–8.52 and the redox potential in the range of 45–259 mV. 3.3. Water levels in the LSWB in autumn 2016 The water levels in relation to the initial water level in the LSWB are displayed in Fig. 4. As demonstrated in Table 4, the precipitation between application and sampling varied among the LSWB. The group of LSWB A2, A4, A6, A9 and A10 were sampled at the same dates and precipitation sums were identical, the changes of the water level varied considerably. As a second group, A5 and A8 were sampled and showed decreasing/slightly increasing water levels which may be related to the lower amount of precipitation in comparison to the other LSWB. The unintended extraction of the rods led to missing values in these LSWB. A7 had again a different sampling scheme due to the late date of application. Overall, the sum of precipitation was almost 20 mm lower than for the other LSWB but the increase of the water level is the second highest increase of all LSWB. 4. Results and discussion of pesticide analyses 4.1. Pesticide target screening after spring application The analyses showed that from the measured 108 compounds, ten compounds in 2015 and twelve compounds in 2016 were quantified above the LOQ (Fig. 5). Most of the compounds with positive findings were detected in one or few LSWB, but metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylterbuthylazine were found in each LSWB. Comparing both years, azoxystrobin, cyproconazole, diflufenican were measured solely in 2016, while pirimicarb was found only in 2015. The pesticide concentrations in 2015 were close to the LOQ with four exemptions clearly above 0.1 μg L⁻¹. In 2016, seven findings were higher than 0.1 μg L⁻¹. The highest detected concentration after the spring application was 0.63 μg metolachlor L⁻¹ in A10. Multiple-pesticide contaminations from 3 to 7 compounds were observed in the single LSWB whereas the number of contaminants increased from 2015 to 2016. The highest number of compounds was observed in A7 with 6 compounds in 2015 and 7 compounds in 2016. Due to their high uncertainty, the values of methyldesphenylchloridazone were not considered. Within the twelve compounds detected in concentrations higher than the LOQ, there are four herbicides, three fungicides, three insecticides and two TP of herbicides. Their properties vary concerning mobility and persistence in a broad range (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016;) so that inputs cannot be addressed to certain physicochemical characteristics. Considering the land use, none of these compounds had been applied in that year directly to the fields in which the LSWB were located as the crops grown there did not require them. However, in all cases these pesticides had been applied to the crops on either one of the neighbouring fields that year or in autumn/spring of the previous year to the LSWB field. Hence, the pesticide inputs may originate from these adjacent fields or former applications. Exemplarily, diflufenican is a herbicide which is applied in autumn and is part of a widely distributed product. In autumn 2015, this product was applied to field A7 (winter grain) so that the measured concentration in A7 in spring 2016 may result from that application. The same product was applied to A1, A3, A6 and A10 as well in 2015, but residues in July 2016 were not found. These results may lead to the assumption that A7 is more susceptible to pesticide inputs than the other LSWB of the study. The key results of the target screenings are that (i) metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethyltriazine were found in all LSWB and that (ii) the concentrations of the twelve compounds were lower in 2015 than in 2016. (i) Metolachlor and terbuthylazine are herbicides which are applied to corn. However, they were neither applied in 2015 nor in 2016 and often not for years to the fields of the ten LSWB. In most of the LSWB, the three compounds were detected in both years in background concentrations.01–0.03 μg L⁻¹. In 2016 in A10, 0.315 μg L⁻¹ terbuthylazine and 0.63 μg L⁻¹ metolachlor were found. Since a field with corn cultivation in 2016 is next to A10, it can be assumed that these concentrations are caused by the release from this field to A10. There were no further fields with corn cultivation close to the other LSWB which could explain the findings of terbuthylazine and metolachlor. Sandin et al. In addition to water-related transport into water bodies, atmospheric deposition has to be considered as a potential input pathway as well. Several studies show that pesticides can be transported via air or rainfall to non-target areas (Epple et al., 2002; Sauret et al., 2009; Jiménez et al., 2015). Metolachlor, terbuthylazine and desethylterbuthylazine were mainly detected in wet deposition in amounts of 0.01–1.39 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹, 0.04–1.11 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹ and 0.08 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹, respectively (Sauret et al., 2009; Kreuger et al., 2017). Especially for triazines like terbuthylazine and its TP, long-range transport is observed due to their high persistence in air (Epple et al., 2002; Kreuger et al., 2017). As a consequence of the use of metolachlor since 1976 and terbuthylazine since 1971 it becomes probable that they have spread ubiquitously over time and cause the low but permanent background concentrations. These background concentrations have been recognized in studies with a large number of sampling points and sampling dates (LFU, 2014; LLUR, 2014; Schreiner et al., 2016). As a consequence of the long period of terbuthylazine application, its TP desethylterbuthylazine, was measured in background concentrations of 0.01–0.03 µg L⁻¹ and up to 0.114 µg L⁻¹ in A6 in 2016. Lischeid et al. (2017) observed natural ponds to identify external drivers of their water quality. The results obtained reveal that size and location of the ponds' catchment is of crucial importance and that it is often related to shallow groundwater systems. Especially at small scale and without flowing water bodies, topography and groundwater levels are not sufficient for the delineation. Lischeid et al. (2017) showed that subsurface catchments of these LSWB can exceed sizes of 2 ha. In consequence, the residence time of dissolved compounds such as pesticides in subsurface flow can be high. Sandin et al. (2018) explained their findings of formerly applied pesticides by intermittent transport processes which relocate the pesticides to the subsoil where degradation is slower than in topsoil. In the subsoil, pesticides can be stored and slowly released so that they cause a signal over a long period. The results of these two studies explain that the corn-herbicide findings in our LSWB may originate via hydraulic subsurface connection and slow transport in the subsoil from former applications in larger distance. (ii) To explain the concentration differences between the years, the amount and distribution of the precipitation from 1st April to 5th July were compared. The precipitation sum was 149 mm in 2015 and 299 mm in 2016 in 8 km distance, and 169 mm (2015) and 214 mm (2016) in 2–4 km distance. The overall amount of rainfall was clearly higher in 2016 than in 2015. The distribution shows higher rainfall amounts in April and June in 2016, but higher ones in May 2015. In general, the herbicides metolachlor and terbuthylazine are applied to corn in May while the fungicide tebuconazole is applied to rape in April/May and to grain from April to middle of June. The higher precipitation in 2016 caused a more frequent application of tebuconazole than in 2015: six of eight fields were sprayed in 2016, while in 2015, two of five fields were sprayed. Two rainfall events of 30–50 mm at the end of June 2016 may have caused enhanced relocation especially of metolachlor, tebuconazole and terbuthylazine. According to their properties (water solubility, log P, Kfoc, DT50 soil) (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016), they are assessed to be moderately mobile and moderately or non-persistent so that a higher potential for discharge cannot be derived. Hence, the combination of the rainfall pattern and the time of application may have caused the differences of pesticide findings in 2015 and 2016. 4.2. Analyses of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in autumn samples 2015 and 2016 4.2.1. Transport and transformation of metazachlor in LSWB located in rape fields Five LSWB were monitored in 2015 for metazachlor and its TP concentrations. Metazachlor was not detected in concentrations higher than LOQ before application (Fig. 6). After application, the maximum concentration amounted to 0.62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in A8 after the second rainfall event. The following observations were made: In all 5 LSWB, metazachlor concentrations were highest after the 1st rainfall event following the application. Over time, the concentrations decreased. We assessed this as prevalent patterns. However, the reduction of concentration varies between the LSWB from 20 to 90% from the first to the third sampling after application (47 days). Observations from two LSWB of a different study show metazachlor concentrations of 0,764–10.24 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) (LELF, 2014) considerably higher than those in our study with a maximum of 0,62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\). The metazachlor TPs were quantified in maximal concentration of up to 1.8 \( \mu \)g OA L\(^{-1}\) and 4.8 \( \mu \)g ESA L\(^{-1}\). Both TPs show the same patterns just vary in concentration: the concentrations increase overtime to the highest value in the third sample after application in A4, A5, A8. But in A2 and A9, the concentrations were at a constant value and did not change considerably. Metazachlor-ESA concentrations are in general higher than those of metazachlor-OA which can be explained by the ESA's higher occurrence fraction, a higher DT50 in soil and a very low k_foc displaying a very high mobility (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016). However, positives in the range of 0.49–4.2 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in the samples collected before application cannot be explained. The physicochemical properties, if available, do not predict this persistence. In addition, there was no application of metazachlor in the previous year 2014. This leads to the conclusion that either the TPs are very persistent and are still detectable two years later or transported from former applications at other sites to the LSWB below surface according to the assumptions of Lischeid et al. (2017). Fig. 6. Concentrations of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in LSWB located in rape fields in autumn 2015, event 0 = before application; I–III = event based samples after application. To explain the variability of the concentrations in the LSWB, the rainfall following the application is considered. For most of the LSWB, some dry days followed the application, but at the A9 and A2 fields, rainfall events of 15 mm and 4 mm, respectively, were observed at the day after application and may have led to the highest metazachlor concentrations in the first rainfall. The relevance of rainfall events after application has been pointed out in several studies (Fohrer et al., 2014; Lewan et al., 2009). The shorter the period between application and rainfall event is and the higher the rainfall intensity/amount, the higher is the potential for pesticide relocation from the fields since time for degradation processes is reduced. The results of our study support these findings. While the rainfall after application was a crucial factor for A2 and A9, the overall maximum concentration was measured in A8 in the second sample after application. Hence, the pesticide transport here was slower. Either the single transport pathways are of different relevance for A8 and A2/A9, or the connection between soil and water body at A2/A9 e.g. by lateral flow are faster at A2/A9 than at A8. Residues of flufenacet-TPs from the application in 2014 occurred in all LSWB except of A9 in more or less constant mean concentrations of 0.024 (OA) and 0.069 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) (ESA) due to the winter barley cultivation on these sites. The mother compound flufenacet was detected only once at concentrations of 0.026 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) due to its shorter dissipation time and lower mobility compared to those of the TPs. Fig. 7. Concentrations of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in LSWB located in winter grain fields in autumn 2015, event 0 = before application; I–III = event based samples after application. 4.2.2. Transport and transformation of flufenacet in LSWB located in winter grain fields In 2015, five LSWB were sampled for Flufenacet and its TP exposure. In A6 and A10, no contamination was determined (Fig. 7). The other LSWB show different patterns: the flufenacet concentrations varied in the range of 0.02 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) within each LSWB showing slightly decreasing (A1), increasing (A3) or fluctuating values. These slight differences may also be attributed to the uncertainty of the values. For flufenacet, the highest concentration amounted to 0.69 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in A7 after the second rainfall event. The flufenacet-TP concentrations increased in different patterns, but the final concentration was the highest in each LSWB. Similar to the metazachlor-TPs, flufenacet-OA and -ESA concentrations showed the same behaviour and increased but in different rates. In every sample, ESA concentrations were higher than OA due to a slightly lower \( k_{foc} \) and considerably higher DT\(_{50}\) in soil (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016). In total, the concentrations of flufenacet and its TPs were considerably higher in A1 and A7 than those in A3, A6, A10. Considering the rainfall events in the days following application, events of 11 and 14 mm/d occurred one/two days after application to field A1 and a rainfall event of 20 mm was detected 4 days after application to A7 field. In contrast, several days without any rainfall followed the applications on the other fields. Residues of metazachlor were not detected but metazachlor-OA concentrations were measured in A1 and A7 with 0.55 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) and 0.1 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) before application and after application up to 0.41 in A1. Metazachlor-ESA was detected in every sample with highest concentration of 1.9 in A1. The considerable contamination with metazachlor-TPs of A1 can be explained with the crop rotation and the growing of rape including a metazachlor application in autumn 2014. However, residues in A3 cannot be explained since metazachlor was neither applied in 2014 at this field nor to adjacent fields in 2015. 4.2.3. Analyses of flufenacet and its TPs in autumn samples 2016 The results from 2016 demonstrate that flufenacet is transported into the LSWB with no consistent patterns and in various temporal dynamics (Fig. 8). A concentration increase was measured in A4 and clearly in A10 to 0.304 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\), which is the maximum concentration of this sampling campaign. For the TPs, an increase of concentration was observed in three LSWB (A5, A7, A8) in the second sample after application, in two LSWB (A4, A10) in the third sample after application and in two LSWB (A6, A9), TPs were not detected above the LOQ. Hence, the various temporal dynamic of the mother compound can be observed for the TPs as well. Every day after application, there was rainfall until the sampling. Hence, high flufenacet concentrations were detected in the samples. This counts for 5 of 8 LSWB: 10–13 mm/d were measured for A7, A9, A10 and 5–8 mm/d for A5/A8. For the other 3 LSWB, there was no rainfall right after application. Hence, the flufenacet concentrations here are lower than in the LSWB with rainfall after application. Again, the date of application in conjunction with the rainfall events shortly after it, prove to be a crucial factor for fast pesticide transport. Low metazachlor concentrations were measured in A6 in the samples I to III and may originate from an adjacent rape field which is separated from the A6 field by a road. Residues from former usages determined in the samples before application in 2015 were metazachlor-TPs in A1 and in lower concentrations in A7. While the previous crop in 2014 at the A1 field was winter rape and explains the residues, corn was cultivated on the A7 field where metazachlor was not applied so that the source of the TPs is either an application before 2014 or a different field. In 2016, metazachlor-TP positives were detected in high concentrations before application in all LSWB where the cultivation of winter rape and the associated application of metazachlor in 2015 took place (A2, A4, A5, A8, A9). Again, metazachlor-TPs were observed in A7 in 2016 without an application of metazachlor in the previous two years. However, positives of flufenacet-TPs in A7 and A6 before application can be explained with the flufenacet application in autumn 2015. 4.3. Comparison of the results in 2015 and 2016 Comparing the results of flufenacet and its TPs in 2015 and 2016, highest contamination was recorded in both years for A7. A8 showed also high contaminations in 2016, but was exposed to metazachlor and its TPs in 2015. Nevertheless, A8 seems to be susceptible to pesticide inputs like A7 since highest metazachlor and -TP contaminations in the rape LSWB were measured in A8 in 2015. The concentrations of flufenacet and its TPs were higher in 2015 than in 2016, either maximum values or average values. This can be explained with the hydrological parameters: the precipitation in 2015 was at all sampling events ![Bar charts showing concentrations of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in LSWB located in winter grain fields in autumn 2016, event 0 = before application; I–III = event based samples after application.](page_120_1342_1708_1012.png) Fig. 8. Concentrations of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in LSWB located in winter grain fields in autumn 2016, event 0 = before application; I–III = event based samples after application. twice as high as in 2016 (see Table 3, Table 4). In addition, the precipitation in the four weeks before application (July) of 77 mm in 2016 was much lower than in rainy late summer 2015 with 143 mm, hence, a lower soil water content can be assumed in 2016. Comparing the individual precipitation sums of each LSWB 14 days prior to application, the sums range from 7 to 60 mm (average 36,6 mm) in 2015 and 8,5 to 32 mm (average 17,6 mm) in 2016. Lewan et al. (2009) stated that the initial soil water content is a crucial factor effecting pesticide transport. A high initial soil water content enhances macropore flow, and thus, pesticide leaching (Jarvis, 2007; Kahl et al., 2008). Overall, concentrations of metazachlor and its TPs were higher than those of flufenacet and its TPs which is attributed to different amounts of application. In general, metazachlor is applied with 500 g ha\(^{-1}\), while 130–240 g flufenacet/ha are applied to winter grain fields. Furthermore, metazachlor is assessed to be more mobile than flufenacet due to its physicochemical properties (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016) and is hence, transported into water bodies to a higher extent. Independent of the applied herbicide, contaminations were highest in the LSWB A7, A8 and A10 in both years. Hence, these LSWB can be assessed to be more prone to pesticide inputs than the other LSWB. 4.4. Transport pathways of pesticides into LSWB Pesticides enter surface water bodies as drift via air transport during application or after it, by surface runoff, lateral flow and by interaction with shallow groundwater. Our results indicate that the LSWB are mainly surrounded by tall vegetation which is supposed to reduce pesticide inputs via spray drift during the application procedure. Correlations of the concentration and the share of tall vegetation at the bank of the LSWB were not significant (see chapter 4.5). Furthermore, A6 with a low share of tall vegetation showed very low contaminations in both years, and A9 with a high percentage of surrounding vegetation is one of the most contaminated LSWB. It is assumed that the input via air is of minor relevance in our study. Nevertheless, the findings of atmospheric deposition from Epple et al. (2002), Sauret et al. (2009), Jiménez et al. (2015) and Kreuger et al. (2017) should be considered when input pathways are to be identified. The slopes of the investigated fields are in the range of 1.14 to 3.69% which is typical for a lowland region. These slopes generate surface runoff in constrained areas and under specific rainfall patterns so that surface runoff at the sites of the investigated LSWB is limited. Furthermore, the LSWB are surrounded by a furrow/dam of approximately 30–40 cm height. The furrow/dam originates from field management practices such as ploughing and hampers inputs via surface runoff (Fig. 9). This is supported by the findings in A7: observations in 2015 showed that A7 overflowed the southerly bank and extended into the field due to incessant precipitation. Hence, the water phase of the LSWB was in direct contact with the soil surface, where flufenacet was applied, and caused highest concentrations of flufenacet and its TPs. One may blame the narrow buffer strip of approximately 2 m for the contamination, but in summer 2016, the farmer built a small embankment at this location to prevent overflow, but the flufenacet/TP concentrations were still the highest of all LSWB in 2016. Hence, other water paths than surface runoff seem to play an important role. Beside inputs by pathways above/on surface, subsurface inputs via lateral flow or shallow groundwater need to be considered as well. The water level changes reveal water inflow and outflow below the surface and hereby, pesticide transport into/out of the LSWB. Since lateral flow is limited to times of a rainfall event in the unsaturated zone (Du et al., 2016; Fares, 2016; Sophocleous, 2002), the interaction with the shallow groundwater takes place over a longer period. Hence, it is assumed to be a relevant subsurface pathway. In our study, the same water level change (increase or decrease) caused contrary effects: high inflow of water was accompanied either with a dilution of pesticide concentrations in A6 or an increase of concentrations in A7. In A2, a constant water level and constant concentrations were detected. Whereas water level and concentration fluctuated in A4. These examples show the broad variety of transport processes taking place in and around an LSWB, effecting pesticide transport and transformation. They support the findings of Lischeid et al. (2017) and Lischeid and Kalettk (2012) that the understanding of the hydrology/hydrogeology of sites is essential to understand the spatial and temporal water flow into LSWB and hence, pesticide transport. The results indicate that the input of the pesticides into LSWB is controlled by a complex system of different processes whose relevance has not been understood yet. 4.5. Correlations between target compounds and physicochemical parameters/site characteristics The following figure shows the correlations between the concentrations and the physicochemical as well as site parameters (Fig. 10). For the samples I to III, only values higher than LOQ were considered, leading to a data base of 53 samples (n = 15 for rape 2015; n = 14 for grain 2015; n = 24 for grain 2016). The concentrations of the target compounds are not normally distributed. Exemplarily, the results of the LSWB located in grain fields are displayed. The statistical analyses reveal correlations of up to r = 0.662 between the herbicides/their TPs and physicochemical parameters of the water samples. The physicochemical parameters varied just slightly and showed only minor differences between the LSWB which could not explain variations of the pesticide concentrations. Furthermore, the higher correlations of e.g. flufenacet-ESA and conductivity are caused by outliers which create artificially elevated correlation values. None of the included variables showed a significant correlation and explain the input/transformation of the target compounds in our study. The correlation between the pesticide concentrations and the site characteristics does not demonstrate any significant dependencies for the same reasons as described before. The sites did not differ noticeably in soil type, slope or organic carbon content (Table 4). Schulz (2004) investigated the effect of catchment size of up to 100.000 km\(^2\) on insecticide concentrations in water bodies and showed that water bodies in smaller catchments are more harmed than those in larger catchments. Brinke et al. (2015) investigated the effect of topographic catchment size on pesticide concentrations in lotic SWB from 1 to 100 km\(^2\) and found slight tendencies for higher contamination risk in catchments smaller than 30 km\(^2\). Data for lentic SWBs were too scarce for analyses. Our study was carried out at a considerably smaller scale (LSWB surface area of from 41 to 647 m\(^2\)) than that of Brinke et al. (2015). Since the correlation between concentrations and catchment size could hardly be detected at larger scale, it is unlikely to observe such effects at the scale of our study and its data base. 4.6. Assessment of findings To assess the exposure of the LSWB, environmental quality standards (EQS) of Germany are considered. The relevant standards for Fig. 10. Correlation between measured target compound concentrations and physicochemical parameters (a) and between median target compound concentrations and site characteristics for LSWB located in grain fields 2015 and 2016. short-term exposure are listed in Table 7, the EQS annual mean concentration cannot be applied but are listed as additional information. EQS for the TPs in surface water are not available. The maximum observed metazachlor concentration was for 0.13 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \) and is clearly below the regulatory acceptable concentration (RAC) and the EQS. For flufenacet, the maximum allowable concentration was exceeded in A8 (0.277 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \)) and A10 (0.304 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \)) in the third samples after application in October 2016. Comparable data of pesticide contamination in LSWB are scarce but concentrations from LSWB in the eastern part of Germany, in Brandenburg, can be used for comparison. For metazachlor, in four of ten samples concentrations of 0.764 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \) up to 10.24 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1} \) were measured in autumns 2012/3. Flufenacet data for comparison are not available since either it was not included in the analytical spectrum of the study or values were below the LOQ (LELF, 2014). The results of metazachlor findings in our study are considerably lower than in the other study. 5. Conclusion The key findings of the study indicate a high temporal and spatial variability in the inputs of the herbicides metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs into the LSWB. Few similar transport patterns were observed for metazachlor, but not for flufenacet. Despite of closely resembling hydrological data and site characteristics such as soil type, humic content and slope, a considerable spatial heterogeneity is displayed by the almost unique kind of pesticide concentrations in the LSWB over time. The transformation of the mother compounds showed correspondences in the manner of highest TP concentrations in the last sample of the campaign, but TP concentrations varied in the intermediate samples. The TPs of the mother compound applied in the previous year were clearly detected in the following year. This applies in particular for metazachlor-ESA which can be assessed as a permanent exposure in each water body of the study. The analysis of the target compounds' physicochemical properties reveal that the TPs, especially the ESA-TPs, have a higher mobility and persistence than the mother compounds metazachlor and flufenacet. Metazachlor-ESA was detected in almost every sample, even one or two years after application of the mother compound. In contrast, the mother compounds were only measured after application due to their lower DT\(_{50}\). Further results indicate that hydrological parameters are more relevant for pesticide transport than properties of the pesticides or the site characteristics. The rainfall amount and patterns strongly influence the transport of the pesticides. Thereby, the rainfall following application seems to be of higher importance than the antecedent rainfall which effects the initial soil water content. The recording of the water level changes in 2016 clearly demonstrate that the transport of water and hence, of pesticides into LSWB is strongly related to inflow via subsurface flow and becomes apparent to be of high relevance. The target screenings after spring application reveal findings of the pesticides metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylatrazine in each LSWB, which may originate from former applications in larger distance. Furthermore, the site characteristics do not explain sufficiently the variations of the concentrations. The same applies for the correlation between physicochemical properties of the water samples such as pH, oxygen content, redox potential and the concentrations of the target compounds. Small-scale characteristics such as subsurface transport via lateral flow and interaction with the shallow groundwater as well as soil moisture or date of application seem to be of higher relevance for pesticide transport. Lentic small water bodies are of major importance for biodiversity but have a high potential to be harmed by agrochemicals due to their location in agricultural fields. The driving factor controlling the transport of pesticides into the LSWB is the precipitation and related to this, the inflow of water and dissolved pesticides. Moreover, the transport how and from where the pesticides enter the LSWB as well as the importance of interactions with the sediments as potential permanent pesticide releaser need to be elucidated. Since studies reveal atmospheric pesticide inputs into surface water bodies, their concentrations in wet and dry depositions should be considered as well. The data base of pesticide contamination of LSWB has definitely to be enlarged by event-based sampling to get a realistic assessment of their exposure. But in addition, continuous long-term monitoring in high temporal resolution e.g. in daily intervals is essential to recognize the processes responsible for pesticide transport at this scale. Without understanding these processes, an efficient protection of the LSWB cannot be achieved as stated in directives, guidelines and national action plans. Hence, there is an urgent need to fill the knowledge gaps to meet the environmental goals in the near future. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction The environmental fate of pesticides and their effects on non-target areas and organisms has been investigated for many decades (among others Kreuger, 1998; Leu et al., 2004). Due to the European Water Framework Directive (WFD) (2009/128/EC, 2009), a monitoring of pesticide concentrations in rivers with a catchment > 10 km², in lakes with a surface area >50 ha and groundwater has been obligatory in the European member states since 2000. Surface water bodies below these surface/catchment sizes are not considered within the EU-WFD. These so called small water bodies (SWB) are often located in rural areas with intensive agricultural use and have a considerable potential to be harmed by agrochemicals since they are adjacent and in direct contact with agricultural fields (Schäfer et al., 2007; Liess et al., 2008; Bunzel et al., 2014). Potential input pathways are by air and water. Water related transport pathways are by surface runoff, lateral flow in the unsaturated zone or shallow groundwater in the saturated zone (Du et al., 2016; Fares, 2016). However, SWB should receive more attention since they perform important hydro-ecological functions: they collect storm water directly by tile drainages and surface runoff or indirectly by subsurface flow and can interact with groundwater (EPCN, 2010; Céréghino et al., 2014; Golus and Bajkiewicz-Grabowska, 2016). Furthermore, SWB retain pollutants by sorption/sedimentation processes, support microbiological degradation and plant uptake (Steidl et al., 2008; Das Gupta et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016). Due to the changing physicochemical environment in SWB (Lischeid and Kalettka, 2012), they provide a variety of different habitats which leads to a high biodiversity in these ecosystems (Downing, 2010; Biggs et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2016). Especially for amphibians, lentic SWB are of importance since they enable the change between aquatic and terrestrial habitat according to the current life cycle. If SWB are located in an appropriate setting, they act as step stones for migrating species and support genetic exchange as well as meta-populations in habitats (Roe and Georges, 2007; Jeliazkov et al., 2014). Such a patchy spatial arrangement of SWB allows species to migrate to favored habitats when climate change alters environmental conditions (Rosset and Oertli, 2011). According to their high number at global scale, SWB are assessed to be a relevant part of the carbon cycle and contribute significantly to carbon sequestration (Gilbert et al., 2016; Holgerson and Raymond, 2016). So far, SWB have just been protected by the Council Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (92/43/EEC, 1992). Since authorities/researchers are aware of the importance of SWB, they attract more attention by selected monitoring programs (Brinke et al., 2015; Tamis et al., 2017) or legal instruments such as National Action Plans for the sustainable use of Pesticides (NAP). The mentions of SWB s in NAPs of other European states are listed in (Table 1). Considerable pesticide contaminations have been found in lotic SWB with maximum concentrations up to 130 µg L⁻¹ for prosulfocarb, 129 µg L⁻¹ for ethofumesat and 92 µg L⁻¹ for metamitron and several exceedances of environmental quality standards were reported (Neumann et al., 2003; Brinke et al., 2015; Szöcs et al., 2017). However, these studies demonstrate that the data base for SWB is too small to give a representative status of contamination, especially for lentic SWB (LSWB). The collected data are inconsistent in sampling procedure, strategy, amount and selection of the active compound and solely demonstrate the current status at the date of sampling (Schreiner et al., 2016; Ulrich et al., 2015; Brinke et al., 2015). Besides, driving factors of pesticide transport into LSWB and of their transformation processes have not been investigated and are not understood, yet. To better understand pesticide fate at sites with lentic SWB and to protect valuable functions of these water bodies, the objectives of our study are (i) to improve and enhance the data base for pesticide contamination in lentic SWB, (ii) to observe the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of pesticide input into these water bodies within one catchment, (iii) to record transformation patterns of the mother compounds into their transformation products and (iv) to relate physico-chemical characteristics of the target compounds, hydrological parameters and site characteristics to the findings. Despite of several definitions of SWB in terms of size or water levels, the authors refer to perennial rivers/lotic water bodies with catchments <10 km² and lakes/lentic water bodies with a surface area <50 ha based on the EU Water Framework Directive. 2. Material and methods In our study, 10 LSWB were monitored in autumns 2015 and 2016 after pesticide application. Event-based grab samples were analyzed for the applied herbicides flufenacet and metazachlor as well as their transformation products - oxalic acid (OA) and - sulfonic acid (ESA). 2.1. Description of the study site and sampling points The catchment of the lowland river Kielstau is located in the North of Germany, Federal State Schleswig-Holstein (Fig. 1). Briefly summarized, it is a catchment with an area of 50 km² and the river Kielstau has a length of 17 km. The region with plain topography is intensively used for agriculture (63% of catchment area). Due to the lowland character, hydraulic gradients are low and there is a high potential for water retention in the landscape (Kiesel et al., 2010). The groundwater levels are high and the shallow groundwater is in close interaction with surface water (Pfannerstill et al., 2014). Approximately 38% of the agricultural fields are drained to improve management practices and plant growth (Fohrer et al., 2007). The prevalent soil types are Planosols and Luvisols and Gleysols and Histosols in the depressions. The average annual temperature is 8.9 °C, the annual precipitation is 885 mm and the annual sunshine duration is 1631 h (data from 1990 to 2016; DWD, 2017a). The Kielstau catchment was appointed as Unesco demosite in 2010 (Fohrer and Schmalz, 2012). 3.2. Physicochemical parameters of water samples The physicochemical parameters determined in the field show common values of surface water bodies (Fig. 3). The oxygen concentration was in the range of 1.86–12.74 mg L⁻¹, the temperature in the range of 0.4–18.4 °C (not displayed), the conductivity in the range of 151–664 μS cm⁻¹, the pH value in the range of 6.66–8.52 and the redox potential in the range of 45–259 mV. 3.3. Water levels in the LSWB in autumn 2016 The water levels in relation to the initial water level in the LSWB are displayed in Fig. 4. As demonstrated in Table 4, the precipitation between application and sampling varied among the LSWB. The group of LSWB A2, A4, A6, A9 and A10 were sampled at the same dates and precipitation sums were identical, the changes of the water level varied considerably. As a second group, A5 and A8 were sampled and showed decreasing/slightly increasing water levels which may be related to the lower amount of precipitation in comparison to the other LSWB. The unintended extraction of the rods led to missing values in these LSWB. A7 had again a different sampling scheme due to the late date of application. Overall, the sum of precipitation was almost 20 mm lower than for the other LSWB but the increase of the water level is the second highest increase of all LSWB. 4. Results and discussion of pesticide analyses 4.1. Pesticide target screening after spring application The analyses showed that from the measured 108 compounds, ten compounds in 2015 and twelve compounds in 2016 were quantified above the LOQ (Fig. 5). Most of the compounds with positive findings were detected in one or few LSWB, but metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylterbuthylazine were found in each LSWB. Comparing both years, azoxystrobin, cyproconazole, diflufenican were measured solely in 2016, while pirimicarb was found only in 2015. The pesticide concentrations in 2015 were close to the LOQ with four exemptions clearly above 0.1 μg L⁻¹. In 2016, seven findings were higher than 0.1 μg L⁻¹. The highest detected concentration after the spring application was 0.63 μg metolachlor L⁻¹ in A10. Multiple-pesticide contaminations from 3 to 7 compounds were observed in the single LSWB whereas the number of contaminants increased from 2015 to 2016. The highest number of compounds was observed in A7 with 6 compounds in 2015 and 7 compounds in 2016. Due to their high uncertainty, the values of methyldesphenylchloridazone were not considered. Within the twelve compounds detected in concentrations higher than the LOQ, there are four herbicides, three fungicides, three insecticides and two TP of herbicides. Their properties vary concerning mobility and persistence in a broad range (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016;) so that inputs cannot be addressed to certain physicochemical characteristics. Considering the land use, none of these compounds had been applied in that year directly to the fields in which the LSWB were located as the crops grown there did not require them. However, in all cases these pesticides had been applied to the crops on either one of the neighbouring fields that year or in autumn/spring of the previous year to the LSWB field. Hence, the pesticide inputs may originate from these adjacent fields or former applications. Exemplarily, diflufenican is a herbicide which is applied in autumn and is part of a widely distributed product. In autumn 2015, this product was applied to field A7 (winter grain) so that the measured concentration in A7 in spring 2016 may result from that application. The same product was applied to A1, A3, A6 and A10 as well in 2015, but residues in July 2016 were not found. These results may lead to the assumption that A7 is more susceptible to pesticide inputs than the other LSWB of the study. The key results of the target screenings are that (i) metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethyltriazine were found in all LSWB and that (ii) the concentrations of the twelve compounds were lower in 2015 than in 2016. (i) Metolachlor and terbuthylazine are herbicides which are applied to corn. However, they were neither applied in 2015 nor in 2016 and often not for years to the fields of the ten LSWB. In most of the LSWB, the three compounds were detected in both years in background concentrations.01–0.03 μg L⁻¹. In 2016 in A10, 0.315 μg L⁻¹ terbuthylazine and 0.63 μg L⁻¹ metolachlor were found. Since a field with corn cultivation in 2016 is next to A10, it can be assumed that these concentrations are caused by the release from this field to A10. There were no further fields with corn cultivation close to the other LSWB which could explain the findings of terbuthylazine and metolachlor. Sandin et al. Lischeid et al. (2017) observed natural ponds to identify external drivers of their water quality. The results obtained reveal that size and location of the ponds' catchment is of crucial importance and that it is often related to shallow groundwater systems. Especially at small scale and without flowing water bodies, topography and groundwater levels are not sufficient for the delineation. Lischeid et al. (2017) showed that subsurface catchments of these LSWB can exceed sizes of 2 ha. In consequence, the residence time of dissolved compounds such as pesticides in subsurface flow can be high. Sandin et al. (2018) explained their findings of formerly applied pesticides by intermittent transport processes which relocate the pesticides to the subsoil where degradation is slower than in topsoil. In the subsoil, pesticides can be stored and slowly released so that they cause a signal over a long period. The results of these two studies explain that the corn-herbicide findings in our LSWB may originate via hydraulic subsurface connection and slow transport in the subsoil from former applications in larger distance.

(ii) To explain the concentration differences between the years, the amount and distribution of the precipitation from 1st April to 5th July were compared. The precipitation sum was 149 mm in 2015 and 299 mm in 2016 in 8 km distance, and 169 mm (2015) and 214 mm (2016) in 2–4 km distance. The overall amount of rainfall was clearly higher in 2016 than in 2015. The distribution shows higher rainfall amounts in April and June in 2016, but higher ones in May 2015. In general, the herbicides metolachlor and terbuthylazine are applied to corn in May while the fungicide tebuconazole is applied to rape in April/May and to grain from April to middle of June. The higher precipitation in 2016 caused a more frequent application of tebuconazole than in 2015: six of eight fields were sprayed in 2016, while in 2015, two of five fields were sprayed. Two rainfall events of 30–50 mm at the end of June 2016 may have caused enhanced relocation especially of metolachlor, tebuconazole and terbuthylazine. According to their properties (water solubility, log P, Kfoc, DT50 soil) (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016), they are assessed to be moderately mobile and moderately or non-persistent so that a higher potential for discharge cannot be derived. Hence, the combination of the rainfall pattern and the time of application may have caused the differences of pesticide findings in 2015 and 2016.

4.2. Analyses of metazachlor, flufenacet and their TPs in autumn samples 2015 and 2016

4.2.1. Transport and transformation of metazachlor in LSWB located in rape fields

Five LSWB were monitored in 2015 for metazachlor and its TP concentrations. Metazachlor was not detected in concentrations higher than LOQ before application (Fig. 6). After application, the maximum concentration amounted to 0.62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in A8 after the second rainfall event. The following observations were made: In all 5 LSWB, metazachlor concentrations were highest after the 1st rainfall event following the application. Over time, the concentrations decreased. We assessed this as prevalent patterns. However, the reduction of concentration varies between the LSWB from 20 to 90% from the first to the third sampling after application (47 days). Observations from two LSWB of a different study show metazachlor concentrations of 0,764–10.24 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) (LELF, 2014) considerably higher than those in our study with a maximum of 0,62 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\).

The metazachlor TPs were quantified in maximal concentration of up to 1.8 \( \mu \)g OA L\(^{-1}\) and 4.8 \( \mu \)g ESA L\(^{-1}\). Both TPs show the same patterns just vary in concentration: the concentrations increase overtime to the highest value in the third sample after application in A4, A5, A8. But in A2 and A9, the concentrations were at a constant value and did not change considerably. Metazachlor-ESA concentrations are in general higher than those of metazachlor-OA which can be explained by the ESA's higher occurrence fraction, a higher DT50 in soil and a very low k_foc displaying a very high mobility (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016). However, positives in the range of 0.49–4.2 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\) in the samples collected before application cannot be explained. The physicochemical properties, if available, do not predict this persistence. In addition, there was no application of metazachlor in the previous year 2014. This leads to the conclusion that either the TPs are very persistent and are still detectable two years later or transported from former applications at other sites to the LSWB below surface according to the assumptions of Lischeid et al. (2017).
