Life-cycle phenology of some aquatic insects: implications for pond conservation JÉRÔME CAYROU and RÉGIS CÉRÉGHINO* Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Hydrosystèmes, Université Paul Sabatier, Toulouse, France ABSTRACT 1. Life-cycles and growth patterns were determined for 21 dominant aquatic insect species in small permanent ponds in an arid, karstic region (SW France, site fr7300909 of the Natura 2000 conservation network). The species studied are widely distributed throughout Europe, but some life-cycle patterns are reported here for the first time. 2. The life-history patterns of the 21 species can be divided into five main types: (i) a semivoltine cycle spreading over 2 years; (ii) slow univoltine cycles; (iii) fast univoltine cycles; (iv) multivoltine life-cycles with a long winter generation and two or three summer generations per year; and (v) bivoltine life-cycles with two fast generations per year. Growth was either exponential over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or divided into two or three successive periods during each of which the growth rate was fairly constant. 3. Biodiversity estimates strongly depend on the temporal and spatial scale over which observations are made. Ponds thus provide useful models to show how life-history patterns enable many temporally segregated populations to utilize small ecosystems. Conservation frameworks should therefore carefully consider the time-frame needed to survey ponds, as many species with fast cycles could be overlooked. The spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats and thus preserve pond networks must be broadened, rather than attempting to target individual water bodies for particular management actions. Copyright © 2005 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. KEY WORDS: aquatic insects; wetlands; ponds; life-history; growth; temporal niche segregation; temperature; conservation INTRODUCTION The diversity of habitat types within wetlands allows them to be colonized by a wide range of specialist and generalist species (Masing et al., 2000). Wetlands are thus often considered as ‘hot spots’ of biodiversity within a region or a landscape (Gopal et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2004). However, wetlands and the biodiversity they support are threatened by human activity (e.g. agriculture, industry, urban development), though these ecosystems have significant ecological functions (Dugan, 1990) and recognized social and economic uses (Chapman et al., 2001). During the 20th century, wetland losses reached 40–90% in a number of north-western European countries (Hull, 1997), and in the United States more than 50% of these ecosystems have been destroyed by man (Tiner, 1984; Williams, 1990). Due to such large-scale habitat loss, many species are also endangered. This threat has prompted specific studies aimed at understanding the dynamics of wetland populations. Such an understanding is expected to help in planning conservation efforts such as the creation or restoration of ecosystems (Biggs et al., 1994). Although ponds have only recently started receiving some attention (Oertli, 1995; Hull, 1997; Angélbert et al., 2004), it is now well established that their management and conservation is closely linked to an understanding of the biodiversity and ecology of the biota they host (Gee et al., 1997; Gaston et al., 2005). Many of the models used to predict the consequences of future conservation strategies require life-history data (Rustigian et al., 2003). Therefore, information on the life-cycles of aquatic species is of fundamental importance for virtually all aspects of wetland conservation, including the conservation of ponds. Aquatic insects constitute an important part of animal production within wetlands (Oertli, 1993), and are tightly integrated into the structure and functioning of their habitats (e.g. organic matter processing, nutrient retention, food resources for vertebrates such as amphibians, fish, or birds). In a given area, the spatial and temporal variability of habitat types are key factors influencing the biodiversity of insect communities (Minshall, 1984; Hanquet et al., 2004), and are reflected in the ecological strategies and adaptation exhibited by species (Townsend, 1989; Townsend et al., 1997). In contrast to the large volume of studies in river ecology, very little research has addressed the population dynamics of pond insects. Most attention has instead been paid to patterns of biodiversity such as spatial variations in species richness (Oertli, 1995), or species diversity vs. area relationships (Oertli et al., 2002). Information on the life-history of pond insects is generally sparse, and usually available for a few, separately studied, species (e.g., Di Giovanni et al., 2000). However, there have been no previous attempts to gather – in a single investigation – detailed life-cycle and growth data on a large number of pond insects that are likely to coexist. Such an investigation would provide an overview of life-history traits and would consequently have significant implications for planning management and/or conservation actions in a particular area. In this investigation, the life-cycle phenologies, including growth patterns, of 21 aquatic insect species were determined in three small, permanent ponds in the arid, karstic region of the ‘Causses du Quercy’ (SW France). This area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and the results are discussed with reference to the implications for broader conservation strategies. STUDY AREA Located in south-western France, the ‘Causses du Quercy’ is a 2156 km\(^2\) limestone plateau. This arid area is affected by Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Continental climates, and this is reflected in its distinctive weather conditions and vegetation cover. The dominant plant species found in the area are *Quercus pubescens* Willd. and *Acer monspessulanum* L., while the moorland vegetation is principally composed of *Juniperus communis* L. The area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and is identified as site fr7300909. The plateau has no natural surface fresh water; however, it has more than 300 artificial ponds (typically permanent, rectangular in shape, and shallow, with a density of less than one pond per square kilometre). These ponds, bored into the calcareous rock, were created to hold rain water and support agricultural activities, and it is a technique that has been practised since the 12th century. Abandoned during the 1960s, the ponds are progressively filling with sediment and aquatic vegetation. Although they are now at various stages of natural succession, they support an aquatic vegetation community classified for conservation by the European Fauna-Flora-Habitat guideline 92/43/CEE: ‘22.12X22.44, oligo-mesotrophic calcareous waters with benthic vegetation of Characea’. This study was conducted from November 2000 to November 2001 in three such permanent ponds with a rocky substrate (hereafter called 1, 2 and 3). These three ponds are at different stages of natural succession; their main characteristics are shown in Table 1. A thorough study of their physical and chemical features (together with a fauna and flora species list) can be found in Angélibert et al. (2004). METHODS Sampling In each pond, samples were collected monthly from November 2000 to February 2001, then every 2 weeks from March to November 2001. Different techniques were used to obtain qualitative samples of aquatic insects within each pond. First, samples were randomly taken in each pond and at each sampling date by intensive sweeping of a hand net (mesh size = 250 μm) through the various habitats for 15–20 min. In order to maximize the number of available individuals on each sampling occasion, additional samples were specifically taken from the various substrate types (Table 1), each requiring a specific sampling technique (Oertli, 1993). Thin layers of mud (< 5 cm) deposited on the calcareous substrate and bryophytes were sampled using an air-lift sampler (Boulton, 1985) (sampling area 186 cm², mesh size of the net: 250 μm). Thick layers of mud (> 5 cm) were sampled using a plastic core sampler (sampling area: 28.2 cm²). Specific cores (40 cm high and 4.4 cm in diameter) were used to sample the submerged section of Typha stems. The aerial part of the plant was cut at water level, and the remaining submerged part was quickly enclosed in the core and cut at approximately 35 cm under the surface of the water. Chara beds at mid-depth were sampled by rapidly enclosing plants in a plastic box (7.5 × 16 × 11.5 cm). The Chara plants were then cut with shears.

Life-history and growth Twenty-one species were found in sufficient numbers throughout their developmental period to allow their life histories and growth patterns to be studied. All larvae were divided into size categories (0.1 mm) based either on head capsule width or tibia length of the third leg. Size–frequency plots for life-cycle determination were based on direct identification of larval instars (four species of Heteroptera, seven Coleoptera, five Diptera), or on head or tibia measurements when larval instars could not be easily identified (one species of Ephemeroptera, four Odonata). Sets of larvae (at least 10 individuals) from different size categories were dried at 60°C for 24 h and then weighed. Larval mean individual dry weights (\( W \), mg) were derived from linear regressions (\( \ln W = a + bL \) with 95% C.L.) between the natural log of weight (\( \ln W \)) and tibia length or head capsule width. Mean individual dry weights of cohorts from each site were natural log transformed to generate a series of subsegment linear regressions that represent a generation’s seasonal growth patterns over the year (see, for example, Figure 8). RESULTS Life-history patterns The life-history patterns of the 21 study species (Figures 1–7) can be divided into five main types. (1) The semivoltine life-cycle of Anax imperator began in summer (June–September). It lasted 2 years and ended in late spring (June). There was a large range of larval sizes throughout the year, with two overlapping generations. (2) Five species showed slow cycles with one generation per year. The eggs began to hatch in the spring (Coenagrion scitulum, Libellula depressa, Agabus nitidus, Haliplus lineatocollis) or late summer (Odontomyia ornata), and growth occurred over a long period (9–12 months) before spring or early summer emergences. (3) Ten species exhibited fast univoltine cycles (one generation per year), with hatching periods in late winter (Hygrotus inaequalis, Acilius sulcatus), spring (Chalcolestes viridis, Corixa punctata, Plea leachi, Hygrobia hermanni, Phaenobezzia sp.), or early summer (Haliplus mucronatus, Noterus clavicornis, Stratiomys potamida) with a short growth period (2–4 months), and were adult by spring, summer, or autumn. (4) Three species were multivoltine (two or three generations per year) with a long winter generation (September to May) and one (Culicoides sp., Dicrotendipes tritomus) or two (Cloeon dipterum) short summer generations (from July to August). It should be noted that two additional mayflies, Cloeon simile and Caenis luctuosa, occurred in pond 1 (but not in ponds 2 and 3). Their life-cycle patterns were previously described in Cayrou and Céréghino (2003): both species had a long winter and a short summer generation. (5) Two species were clearly bivoltine, with two short generations per year, i.e., in spring and summer (Naucoris maculatus), or both in spring (Notonecta maculata). DISCUSSION Compared with previous reports, some species seemed to exhibit flexible life histories. Cloeon dipterum occurs throughout much of Europe, and most authors have described univoltine and bivoltine (with a short summer generation) life-cycles (Clifford, 1982), whereas three generations per year were recorded in ponds 2 and 3 (see also Elliott et al., 1988). Libellula depressa was clearly univoltine in ponds 2 and 3. However, Di Giovanni et al. (2000) noted that Libellula depressa had a 2-yr life-cycle, although some more rapidly growing individuals were able to emerge after 1 yr. The data in the present study suggested that Anax imperator had a 2-yr life-cycle. However, in colder regions (e.g. Germany, United Kingdom), A. imperator shows larval cycles extending either over 1 or 2 yr (Corbet, 1955; Sternberg and Buchwald, 2000), even at a given locality (which remains likely in our study area). Corixa punctata is mostly univoltine, but a second generation was observed by Papáček and Bohoněk (1989). According to Svensson et al. (2000), Notonecta maculata has one generation per year in Sweden, with adult emergence in August (compared with two generations per year and emergence from May to July in this study). Acilius sulcatus grew from February to June in pond 2 (this study), but from May to June in Wisconsin, USA (Hilsenhoff, 1993). Finally, previously undescribed life-cycle and growth patterns were detailed for the following species: Naucoris maculatus, Haliplus lineatocollis, Haliplus mucronatus, Hygrotus inaequalis, Noterus clavicornis, Odontomyia ornata, Stratiomys potamida, Dicrotendipes tritomus – thus contributing further to an understanding of the population dynamics of wetland insects. As wetland habitats, ponds have only recently started receiving some attention, and most of the current research still focuses on assessing the biodiversity they support (Briers and Biggs, 2003; Angélbert et al., 2004) or are likely to host (Davies et al., 2004; Gaston et al., 2005). Among wetland inhabitants, aquatic insects have the potential to be relevant ecological indicators. Indeed, they are already widely used to reveal short- and long-term environmental changes in both running and still waters (Céréghino et al., 2003; Verneaux et al., 2004), most notably through the strong influence of human disturbance on the species richness of aquatic insects (Rosenberg and Resh, 1993). Such disturbances usually lead to losses of taxa (Compin and Céréghino, 2003). However, in a given area, biodiversity estimates (e.g. species richness, evenness, etc.) strongly depend on the spatial scale (type of habitat) and temporal scale (week, month, or season) over which observations are made. Water temperature is usually considered to be the major abiotic factor affecting the life-cycle phenology of aquatic invertebrates (Vannote and Sweeney, 1980; Sweeney et al., 1986), influencing the seasonality and development patterns of aquatic insects through growth, adult size, and fecundity (Lavandier, 1988; Giberson and Rosenberg, 1992; Pritchard and Zloty, 1994). This study suggested that the increased growth of those species with long generations (e.g., Cloeon dipterum) seemed to correspond to the rise in water temperature in spring (March), and that the warmest period (spring–summer) favoured the hatching and rapid development of short summer generations in most species. Whatever the biotic and/or abiotic factors controlling the life-cycle phenologies, and, subsequently, the temporal patterns of aquatic insect communities within ponds, this study clearly emphasizes the temporal dimension of biodiversity in small bodies of water. The seasonality of wetland-dependent insects in particular may influence the biodiversity ponds may support. Similar recommendations are already part of protocols for sampling and assessment of both riverine and wetland habitats, e.g. RIVPACS sampling for rivers (Wright et al., 2000), and UK National Pond Survey methods (Pond Action, 1989). Life-cycle attributes (e.g., reproduction, hatching and emergence periods) need to be carefully considered when restoring, managing and/or creating new ponds for conservation purposes (Ripley et al., 2004). Owing to the difficulty of pond creation in the study area (a limestone plateau), dredging the abandoned ponds is the only option for wetland restoration. Therefore, environmental managers should minimize the likelihood that dredging will eliminate populations (e.g., during the main growth or hatching periods). Theoretically, the acceptable period for dredging would be between adult emergence and egg-laying, i.e. during the flight and reproduction period. Given that most populations show a temporal sequence of species replacements (e.g. certain Coleoptera, Heteroptera), or have delayed life-cycle events (certain Odonata), defining an optimal period for dredging seems to be an impossible task. As an alternative, a plan of pond management should be envisaged over a large spatial scale to maintain the heterogeneity of pond networks in the area. Such a plan would imply promoting the conservation of all ponds, regardless of their successional stages. This is especially important when the density of ponds in the network is very sparse. Indeed, a recent study in the same area (Angélibert and Giani, 2003) on the dispersal capability of Odonata showed that dispersal phenomena were low because of the distance separating ponds. Thus, after dredging, species adapted to late succession ponds have little hope of finding suitable conditions in other ponds to ensure their development. Broader conservation strategies should therefore ensure that such currently common organisms do not become the endangered species of the future (Rustigian et al., 2003). Ponds also provide useful models for studying how life-history patterns enable many populations to utilize small ecosystems, temporal segregation and/or differences in the size of coexisting nymphs certainly reducing interspecific competition for food and habitat resources (Svensson et al., 2000; Cayrou and Céréghino, 2003). Subsequently, interesting ideas and/or alternative strategies can be derived for conservation planning. Because the growth of most species is markedly seasonal and many species are temporally segregated, the spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats must be enlarged. Thus, when possible, pond networks should primarily be preserved rather than attempting to target some bodies of water for particular management actions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We wish to thank N. METHODS Sampling In each pond, samples were collected monthly from November 2000 to February 2001, then every 2 weeks from March to November 2001. Different techniques were used to obtain qualitative samples of aquatic insects within each pond. First, samples were randomly taken in each pond and at each sampling date by intensive sweeping of a hand net (mesh size = 250 μm) through the various habitats for 15–20 min. In order to maximize the number of available individuals on each sampling occasion, additional samples were specifically taken from the various substrate types (Table 1), each requiring a specific sampling technique (Oertli, 1993). Thin layers of mud (< 5 cm) deposited on the calcareous substrate and bryophytes were sampled using an air-lift sampler (Boulton, 1985) (sampling area 186 cm², mesh size of the net: 250 μm). Thick layers of mud (> 5 cm) were sampled using a plastic core sampler (sampling area: 28.2 cm²). Specific cores (40 cm high and 4.4 cm in diameter) were used to sample the submerged section of Typha stems. The aerial part of the plant was cut at water level, and the remaining submerged part was quickly enclosed in the core and cut at approximately 35 cm under the surface of the water. Chara beds at mid-depth were sampled by rapidly enclosing plants in a plastic box (7.5 × 16 × 11.5 cm). The Chara plants were then cut with shears.

Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). 550 L. Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Springer Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in 552 L. E. Mosscrop et al. DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first ($\lambda = 0.36$) and second ($\lambda = 0.21$) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO$_4$, and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability.

Site codes (left panel) are found in Table 1, and species codes (right panel) are found in Table 2. For plotting purposes, the environmental vectors have been multiplied by factors of 2 and 0.5 for the sites and species biplots, respectively For example, despite being shallow, some of the study lakes were stratified at the time of sampling (mid-summer), with observed differences in water temperature of more than 10 °C across the water column (Mossocrop 2013). Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Specifically, decreases in the relative abundance of pelagic, Daphnia Fig. 5 Comparison of the relative abundances of the dominant cladoceran taxa in modern and pre-industrial sediments from 26 lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Modern and pre-industrial cladoceran relative abundances are shown as solid and open bars, respectively spp. that require more Ca were related to declines in lake water Ca concentrations, a finding supported by laboratory evidence (Ashforth and Yan 2008), field data (Cairns 2010), and other paleoecological studies in the Muskoka-Haliburton region (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2012a, b). Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Thus, while it is possible that climate may be an important factor influencing cladocerans in some lakes, we believe that it has played a less important role than long-term ![Boxplots comparing deep and shallow values for various water quality parameters: NO3/NO2, TP, Ca, Mg, SO4, spec. conductance, pH, DOC, surface area, and maximum depth.](page_0_0_2048_2048.png) Fig. 6 Box plots comparing ten physical or chemical variables in 30 shallow (this study) and 41 deeper (DeSellas et al. 2008) lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes Springer in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Springer

Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 446 Anne-Mette Jespersen and Kirsten Christoffersen 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 µE m⁻² s⁻¹. The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used.

All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction.

To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts.

To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. As a consequence, it is suggested that interference from chlorophyll-b in ethanol extracts may be ignored when chlorophyll-a is determined from phytoplankton. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested.
