The biomass of instar \( i \) (\( B_i \)) was determined as indicated previously. Following Cressa and Lewis (1986), we calculated \( C_i \) as \[ C_i = (R_i + G_i)/\mathrm{AE}_i, \] where \( R_i \) and \( G_i \) are respiration and growth of the \( i \)th instar, and \( \mathrm{AE}_i \) its assimilation efficiency, the last term accounting for fecal output. Estimation of R, G, and AE Invertebrate respiration rates are principally a function of animal activity, size, and temperature (Lampert 1984). We ignored the respiratory cost of the daily migration of \( C. punctipennis \). It is a minor component of the energy budget of Chaoborus in shallow lakes such as Swan Lake (Giguère and Dill 1980). At constant temperature, whole animal respiratory rates may be represented as a power function of animal mass (\( M \)), i.e., \( R = aM^b \). The constants \( a \) and \( b \) are obtained by linear regression fit to the log-transformed, mass-specific version of the equation: \[ \log(R/M) = \log a + (b - 1)\log M. \] Respiratory rates of all four larval Chaoborus instars have been measured only for the tropical species \( C. brasiliensis \) (Cressa and Lewis 1986). Fortunately, this is a small species similar in size to \( C. punctipennis \), the dominant species in Swan Lake. Therefore, we solved Eq. 3 using Cressa and Lewis' reported mean values for each instar of \( C. brasiliensis \) (their Table 2), and used the resulting model (Eq. 4) to calculate larval Chaoborus respiration (in microlitres \( O_2 \) per milligram larvae per hour) at 26\( ^\circ \)C, Cressa and Lewis' exposure temperature: \[ \log(R/M) = -0.11 - 0.33 \log M \quad (r^2 = 1.00). \] Estimates of respiration at 26\( ^\circ \) were then corrected to the in situ temperature of exposure (\( T \)) in Swan Lake by use of a multiplication factor (\( 0.0768 e^{0.10227T} \)) fit to Krogh's normal curve (Lampert 1984: 451). By example, this correction has the effect of reducing mass-specific respiration by a factor of \( \approx 5 \) with a drop in temperature from 25\( ^\circ \) to 10\( ^\circ \), a change in agreement with the measured temperature dependence of respiration in \( C. trivittatus \) (Swift 1976). The temperature of exposure (\( T \)) was taken to be the volume-weighted mean lake temperature calculated from lake morphometry and temperature profiles (Fig. 2) for first- and second-instar \( C. punctipennis \) and all \( C. americanus \) larvae. It was always within 2\( ^\circ \) and usually within 1\( ^\circ \) of the epilimnetic temperature. We calculated \( T \) for third- and fourth-instar \( C. punctipennis \) on the assumption that they occupied the epilimnion at night and the hypolimnetic waters and sediments during the day. This distribution was confirmed on one occasion. Finally, consumption of oxygen was converted to consumption of prey biomass assuming that 1 mL \( O_2 = 0.536 \) mg C at a respiratory quotient of 1 (Lampert 1984), and that carbon comprises 47.3% of prey dry mass (Hall and Likens 1981). Although Sigmon et al. (1978) have measured respiration of \( C. punctipennis \), the dominant species in Swan Lake, we did not use their respiration values because they were unusually high. This was perhaps a consequence of their measurement of respiration of crowded larvae, \( \approx 350 \) fourth-instar animals per litre. ![Isotherm diagram for Swan Lake in 1983. Growth (\( G \)) of instars I–III of C. punctipennis was calculated as the exponential rate of increase in mass required to attain the observed mean mass of each instar at stations 1–3 (Fig. 3) over its development time (\( D_i \)). \( D_i \) was calculated from the temporal centers of mass, i.e., the abundance-weighted mean dates of occurrence (\( t_i \)), of each instar at stations 1–3. Lewis’s (1979: 51–53) methods were used to calculate \( t_i \) and, hence, \( D_i \). To calculate \( G \) for fourth-instar C. punctipennis, we assumed growth was 0 before 8 August 1983 because mean mass never increased prior to that date (Fig. 3). Growth of fourth-instar C. americanus was estimated in a similar way, but only when enough animals were captured that their abundance was reliably estimated, i.e., after 23 August 1983. Reported assimilation efficiencies (AE) for Chaoborus range from 0.52 to 0.91 (Cressa and Lewis 1986) and vary with larval development, prey type, and meal volume (Giguère 1981, Cressa and Lewis 1986). Values have not been determined for C. punctipennis or C. americanus. Because interpretation of our consumption data was not influenced by the choice of AE values spanning the range reported in the literature, we used Swift’s (1976) value of 0.67, for compatibility with Elser et al. (1987). First-order error analysis (Carpenter 1984) was used to calculate 95% confidence intervals in consumption from errors in estimates of larval Chaoborus growth and respiration. Variance in production of prey should be calculated from errors in estimates of prey biomass and birth rates. Because we pooled zooplankton samples from the three stations prior to enumeration, we estimated errors in production from errors in estimated birth rates alone (calculated following DeMott 1980). Therefore, the estimated errors for consumption of prey by Chaoborus and production of the prey should be considered minima, the former because they were calculated by error propagation, the latter because the contribution of spatial variation in prey biomass was not considered. RESULTS Plankton community structure The phytoplankton community of Swan Lake was very simple. Green algae, principally Oocystis parva West and West, were the dominant taxa in the early summer of 1983. Dinoflagellates, especially Peridinium inconspicuum and a large (30 \( \mu \)m diameter), spherical, unidentified Gymnodinium, formed virtually all of the biomass for much of the rest of the year. There was a large bloom of the chrysophyte Dinobryon bavaricum in November (Fig. 4). The zooplankton community was simple and unusual. The biomass of planktonic Rotifera was, on average, an order of magnitude higher than that of Crustacea (Fig. 4). Polyarthra spp. and Keratella tau-rocephala were the dominant rotifers, although the abundance of the latter species was much reduced from 1977 when the lake was more acidic (MacIsaac et al. 1986). Trichocerca similis was also very abundant (averaging 107 animals/L), but because of its small size (Table 1) it contributed little to total rotifer biomass. The small, acid-tolerant, herbivorous cladoceran Bosmina longirostris was the dominant crustacean zooplankter. Its biomass was quite variable. Maximum values were observed in the early spring (Fig. 4), an unusual time in a temperate lake. Daphnia spp. and Holopedium gibberum were absent from the lake. This is typical of acid and metal-contaminated lakes near Sudbury (Yan and Strus 1980), and is probably a direct consequence of the acid sensitivity of Daphnia (Keller et al. 1990) and the metal sensitivity of H. gibberum (Lawrence and Holoka 1987). The ubiquitous calanoid copepod Diaptomus minutus was present, although its contribution to total biomass was negligible. Orthocyclops modestus was the only cyclopoid copepod observed in the lake (Fig. 4). Phytoplankton, rotifer, and crustacean assemblages observed in 1983 were similar to those observed in 1982 and 1984 (W. Keller, H. J. MacIsaac, and N. D. Yan, personal observations). There were an average of 0.19 Chaoborus punctipennis/L and 0.009 C. americanus/L during the ice-free season of 1983. Monthly samples collected in 1982 produced somewhat higher average densities of 0.49 and 0.04 larvae/L, respectively. The seasonal patterns of abundance of C. punctipennis were similar at the Fig. 4. Adults emerged over the entire summer with peak emergence during July and August. The substantial decline in the measured planktonic abundance of \( C. punctipennis \) in the fall is most likely attributable to the failure of the larvae to migrate into the water column at that time of year (Wood 1956). Abundances of the early instars of \( C. americanus \) were clearly underestimated (Fig. 4). We assumed they must have inhabited either extremely shallow waters or the relatively large areas of the lake we did not sample (Fig. 1). Rotifers contributed a remarkable 62% of the average zooplankton biomass (including Chaoborus) during the ice-free season in Swan Lake in 1983. Chaoborus larvae contributed 32%, and crustacean zooplankton the remaining small fraction (6%) of the total biomass (Fig. 4). The Crustacea : Chaoborus ratios are not unusual for acid lakes in Canada supporting populations of \( C. americanus \) (N. D. Yan, personal observation). Chaoborus diet The relative numbers of organisms identified in the crops of \( C. punctipennis \) changed both within and among developmental stages. Excluding algae, the crops of first-instar animals contained only rotifers, and those of second-instar animals contained little but rotifers (Fig. 6). The relative abundance of \( K. taurocephala \) in the crops increased with larval stage. In contrast, the importance of the smaller Trichocerca sp. in the diet declined in older larvae. \( B. longirostris \) was virtually the only crustacean zooplankter consumed. It formed roughly 30% of animals encountered in the crops of third-instar and young fourth-instar larvae, but the older fourth-instar larvae, those captured in the spring and late fall, fed almost exclusively on \( B. longirostris \) (Fig. 6). DISCUSSION Chaoborus diet While identification of the prey of Chaoborus was not the major objective of this study, such information is rare enough for the widely distributed C. punctipennis that some discussion of its crop contents is warranted. In midsummer collections from Post Pond, New Hampshire, Moore (1988) recorded a diet of C. punctipennis remarkably similar to that observed in Swan Lake animals. She observed large algae and rotifers in the crops of all instars. The contribution of rotifers to total crop biomass declined monotonically with increases in larval development, as in Swan Lake. Crustacea, including B. longirostris, were only observed in III- and IV-instar larvae, as in Swan Lake. In summary, it is clear that C. punctipennis from Swan Lake can maintain a diet resembling that of a nonacidic lake despite the impoverishment of the plankton assemblages of the lake. Dinoflagellates were observed in the crops of many young C. punctipennis in Swan Lake. While it has generally been assumed that Chaoborus is zooplanktivorous, it is now clear that large algae, dinoflagellates in particular, may often be important in the diet of small Chaoborus species such as C. punctipennis (Elser et al. 1987, Hare and Carter 1987, Moore 1988). Early Chaoborus instar mortality is usually very high in oligotrophic lakes (Neill and Peacock 1980). Dinoflagellates, particularly *Peridinium limbatum* and *Peridinium inconspicuum* commonly dominate the phytoplankton of acidified, north-temperate lakes (Fig. 4; Stokes 1986). *Impact of Chaoborus predation on zooplankton* There is no doubt that *Chaoborus* can dramatically alter zooplankton community structure and standing stocks in nutrient-rich lakes in the absence of fish. A large proportion of early-instar larvae survive because food is plentiful (Neill and Peacock 1980), and older larvae prosper in the absence of predation from fish. The resulting large *Chaoborus* populations can decimate a zooplankton community (Lynch 1979, Neill and Peacock 1980, Yan et al. 1982). Predation by *Chaoborus* may also be important in oligotrophic lakes in the absence of fish (Dodson 1972, Vanni 1988); however, Neill (1981) indicated that the zooplankton community structure of a fish-free, oligotrophic lake in western Canada was rarely influenced by resident *Chaoborus* populations. Therefore, the absence of fish from oligotrophic lakes does not guarantee that zooplankton community structure will be regulated by *Chaoborus*. The evidence supporting the hypothesis that *Chaoborus* regulate zooplankton community structure in acidified lakes is actually quite weak. While Nyman et al. (1985) purported to test the hypothesis, their experiment was not performed in an acidic lake, and it was of unrealistically short duration (3 d). Yan et al. (1982) showed that *Chaoborus* regulated zooplankton community structure and biomass in an acidic lake after it was fertilized, but fertilization produced such unusually large populations of *Chaoborus* that the data set is of limited use. Stenson and Oscarson (1985) argued that the biotic changes that followed the additions of rotenone to a nonacidic lake (Stenson et al. 1978) provided support for the hypothesis. However, there is no reason why community changes induced by the addition of rotenone to nonacidified lakes must match those changes accompanying the acidification of lakes. Nyberg (1984) attempted the only previous quantification of the impacts of predation by *Chaoborus* on the zooplankton of lakes acidified by atmospheric deposition of strong acid. Prior to the addition of neutralizing agents and fish to Lakes Iglafallssjön and Blanksjön in Sweden, Nyberg estimated consumption rates of third- and fourth-instar *Chaoborus* larvae using Kajak and Rybak's (1979) methods. Our Swan Lake analyses indicate that consumption from these instars should approximate total consumption (Fig. 8). Nyberg concluded that, from May to October, *Chaoborus* predation exceeded prey production in the former but not the latter lake, prior to treatment. Because he recorded an average of only 0.033 *Chaoborus*/L in Iglafallssjön over the time period, while there were an average of 0.154 larvae/L of the same developmental stages in Swan Lake (calculated from Fig. 5), we should not be surprised if *Chaoborus* influence zooplankton community structure in Swan Lake. The Swan Lake analyses suggest that *Chaoborus* regulated the abundance of *B. longirostris* in Swan Lake for much of the ice-free season of 1983 (Fig. 9). Further, a comparison of loss rates of Crustacea to *Chaoborus* (\( L \) in Fig. 10) with published production/biomass (\( P/B \)) ratios of the planktonic Crustacea of lakes of nutrient status comparable with Swan Lake suggests *Chaoborus* probably maintain the unusually small crustacean zooplankton biomass in the lake. For example, Makarewicz and Likens (1979) reported daily \( P/B \) values for crustacean zooplankton of 0.04, 0.04, 0.05, and 0.06 for Mirror Lake, Lakes 239, Clear, and Naroch, respectively. Values of \( L \) in Swan Lake exceeded these values on all but the first visit to the lake (Fig. 10). While all *Chaoborus* instars consumed rotifers, the abundance of *K. taurocephala*, the favored rotifer prey, was apparently not regulated by *Chaoborus* (Fig. 9). Further, it is unlikely that *Chaoborus* predation controlled total rotifer biomass. Estimated daily rates of loss of rotifer biomass to *Chaoborus* never exceeded 0.1 and were frequently <0.01 (Fig. 10). In contrast, Makarewicz and Likens (1979) recorded much higher average daily \( P/B \) ratios of planktonic rotifers in oligotrophic lakes, e.g., 0.11 in Mirror Lake and 0.35–0.37 in Clear Lake and Lake 239. The validity of these conclusions hinges largely on the accuracy and precision of the estimated consumption rates, which in turn depend on the estimates of growth, respiration, and assimilation, and on the identification of *Chaoborus* prey. Our choice of assimilation efficiency is not worrisome, because the differences be- tween consumption and production rates were generally so large (Fig. 9), that a selection of values covering the published range for nonsatiated larvae (0.6–0.9) did not alter our conclusions. We cannot verify the accuracy of our respiration estimates because the influence of temperature and stage of development on the respiration of C. punctipennis has not been determined. Nonetheless, because the value of \( b \) in Eq. 3 (0.67, \( b - 1 = -0.33 \)) lies satisfyingly near the midpoint of the range of values reported for aquatic invertebrates (0.52–0.88, Lampert 1984), we do not think our respiration estimates bias our conclusions. In contrast, the consumption estimates of Rotifera and Crustacea are biased to high values by our failure to include consumption of algae in the calculations. Because Elser et al. (1987) and Moore (1988) observed that algae contributed an average of only \( \approx 10\% \) of the biomass of the crop contents of third- and fourth-instar C. punctipennis, we think the magnitude of this bias is probably small. Our estimates of Chaoborus growth are the most worrisome component of the calculations. The problem is not that the estimated rates of growth (Table 3) are impossibly high. From Pawson and McEachern’s (1987) length-mass relationships of Chaoborus flavicans and Hanazato and Yasuno’s (1989) reported body lengths and development times of this species cultured at saturating food conditions, we estimate that the mass of instar II and III C. flavicans can increase at 50–60%/d at 20°C, growth rates comparable with subtropical larval chironomids (Stites and Benke 1989). Clearly, Chaoborus can grow at rates exceeding those we calculated in Swan Lake (Table 3). Indeed, our estimates of growth of C. punctipennis in Swan Lake may be too low, because our weakest assumption was that C. punctipennis was univoltine (Fig. 5). While the species is usually univoltine at north-temperate latitudes (Hilsehnoff and Narf 1968, Carter and Kwik 1977, von Ende 1982, Sardella and Carter 1983), a bivoltine population has been described (Miller 1941). Our assumption of univoltinity produces conservative estimates of larval growth. Therefore, potential consumption rates of Crustacea may actually be higher than indicated in Fig. 9. It would clearly be useful to have laboratory measurements of both growth and respiration of C. punctipennis. Yan and Geiling (1985) suggested that the unusually high biomass of rotifers observed in Swan Lake in 1977, might be attributable to an abundant food supply linked to unusually low densities of crustacean competitors. Hurlbert and Mulla (1981), Neill (1984), and MacIsaac and Gilbert (1989) provide strong experimental support for such an hypothesis. However, Yan and Geiling could not explain the unusually low crustacean zooplankton biomass in the lake. The results presented herein indicate that predation by Chaoborus can account for the currently low crustacean zooplankton biomass of Swan Lake. In this report, we wished to investigate not the frequency with which Chaoborus regulate zooplankton community structure in acidified lakes, but the possibility of such regulation. Therefore, we selected a study lake we thought likely to show the effect, a mesotrophic, acidic lake with abundant Chaoborus. Apparently Chaoborus do not have much impact on zooplankton community structure in north-temperate lakes at abundances <30–50 individuals/m³ (Allan 1973, Nyberg 1984). Chaoborus abundance was lower than this threshold in four of five fish-less, acidified lakes (the exception being Swan Lake) surveyed by Yan et al. (1985). Therefore, while we support Nyberg’s (1984) demonstration that Chaoborus can regulate community structure in acidified lakes, an assessment of the frequency of occurrence of such control must await the assessment of Chaoborus population size in many more acidified lakes. Investigators planning such surveys should consider both presence of fish and lake nutrient status during lake selection, because both influence the abundance of Chaoborus (Neill and Peacock 1980, Yan et al. 1985). Further, such surveys should not be focused solely on the nonmigratory species of Chaoborus that are more sensitive to fish predation. In Swan Lake and in Nyberg’s Lake Iglafallssjön, the species of Chaoborus that were the major zooplanktivores were C. punctipennis and C. flavicans, respectively. Both are migratory species (Borkent 1981). Many of the biological changes that accompany the acidification of lakes are directly attributable to the toxicity of acid lake waters (Holtze and Hutchinson 1989, Keller et al. 1990). However, there is increasing evidence that other changes may be indirectly related to habitat acidification (reviewed by Stenson and Eriksson 1989). Examples of indirect agents of community change include alterations in lake thermal regimes (Yan 1983), reductions in nutrient supply (Jansson et al. 1986), increased prevalence of parasites (France and Graham 1985), and alterations in magnitude and type of competitive (Eriksson 1979) and predatory (Stenson and Eriksson 1989) pressures. In this report we have provided quantitative support for a biological change accompanying acidification that has an indirect cause, unusual zooplankton community structure maintained by invertebrate predation. DESCRIPTION OF SWAN LAKE

Many lakes located near Sudbury, Ontario, are acidic and contaminated with trace metals attributable to emissions of SO_2 and metals into the atmosphere from local Cu and Ni smelters (Conroy et al. 1976). Swan Lake (46°22' N, 81°04' W) is a small (area 5.8 ha), shallow (mean depth 2.8 m, maximum depth 8.8 m), lake located 13 km south of Sudbury (Fig. 1). In the mid-1970s, the lake was very acidic (pH 3.97). Metal levels were elevated (Cu 64 \( \mu \)g/L, Ni 301 \( \mu \)g/L; MacIsaac et al. 1986), and the lake supported no fish (Yan and Miller 1984). Recently, the water quality of many lakes in the Sudbury area has improved in response to reductions in emissions from local smelters (Keller and Pitblado 1986). The average pH, Cu and Ni levels of Swan Lake had improved to 5.0, 12, and 80 \( \mu \)g/L, respectively, by 1983 (MacIsaac et al. 1986). Despite these improvements the lake still supports no fish (W. Keller and J. M. Gunn, personal observations).

Yan et al. (1985) recorded large populations of both C. americanus and C. punctipennis in Swan Lake in 1982. They attributed the presence of C. americanus to the lack of fish, but the size of the populations to the nutrient status of the lake. Total phosphorus (TP) concentrations in the lake averaged 10–12 \( \mu \)g/L in 1977 and from 1982 to 1983 (MacIsaac et al. 1986). Most clear-water, acidified lakes in Ontario have lower TP levels (<5 \( \mu \)g/L, Yan et al. 1985).

METHODS

Plankton community description

We measured water temperatures at 1-m intervals of depth, collected water samples for chemical analyses and collected phytoplankton, zooplankton, and Chaoborus from Swan Lake every 2 wk in 1983. Phytoplankton samples were collected using a Van Dorn bottle at station 2 (Fig. 1) at 1-m intervals from 0.5 m to a depth equivalent to twice the Secchi transparency. A composite sample corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth was generated, preserved with a Lugol’s iodine solution, and saved for subsequent analysis. To match the earlier sampling methods of Yan and Geiling (1985), planktonic Rotifera and Crustacea were collected at depths of 1 and 4 m at stations 1 and 3, and at 1, 4, and 7 m at station 2 (Fig. 1) with a 31.9-L plexiglass trap (Schindler 1969) equipped with 30-\( \mu \)m mesh. Trap hauls collected from the same depth at the three stations were combined prior to enumeration.

In a preliminary survey, abundances of C. punctipennis in the plankton were much greater at night than during the day; therefore, Chaoborus were routinely collected between 0.5 and 2 h after sunset. Samples were taken at five stations (Fig. 1) in single-to-multiple vertical hauls, depending on animal density, from 1 m above bottom to the surface with a 30 cm diameter, 153-\( \mu \)m mesh conical tow net with a 3:1 length-to-mouth diameter ratio. A capture efficiency of 80% was applied to all Chaoborus data. This correction was the mean (range of 55–100% for all larvae) of six comparisons of net vs. plexiglass trap collections, the latter assumed to capture Chaoborus with 100% efficiency, conducted in May and August 1983. Zooplankton and Chaoborus samples were preserved with 4% sugar-formalin.

Nicholls and Carney (1979) and MacIsaac et al. (1987) describe the methods employed for enumeration of phytoplankton and rotifer samples, respectively. Rotifer biomass was subsequently calculated using individual masses listed in Table 1. Crustacea and Chaoborus were enumerated and their sizes simultaneously determined using electronic callipers (Sprules et al. 1981). Chaoborus were identified following Sæther (1972). Head capsule lengths were used to separate larval Chaoborus instars (Yan et al. 1982, Lasenby et al. 1986). Animal masses were calculated from body lengths using the regressions of McCauley (1984) for Crustacea and Yan et al. (1982) and Pawson and McEachern (1987) for Chaoborus. Depth-integrated estimates of the biomass of planktonic Rotifera and Crustacea were calculated by weighting the 1-, 4-, and 7-m data for diminution of lake volume with depth.

Birth rates of Bosmina longirostris (O.F. Müller) and Keratella taurocephala (Myers) were calculated for reasons outlined below (Methods: Estimation of prey production and Chaoborus predation). To ensure accuracy in their determination, we enumerated an average of 92 B. longirostris, 36% of which were gravid, and an average of 113 K. taurocephala, 19% of which were gravid, from each of the 1-, 4-, and 7-m samples.

Estimation of prey production and Chaoborus predation

When measured in small enclosures, estimates of prey consumption by aquatic macroinvertebrate predators may often be biased toward low values (Lewis 1979, O’Brien 1988). Therefore, we employed the literature on Chaoborus bioenergetics (Swift 1976, Giguère 1980, 1981, Cressa and Lewis 1986) to provide indirect but, we hope, unbiased estimates of losses of zooplankton to Chaoborus. We calculated potential rates of consumption of prey by Chaoborus larvae from estimates of Chaoborus biomass, respiration, growth, and assimilation. Then we apportioned consumption among prey species based on their contribution by mass to larval crop contents. Finally, estimated consumption rates were compared with estimated rates of prey production. Similar approaches have been successfully employed to examine impacts of larval Chaoborus on zooplankton in a tropical lake (Saunders and Lewis 1988) and in north temperate lakes with manipulated food webs (Elser et al. 1987).

Box 27 (Viikki, C), FIN-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland, Finnish Game and Fisheries Research Institute, Evo Game Research Station, Kaitalammintie 75, FIN-16970 Evo, Finland and Department of Animal Ecology, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, S-901 83 Umeå, Sweden Abstract. Breeding waterfowl, habitat diversity and food diversity were studied in 31 boreal lakes in Finland and Sweden. Lakes were 2–48 hectares in size, and had zero to eleven waterfowl species each. In all, sixteen species of Gaviiformes, Podicipediformes, Anseriformes and Fulica were recorded. The observed species distribution deviated from the ‘null’ expectation derived from a model of random placement, indicating a low importance of lake area per se. However, lake area was found to be a better predictor of species number than was length of shoreline, and lake area–species number regressions gave values between 0.255 and 0.345. We further evaluated ‘the area per se (sampling)’ hypothesis and ‘habitat diversity’ hypothesis separately by multiple stepwise regressions, in which lake area explained most of the variation in species number in species dependent on the lake for brood-rearing. Richness of more mobile species and of all species was best explained by the number of prey taxa encountered in the lake. Key words. Sampling hypothesis, habitat diversity hypothesis, island biogeography, waterfowl, lake area. INTRODUCTION Among other early workers, Palmgren (1930) made the observation that big survey areas generally support more bird species than small (see Coleman, et al., 1982, and Ås, Bengtsson & Ebenhard, 1992, for further examples). Palmgren also discussed the processes behind the pattern, explicitly in the context of adaptation to edaphic factors and interspecific competition, and implicitly in relation to habitat heterogeneity. The topic was later treated within a more rigid and unified theoretical framework by MacArthur & Wilson (1967), who used archipelagos as a model system, and who theorized that colonization-extinction dynamics is the process behind the pattern. One of the disputed questions of island biogeography is whether there is an ‘island size effect’ as such, or whether big islands support more species than small islands simply because they have a greater diversity of habitats (Abbott, 1978 v. Tonn & Magnuson, 1982; Williamson, 1981; Price, 1984; Blake & Karr, 1987; reviews in Begon, Harper & Townsend, 1990, and Ås et al., 1992). With special reference to birds, which are good dispersers, Lack (1976) argued that habitat heterogeneity is crucial as to whether a species will become established on an island or not. Williamson (1981), Coleman et al., (1982) and Haila (1983), among others, have discussed shortcomings of the theory of island biogeography. Nevertheless, it has proven to be of immense heuristic value, and it is now being widely applied in conservation biology and in management of biodiversity (e.g. Harris, 1984; Hansson, 1992; but see Ashton, 1992, for a review of competing paradigms in plant ecology). As Haila (1983) and Wiens (1989) have pointed out, there are still relatively few studies of species number–island area relationships in birds which include direct measurements of several aspects of habitat diversity. In this paper we examine patterns of species richness in breeding assemblages of migratory waterfowl in North Europe in relation to characteristics of lake size, habitat diversity and food diversity. After testing the observed pattern of species richness against a null model of random placement (cf. Coleman et al., 1982; Möller, 1987) we evaluate alternative predictions supposed to operate in ecological time, namely that species number increases with the following. 76 Johan Elmberg et al. Sampling When not given here, the dates and details of the methods are the same as in Elmberg et al. (1993). In brief, we did the following. All field data were gathered with identical methods in 1990 (Västerbotten, Häme and Karjala) and 1991 (Lappi). For the justification of using data from 2 years, see Elmberg et al. (1993). Many of the species in this study place their nest on land. In some of them, adults as well as broods forage mainly in shallow water along the shore. Therefore it can be argued whether the appropriate measure of 'island area' is the lake's area or the length of its shoreline. Hence, we estimated both from topographical maps (scale 1:10,000 in Sweden, and 1:20,000 in Finland). We used the point count method of Koskimies & Väisänen (1991) to census waterfowl, i.e. all Gaviiformes, Podicipediformes, Anseriformes, and coot (Fulica atra L.). This was done four times in the early part of the breeding season, when pairs had arrived on the lakes and breeding had started. The total number of species recorded in a lake is here referred to as 'all waterfowl'. However, it is a heterogeneous group, comprising species with different food preferences. Our method of sampling invertebrates (see below and Elmberg et al., 1992) well reflects the availability of food preferred by dabbling ducks (genus Anas), some diving ducks (genera Aythya and Bucephala), and coot. If food diversity is important to species number, we would expect a stronger correlation with species number in this group than, say, with the number of species of loons (Gavia), grebes (Podiceps), (1) Increasing lake size. (2) Increasing vegetation heterogeneity of the habitat. (3) Increasing food resource diversity. In his review of the literature about species–area relationships in birds, Wiens (1989) concluded that functionally different groups may differ from one another in their response to area. Here we use different subsets of the waterfowl species pool to evaluate such patterns, also in relation to utilization of surrounding areas (see Möller, 1987). METHODS Study area The theory of island biogeography is based on the assumption that the archipelago studied has been colonized by species belonging to the same species pool (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967). Out of a larger data set from sixty lakes in Sweden and Finland (Elmberg et al., 1993) we therefore selected thirty-one lakes in four regions well within the boreal forest zone (Fig. 1). Apart from sharing the same general species pool and not being just parts of larger lakes, the study lakes (Appendix 1) are thus characterized by being: (a) ice-covered in winter, (b) permanent, with slight between-year variations in water level, and (c) inhabited by completely migratory waterfowl populations. The species studied are closely tied to lake habitats for nesting, brood-rearing as well as for post-breeding molt. Since they are migratory every lake is colonized anew each year. Hence, the study lakes are functional islands to breeding waterfowl from a resource point of view, but they are not very typical islands from an immigration and emigration point of view (cf. Brown & Dinsmore, 1988; Haila, 1990). FIG. 1. Study areas. 1, Lappi; 2, Västerbotten; 3, Häme; 4, Karjala.

In his study of woodlot 'islands' in an agricultural landscape, Möller (1987) distinguished between patch foragers and species which forage also outside the patch ('island'). A similar distinction can be made here. Among the species studied, dabbling ducks and Whooper swan (Cygnus cygnus L.) easily and frequently move their brood to another lake to forage (the subset here called 'lake changing species') (Beard, 1964; Talent, Krapu & Jarvis, 1982; Duncan, 1987; own observations). Diving ducks (Aythya, Bucephala and Mergus), on the other hand, do not undertake such movements so often (here called 'intermediate species') (Eriksson, 1978; Pöysä & Virtanen, in press). Artic loon (Gavia arctica L.), grebes and coot, finally, do not move their young over land at all ('one-lake species'). Further, chicks of dabbling ducks have a shorter fledging period than chicks of the 'intermediate' and 'one-lake species' (mean for species in this study 41, 58, and 63 days, respectively; data from Cramp & Simmons, 1977, 1980). Hence, the three subsets can be supposed to differ markedly in their dependence on the patch (lake). Table 2 shows all five measures of bird species richness used. Lake vegetation was mapped in July, when conditions are representative for the late nesting and brood-rearing phases of most species. Statistical procedures To meet the requirements of parametric correlation analysis, stepwise multiple regression, and analysis of variance, all variables except for PCA scores were transformed according to the formula: \( x' = \ln(x + 1) \). RESULTS Lake area, length of shoreline, size of species pool and habitat structural diversity did not differ between regions (One-way analysis of variance; \( F \)-ratio 0.554, 0.174, 0.646, and 3.163, respectively; \( P > 0.05 \) in all cases; \( N = 4 \) regions, with a total of 31 lakes), thus warranting pooling of data among regions. The species richness pattern among the lakes deviated significantly from what could be expected if species number was determined by lake area only (equation ten in Coleman et al. (1982); \( G \)-test, \( G = 49.39, \ df = 30, P = > 0.05 \); Fig. 5). Some general patterns emerged from the pairwise correlations between waterfowl species richness and characteristics of the lakes (Table 3). DISCUSSION As the observed species-richness patterns did not fit the random placement null model, we proceed to evaluating the role of different aspects of food and habitat diversity. Our method of sampling aquatic prey best reflects the availability of that consumed by the 'non-piscivore' species group (e.g. Cramp & Simmons, 1977, 1980). If food diversity is important to the number of species, we predict the number of species in this group to be: (a) correlated with the number of prey taxa, (b) correlated with prey size diversity, and (c) less or not correlated with lake area. Predictions (a) and (c) were met, and the notion that the number of prey taxa is important to species number was further sustained by the results of the stepwise regression analysis. In agreement with Möller (1987) our data indicate that patch area is the more significant determinant of species number the more functionally dependent the species are on the patch (see also Blake & Karr, 1987). Pairwise correlations as well as stepwise multiple regression analysis showed that area is an important determinant of species number in the two subsets of species which are most dependent on the lake for brood-rearing. On the other hand, richness of 'lake-changing species' (= 'non-patch' species) was not correlated with lake area. Instead, food diversity and habitat structural diversity were crucial. Further, our study warrants the following generalizations: (a) aspects of food diversity, i.e. the number of prey taxa, may generally be as important as lake area to species richness. Nilsson & Nilson (1978) argued similarly with respect to the general productivity of lakes. (b) The relatively low \( R^2 \) values obtained in the final models imply that other factors than the two measures of size and the four diversity variables may be important to species number. What might such other factors be? Abundance of prey is a likely complement (Nilsson & Nilsson, 1978; Haila, 1983). In a previous analysis of local assemblages of dabbling ducks in a larger number of lakes, we presented a model which explains more of the variation in species number than does the model in the present paper (Elmberg et al., 1993). The former model includes two measures of prey abundance a well as a composite (PCA) measure of habitat structural diversity. In the waterfowl community studied area as well as habitat diversity (cf. Ås et al., 1992, p. 220) thus appear important to species richness, sometimes each by itself and sometimes both at the same time, but area per se only in smaller groups of species strongly functionally dependent on the lake (island). Seasonal succession in fishless ponds: effects of enrichment and invertebrate predators on zooplankton community structure

Christopher F. Steiner1,2 & Allison H. Roy3
1W. K. Kellogg Biological Station and the Department of Zoology, Michigan State University, Hickory Corners, MI 49060, U.S.A.
2Present address: Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Natural Resources, Cook College, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ 08901, U.S.A.
E-mail: csteiner@rci.rutgers.edu
3Institute of Ecology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602, U.S.A.
E-mail: aroy@uga.edu

Received 26 February 2002; in revised form 6 August 2002; accepted 20 November 2002

Key words: competition, Daphnia, enrichment, Notonecta, seasonal succession, size-efficiency hypothesis

Abstract

Size-selective predation by fish is often considered to be a primary driver of seasonal declines in large-bodied Daphnia populations. However, large Daphnia commonly exhibit midsummer extinctions in ponds lacking planktivorous fish. A number of empirical and theoretical studies suggest that resource competition and its interaction with nutrient enrichment may determine variable dominance by large Daphnia. Low resource levels may favor competitive dominance by small-bodied taxa while large Daphnia may be favored under high resource conditions or following a nutrient/productivity pulse. Nutrient enrichment may also influence the strength of invertebrate predation on Daphnia by affecting how long vulnerable juveniles are exposed to predation. We investigated these hypotheses using an in situ mesocosm experiment in a permanent fishless pond that exhibited seasonal losses of Daphnia pulex. To explore the effects of nutrient enrichment, Daphnia plus a diverse assemblage of small-bodied zooplankton were exposed to three levels of enrichment (low, medium, and high). To explore the interaction between nutrient enrichment and invertebrate predation, we crossed the presence/absence of Notonecta undulata with low and high nutrient manipulations. We found no evidence of competitive reversals or shifts in dominance among nutrient levels, Daphnia performed poorly regardless of enrichment. This may have been due to shifts in algal composition to dominance by large filamentous green algae. Notonecta had significant negative effects on Daphnia alone, but no interaction with nutrient enrichment was detected. These results suggest that Daphnia are not invariably superior resource competitors compared to small taxa. Though predators can have negative effects, their presence is not necessary to explain poor Daphnia performance. Rather, abiotic conditions and/or resource-based effects are probably of greater importance.

Introduction

A commonly observed successional pattern in planktonic communities is a seasonal shift from early season dominance by large-bodied species of Daphnia to late season dominance by small-bodied Cladocera (such as Diaphanosoma and Ceriodaphnia) and copepods (Sommer et al., 1986; Gliwicz & Pijanowska, 1989).

To date, this seasonal dynamic has been investigated primarily in lake communities with an associated emphasis on size-selective predation by fish as a principal determinant of zooplankton size-structure (e.g. Sommer et al., 1986; Gliwicz & Pijanowska, 1989; Tessier & Welser, 1991), a view rooted in the size-efficiency hypothesis (SEH) of Brooks & Dodson (1965). SEH postulates that large-bodied zooplankton, compared

</page>

<page number="1">

to small-bodied taxa, are superior resource competitors and consequently dominate in the absence of predators. Size-selective predation by fish can reduce the abundance of large taxa, permitting dominance by small-bodied zooplankton. However, in small permanent ponds where fish are absent, zooplankton communities frequently exhibit early season peaks followed by midsummer losses of large-bodied *Daphnia*, despite the absence of the presumed key determinant (e.g. Fig. 1A; see also Hall et al., 1970; Lynch, 1978; Steiner, 2001). Furthermore, seasonal patterns of *Daphnia* relative biomass can vary greatly among these water bodies, with some systems being dominated by *Daphnia* for the entire growing season, some showing successional patterns, and some having little or no *Daphnia* (Steiner, 2001). The determinants of this variation are unknown and hint at a biological complexity not encompassed within the conventional top-down view.

Despite the appeal of SEH, a sizable body of evidence suggests that variable dominance by large *Daphnia* may be dependent on interspecific competition and its interaction with environmental context, independent of fish predator presence or absence (see DeMott, 1989). For example, a number of studies have emphasized the importance of resource concentration and system productivity on differential performance of large versus small-bodied Cladocera (e.g. Goulden et al., 1978; Tillmann & Lampert, 1984; Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985; Tessier & Goulden, 1987). Low rates of algal-resource supply can favor small-bodied taxa by exposing starvation-prone juvenile *Daphnia* to demographic bottlenecks (Neill, 1975a; Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985). High resource availability (or a pulse of food) can allow *Daphnia* populations to accrue a large number of adult stage individuals. These adults could in turn depress resource levels (via high filtration rates) and essentially outstarve small-bodied competitors. This novel mechanism could explain variation in competitive outcomes among ponds as well as seasonally within systems, especially if ponds are prone to mixing events. To date, a number of studies have suggested that competitive outcomes between large and small zooplankton could be dependent on initial algal resource levels or productivity/nutrient pulses during community development (Tillmann & Lampert, 1984; Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985; Bengtsson, 1987). However, these studies, in addition to the general model (sensu Romanovsky & Feniova, 1987), do not consider dynamic algal communities whose composition may change

![Zooplankton seasonal dynamics in P14 during the 1997 growing season. (A) Major zooplankton groupings, including Chaoborus, Daphnia pulex, copepods (cyclopoids and calanoids combined), and small-bodied Cladocera (all taxa combined). (B) Copepods and small-bodied Cladocera ungrouped and depicted separately (Alona, Ceriodaphnia, Bosmina, Scapholeberis, and rotifers were rare, at no time comprising greater than 5% of total biomass, and have been omitted for clarity). Shown is mean biomass (+1) from two vertical tows. Error bars are not depicted to improve clarity.](page_1012_180_1012_1442.png)

Figure 1. Zooplankton seasonal dynamics in P14 during the 1997 growing season. (A) Major zooplankton groupings, including Chaoborus, *Daphnia pulex*, copepods (cyclopoids and calanoids combined), and small-bodied Cladocera (all taxa combined). (B) Copepods and small-bodied Cladocera ungrouped and depicted separately (*Alona*, *Ceriodaphnia*, *Bosmina*, *Scapholeberis*, and rotifers were rare, at no time comprising greater than 5% of total biomass, and have been omitted for clarity). Shown is mean biomass (+1) from two vertical tows. Error bars are not depicted to improve clarity.

in conjunction with enrichment events and/or grazing pressure (e.g., Vanni, 1987; Kerfoot et al., 1988). Shifts in algal composition towards dominance by

</page>

<page number="2">

species resistant to Daphnia grazing could weaken nutrient effects on Daphnia population responses.

Resource effects notwithstanding, top-down effects could also generate mid-summer declines of Daphnia in fishless ponds. For example, salamanders (Notophthalmus and Ambystoma) are common in shallow ponds and can feed preferentially on large-bodied zooplankton (Dodson, 1970; Morin, 1987). However, zooplankton communities may still exhibit seasonal declines in large Daphnia populations even when predaceous salamanders have been excluded (Morin, 1987). Furthermore, in deeper, open water ponds (e.g., Fig. 1A) where salamanders are largely absent in the pelagic zone, successional patterns are still common (Steiner, 2001). Planktivorous invertebrates are also plentiful in pond systems, yet how effective these predators are in shifting the size-structure of zooplankton communities remains equivocal. A number of studies have documented a general preference by invertebrate predators for small or intermediate size classes of zooplankton (Lynch, 1979; Pastorak, 1981; Spitze, 1985), though some species (such as the backswimming bugs, Notonectidae) can feed on larger individuals (Scott & Murdoch, 1983; Murdoch et al., 1984; Arner et al., 1998). The potential impact of invertebrate predators on community size structure is complicated by differential susceptibility of Daphnia life stages; juveniles are more vulnerable to predation but adults may attain a relative size refuge (Swift & Fedorenko, 1975; Vinyard & Menger, 1980; Spitze, 1985). Consequently, seasonal variation in productivity and/or resource quality may enhance top-down effects by affecting how long juveniles are exposed to predators and the ability of individuals to reach a size refuge (Chase, 1999). Just as a pulse of resource production may affect competitive outcomes, high levels of resources may weaken invertebrate predator interactions with Daphnia.

In the present paper we report on an in situ mesocosm experiment in which we explored these hypotheses and processes in a semi-natural pond known to exhibit a seasonal loss of large-bodied Daphnia pulex. The experiment was executed during Daphnia’s midsummer decline. To test effects of a nutrient/productivity pulse on patterns of dominance, we exposed Daphnia plus a diverse assemblage of small-bodied zooplankton to three levels of nutrient enrichment. To examine effects of invertebrate predators and their potential interaction with enrichment, low and high nutrient levels were further crossed with presence and absence of the invertebrate predator Notonecta undulata. If resource abundance, independent of predation, mediates Daphnia performance in the experimental pond, we predict that Daphnia should dominate zooplankton assemblages only in nutrient enriched treatments. Alternatively, if the size-efficiency hypothesis is operating, Daphnia should dominate in the absence of predators at all nutrient levels. Finally, if Notonecta are a primary driver of Daphnia performance, we predict that the presence of the predator should shift dominance towards small-bodied zooplankton. Nutrient enrichment may weaken the shift to small-bodied forms by allowing Daphnia to attain a size refuge from predation.

Study site

The experiment was performed in a single pond (P14) at the W. K. Kellogg Biological Station, experimental pond facility (Hickory Corners, Mich., U.S.A.). This pond is permanent, fishless, and approximately 1.6 m deep, at its deepest point, with a surface area of approximately 700 m². P14 is unstained and has a large open water zone free of submerged macrophyte cover. Hence, light penetration in the water column is high. Trophic state of the pond is in the mesotrophic range, with mean total phosphorus (±S.E.) over three years of 15.3 ± 6.1 \( \mu \)g P l⁻¹. However, this phosphorus level is low when considering the natural range encountered in fishless ponds in the region (Steiner, 2001, 2002). Daphnia pulex (hereafter referred to as Daphnia) is the only Daphnia species found in the pond. Over 5 years of monitoring (1996–2000), P14’s Daphnia population has undergone seasonal succession, peaking in abundance in late spring and then being succeeded by a zooplankton assemblage dominated primarily by Diaphanosoma brachyurum and copepods (e.g. Fig. 1A, B). The pond supports an invertebrate predator assemblage, resident year-round, dominated by the phantom midge larvae (Chaoborus americanus; for densities see Fig. 1A). Backswimming bugs (Notonecta) are also present but attain much lower densities in the experimental ponds (7–70 individuals per 10 000 l; Steiner, unpublished data). Dytiscid beetle larvae have also been commonly observed. Pond temperatures (measured at mid-depth) during the course of the study averaged 23.5 °C (range: 21–25.5 °C).

</page>

<page number="3">

Materials and methods

The experiment was deployed June 23–July 25, 1997 (32 days), during the natural decline phase of Daphnia in this pond (Daphnia were completely absent by the end of the experiment; see Fig. 1A). Our experimental system consisted of impermeable 1200-l polyethylene ‘bag’ enclosures with a 1-m diameter, open at their tops, sealed at their bottoms to exclude sediments, and suspended in the water column by floating frames. Tops of the frames were covered with fiberglass screening (1.3-mm mesh size) to deter insect invasion. Water was pumped from the pond, at mid-depth, into the bags through a 150-μm mesh net to remove the majority of the zooplankton population. A day after enclosures were filled with water we inoculated bags with an equal biomass concentration of Daphnia pulex and a diverse assemblage of small-bodied zooplankton. Small zooplankton were obtained from a neighboring pond (P9) that contained a population of sunfish (Lepomis gibbosus) and thus contained no Daphnia and no invertebrate predators due to planktivory (personal observation). The zooplankton assemblage extracted from this pond included all the major late-season taxa found in P14, including species of Diaphanosoma, Ceriodaphnia, Chydorus, Bosmina, Scapholeberis, calanoid and cyclopoid copepods, and several species of rotifers (dominated primarily by Keratella, Lecane, and Trichocerca). We lab reared all Daphnia pulex to ensure their availability at the time of the experiment. Zooplankton biomass concentrations in Daphnia cultures and P9 were based on length-mass regressions (McCauley, 1984) and determined from samples taken a day prior to inoculation. Total initial zooplankton biomass in the enclosures was 24.5 \( \mu \)g l\(^{-1}\), 42% of the natural biomass level in P14 at the time of the experiment’s initiation.

To explore effects of a nutrient pulse on zooplankton dynamics we subjected enclosures to three nutrient treatments (high, medium and low). To examine effects of invertebrate predators we included treatments with the predator Notonecta undulata at low and high nutrient levels. All treatments were replicated three times for a total of 15 enclosures. Nutrient manipulations consisted of additions of phosphorus (Na\(_2\)HPO\(_4\)) and nitrogen (NaNO\(_3\)) with a N:P molar ratio of 57:1, matched to that of the ambient pond water to minimize changes in algal stoichiometry. High nutrient treatments received a start concentration of 150 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\), medium treatments received 80 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\), and low nutrient treatments received no additions for a start concentration of 10.7 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\). Nutrients were added once, 1 day after zooplankton additions. Notonectids for predator treatments were collected from ponds at the experimental pond facility using horizontal tows with a plankton net. Each predator treatment received 7 adult Notonecta – on the high end of densities found in ponds at the experimental facility but low when considering the range of variation encountered in fishless ponds (J. Chase, Washington University, pers. comm.). Because Notonectids are known to feed preferentially on Daphnia (Scott & Murdoch, 1983), we biased our experiment towards seeing predator effects on the large zooplankter. Predator additions occurred 4 days following zooplankton inoculations.

Beginning on day 8, zooplankton and phytoplankton were sampled every 8 days using an integrated tube sampler that extended to the bottom of the enclosure. Zooplankton were immediately preserved in chilled sucrose formalin and stored for later enumeration. Fifty randomly chosen individuals of each species were also measured to obtain dry mass estimates using length-mass regressions (McCauley, 1984). Water samples (500 ml total) were collected, placed on ice, and later filtered for subsequent analysis of chlorophyll a as a measure of algal biomass (sensu Welschmeyer, 1994). We fractionated samples into two size classes. Half of the water sample was directly filtered onto Gelman A/E glass fiber filters to measure total chlorophyll a. The other half was first filtered through a 35-μm Nitex mesh to measure the ‘edible’ size fraction of algae. Midway through the experiment a mat of filamentous green algae (dominated by Oedogonium and Spyrogyra) appeared on the water surface of the medium and high nutrient enclosures. Surface algae was collected in totality on the final day of the experiment using d-nets, subsampled and filtered to measure chlorophyll a. In all subsequent analyses, we treat surface algae as grazer resistant.

Biomass responses of zooplankton and algae through time were analyzed using univariate repeated measures ANOVA (rm-ANOVA). Analyses of single sample dates were performed using ANOVA. To explore the effects of nutrient enrichment on zooplankton responses, we analyzed low, medium, and high nutrient enclosures (without Notonecta) as a one-way design. To examine the effects of predators and their interaction with nutrient enrichment, we analyzed low and high nutrient enclosures with and without predators as a separate 2 × 2 factorial design. Chlorophyll a measures were \( \log_{10} \) transformed to conform to

</page>

<page number="4">

assumptions of homogeneity of variances. Due to zero values, all zooplankton biomass measures were \( \log_{10}(x + 1) \) transformed. All proportional data (percent relative biomass) were arc-sine square root transformed. Due to potential violations of the assumption of circularity, we present Greenhouse–Geiser (G–G) adjusted probabilities for all repeated measures analyses (von Ende, 1993). Unless otherwise stated all time \( \times \) treatment interactions were not significant. Statistics were performed using Systat Version 8.0.

Results

Algae appeared to respond positively to nutrient enrichment, as indicated by chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations through time (Fig. 2; \( p = 0.057, F_{2,6} = 4.795 \), between subjects effect, rm-ANOVA). Relative biomass of grazer resistant (\( >35\)-\( \mu \)m) algae was calculated as the difference between total and \( <35\)-\( \mu \)m fractions divided by total chlorophyll. Repeated measures analysis of the relative abundance of this size fraction revealed weak effects of enrichment (Fig. 3; \( p = 0.075, F_{2,6} = 4.118 \), between subjects effect, rm-ANOVA). However, these measures do not take into account filamentous surface algae. Its inclusion with day 32 chlorophyll \( a \) revealed a strong positive effect of enrichment on total chlorophyll \( a \) (Fig. 4A; \( p < 0.001, F_{2,6} = 44.57 \), one-way ANOVA) and on the relative abundance of \( >35\)-\( \mu \)m algae (Fig. 4B; \( p < 0.001, F_{2,6} = 36.168 \), one-way ANOVA).

Focusing on zooplankton responses in the absence of predation, nutrient enrichment had weak positive effects on Daphnia biomass (Fig. 5, dashed lines; \( p = 0.090, F_{2,6} = 3.695 \), between subjects effects, rm-ANOVA). Mid-experiment, Daphnia biomass began to drop in all treatments and by day 32 there were no significant differences among nutrient levels detected (\( p = 0.248, F_{2,6} = 1.772 \), one-way ANOVA). No nutrient \( \times \) time interactions were detected (\( p > 0.10 \)). Enrichment had positive and sustained effects on total small-bodied zooplankton biomass (Fig. 5, solid lines; \( p = 0.009, F_{2,6} = 11.539 \), between subjects effect, rm-ANOVA). The small-bodied zooplankton response was largely due to the significant positive responses of Cladocera to enrichment (\( p = 0.007, F_{2,6} = 12.994 \), between subjects effect, rm-ANOVA). There was no effect of nutrients on copepod biomass (\( p > 0.05 \), within and between subjects effects, rm-ANOVA).

In the absence of predators, percent relative biomass of the major components of the zooplankton assemblage varied greatly through time and as a function of enrichment (Fig. 6). Small zooplankton were dominated primarily by Cladocera (of which Diaphanosoma, Bosmina, and Chydorus were the dom-

![Algal responses (not including surface filamentous forms) to low, medium and high nutrient treatments, in the absence of predators. Shown are means (±S.E.).](page_1012_180_484_484.png)

Discussion

As a driver of temporal and spatial variation in zooplankton community size structure, size-selective predation by fish has a formidable body of supporting

evidence (e.g. Hrbacek et al., 1961; Brooks & Dodson, 1965; Gliwicz & Pijanowska, 1989; Mittelbach et al., 1995). However, the importance of top-down effects in fishless ponds is uncertain. Our experiment provided evidence that invertebrate predators can have negative effects on large-bodied Daphnia populations. Notonectids inflicted significant reductions in Daphnia populations, a result consistent with previous investigations (e.g. Murdoch et al., 1984; Arner et al., 1998). Thus, this invertebrate predator has the capacity to play the role that planktivorous fish do in

</page>

<page number="7">

the original formulation of SEH. Nonetheless, while biomass was depressed in the presence of Notonecta, Daphnia at no point dominated the zooplankton community and by mid-experiment had begun to decline in all enclosures, independent of predator presence or absence. This was true regardless of nutrient level; enrichment had no effect on the magnitude or strength of predator effects on Daphnia. Hence, the heart of the size efficiency hypothesis – competitive dominance by large-bodied zooplankton in the absence of predators – was not supported by our experiment. While top-down effects are present and at times strong, variation in Daphnia dominance need not be invariably linked to the presence/absence of predators, a conclusion consistent with previous studies of fishless ponds (e.g. Hall et al., 1970; Lynch, 1978, 1979).

As previously outlined, absolute quantity of resources has been linked to variable Daphnia performance, with several papers suggesting that small-bodied species perform better at low resource levels and large-bodied species at high resource concentrations (Goulden et al., 1982; Tillmann & Lampert, 1984; Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985; Bengtsson, 1987; Tessier & Goulden, 1987). Using simulations, Romanovsky and Feniova (1985) have shown that resource pulses may facilitate competitive reversals by diminishing effects of small-bodied species on Daphnia and strengthening the negative effects of Daphnia on competitors. Variation in nutrient availability, and consequently algal production, might be especially high in shallow water bodies such as ponds in which mixing events extend through the entire water column to nutrient-rich sediments. Thus, this model may account for variation in competition effects among ponds (along gradients of productivity and/or mixing regime) as well as variation in competitor interaction strength within ponds (due to mixing events and seasonal changes in productivity). Though we did not measure the effects of competition directly in our experiment, the small-bodied assemblage was composed largely of Cladocera, species known to compete with Daphnia for shared resources (reviewed in DeMott, 1989). Focusing on relative biomass, Daphnia at no point exhibited clear competitive dominance, comprising a minor fraction of the zooplankton community at all times during the experiment. This was true despite a nutrient pulse an order of magnitude greater than ambient levels. While Daphnia biomass did increase in response to enrichment, the effect was short-term and in clear contrast to the more sustained responses of the small-bodied zooplankton fraction. Furthermore, the lack of dominance does not appear to be an artifact of experimental duration since Daphnia responses peaked mid-experiment and then declined in all treatments.

In order for productivity pulses to generate shifts in competitive outcomes, Daphnia must exhibit a substantial population increase and dominate the zooplankton community during the early onset of community development. During this early community growth phase, adult Daphnia, through their high per capita filtration rates, can drive resources to low levels and out-starve competitors (Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985). This dynamic response was clearly not attained in the present investigation suggesting that abiotic conditions or some aspect of resource quality may have suppressed Daphnia population responses. Though the majority of algal production was in the edible range early in the experiment (surface filamentous forms began to appear by day 16), this course level of resolution can miss important aspects of resource quality and algal size structure. For example, zooplankton taxa can vary in their preferences for different particle sizes and taxa (e.g. Neill, 1975b; Knisely & Geller, 1986; Bogdan & Gilbert, 1987). Compared to large Daphnia species, many small-bodied species are thought to be more efficient in their use of small algal particles and bacteria (taxa < 2\( \mu \)m; Neill, 1975b; Geller & Muller, 1981; Pace et al., 1983). Thus, using a single size-based cut-off to quantify ‘edible’ resources ignores potentially important aspects of algal size and taxonomic composition. More recently, nutritional adequacy (carbon, phosphorus, and nitrogen content) has been recognized as an important aspect of resource quality that may differentially favor zooplankton taxa (Sterner & Hessen, 1994). Daphnia have unusually high phosphorous demands compared to most small-bodied Cladocera and copepods, making them especially prone to phosphorus limitation (Sterner & Hessen, 1994). We did not measure C:N:P content of algal resources. However, the TN:TP ratio in our experimental pond prior to the experiment was 57:1 (molar), indicative of strong phosphorus limitation (Healey & Hendzel, 1980). Thus, stoichiometric conditions of algal resources were likely unfavorable for Daphnia. Finally, resource effects could have interacted with pond temperatures. High temperatures (>25 \(^\circ\)C) are known to have a disproportionately strong negative effect on large-bodied zooplankton, potentially altering competitive outcomes with small-bodied species (reviewed in Moore & Folt, 1993; though see Achenbach & Lampert, 1997). In the first

</page>

<page number="8">

weeks of the experiment, pond temperatures averaged 25 °C, levels at which small-bodied zooplankton should have been favored in competition with Daphnia.

Poor Daphnia performance and declines later in the experiment may have also been due to our use of a dynamic resource community. Prior investigations that have uncovered effects of resource concentration on competitive outcomes have used static algal assemblages (e.g. Tillmann & Lampert, 1984; Romanovsky & Feniova, 1985; Bengtsson, 1987). Phytoplankton community composition is known to change in response to both enrichment and grazing pressure (McCauley & Briand, 1979; Reynolds, 1984; Vanni, 1987; Kerfoot et al., 1988; McCauley et al., 1988). In our study, algae increased in response to enrichment but also exhibited a striking increase in the grazer-resistant size fraction. By the termination of the experiment, much of this was in the form of surface-bound filamentous algae that comprised close to 60% of algal biomass in the highest nutrient treatments. If primary productivity is channeled to species of algae inaccessible to Daphnia, the non-equilibrial dynamics envisioned in Romanovsky & Feniova (1985) may not be approximated. Other studies have shown that allocation of resource production towards less edible forms can attenuate consumer biomass responses to enhanced productivity (e.g. Bohannan & Lenski, 1999). Finally, numerous investigations have shown that filamentous blue-green algae can interfere with feeding of large Daphnia (small-bodied taxa are less susceptible), potentially altering competitive outcomes with small-bodied Cladocera and copepods (e.g., Gliwicz & Siedlar, 1980; Sumner & Dodson, 1983; Gliwicz & Lampert, 1990). In our study, filamentous forms were composed primarily of green algae. Though it is not known whether these species can interfere with Daphnia feeding efficiency, it is certainly plausible. These results do not negate the idea that temporally fluctuating resources may facilitate coexistence among competing zooplankton or that pulses can prolong Daphnia persistence in otherwise unfavorable environments. It does however call into question the capacity of a nutrient pulse to generate alternative competitive outcomes and Daphnia dominated systems in natural pond environments.

Our results showed that top-down effects, while present, are not needed to explain the poor performance of Daphnia following mid-summer declines in ponds. Rather, abiotic conditions, resource quality, or competition with small-bodied taxa (or some combination thereof) appear to be more important. The inability of Daphnia to dominate small-bodied taxa in the absence of predators is further evidence that SEH may have limited applicability in shallow pond systems. Finally, the effects of varying resource levels and productivity on competitive outcomes between large and small-bodied taxa may be insubstantial outside of a laboratory setting (i.e. when applied to systems in which algal composition is dynamic and itself a function of enrichment and grazing events).

Materials and methods

The experiment was deployed June 23–July 25, 1997 (32 days), during the natural decline phase of Daphnia in this pond (Daphnia were completely absent by the end of the experiment; see Fig. 1A). Our experimental system consisted of impermeable 1200-l polyethylene ‘bag’ enclosures with a 1-m diameter, open at their tops, sealed at their bottoms to exclude sediments, and suspended in the water column by floating frames. Tops of the frames were covered with fiberglass screening (1.3-mm mesh size) to deter insect invasion. Water was pumped from the pond, at mid-depth, into the bags through a 150-μm mesh net to remove the majority of the zooplankton population. A day after enclosures were filled with water we inoculated bags with an equal biomass concentration of Daphnia pulex and a diverse assemblage of small-bodied zooplankton. Small zooplankton were obtained from a neighboring pond (P9) that contained a population of sunfish (Lepomis gibbosus) and thus contained no Daphnia and no invertebrate predators due to planktivory (personal observation). The zooplankton assemblage extracted from this pond included all the major late-season taxa found in P14, including species of Diaphanosoma, Ceriodaphnia, Chydorus, Bosmina, Scapholeberis, calanoid and cyclopoid copepods, and several species of rotifers (dominated primarily by Keratella, Lecane, and Trichocerca). We lab reared all Daphnia pulex to ensure their availability at the time of the experiment. Zooplankton biomass concentrations in Daphnia cultures and P9 were based on length-mass regressions (McCauley, 1984) and determined from samples taken a day prior to inoculation. Total initial zooplankton biomass in the enclosures was 24.5 \( \mu \)g l\(^{-1}\), 42% of the natural biomass level in P14 at the time of the experiment’s initiation.

To explore effects of a nutrient pulse on zooplankton dynamics we subjected enclosures to three nutrient treatments (high, medium and low). To examine effects of invertebrate predators we included treatments with the predator Notonecta undulata at low and high nutrient levels. All treatments were replicated three times for a total of 15 enclosures. Nutrient manipulations consisted of additions of phosphorus (Na\(_2\)HPO\(_4\)) and nitrogen (NaNO\(_3\)) with a N:P molar ratio of 57:1, matched to that of the ambient pond water to minimize changes in algal stoichiometry. High nutrient treatments received a start concentration of 150 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\), medium treatments received 80 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\), and low nutrient treatments received no additions for a start concentration of 10.7 \( \mu \)g P l\(^{-1}\). Nutrients were added once, 1 day after zooplankton additions. Notonectids for predator treatments were collected from ponds at the experimental pond facility using horizontal tows with a plankton net. Each predator treatment received 7 adult Notonecta – on the high end of densities found in ponds at the experimental facility but low when considering the range of variation encountered in fishless ponds (J. Chase, Washington University, pers. comm.). Because Notonectids are known to feed preferentially on Daphnia (Scott & Murdoch, 1983), we biased our experiment towards seeing predator effects on the large zooplankter. Predator additions occurred 4 days following zooplankton inoculations.

Beginning on day 8, zooplankton and phytoplankton were sampled every 8 days using an integrated tube sampler that extended to the bottom of the enclosure. Zooplankton were immediately preserved in chilled sucrose formalin and stored for later enumeration. Fifty randomly chosen individuals of each species were also measured to obtain dry mass estimates using length-mass regressions (McCauley, 1984). Water samples (500 ml total) were collected, placed on ice, and later filtered for subsequent analysis of chlorophyll a as a measure of algal biomass (sensu Welschmeyer, 1994). We fractionated samples into two size classes. Half of the water sample was directly filtered onto Gelman A/E glass fiber filters to measure total chlorophyll a. The other half was first filtered through a 35-μm Nitex mesh to measure the ‘edible’ size fraction of algae. Midway through the experiment a mat of filamentous green algae (dominated by Oedogonium and Spyrogyra) appeared on the water surface of the medium and high nutrient enclosures. Surface algae was collected in totality on the final day of the experiment using d-nets, subsampled and filtered to measure chlorophyll a. In all subsequent analyses, we treat surface algae as grazer resistant.

Biomass responses of zooplankton and algae through time were analyzed using univariate repeated measures ANOVA (rm-ANOVA). Analyses of single sample dates were performed using ANOVA. To explore the effects of nutrient enrichment on zooplankton responses, we analyzed low, medium, and high nutrient enclosures (without Notonecta) as a one-way design. To examine the effects of predators and their interaction with nutrient enrichment, we analyzed low and high nutrient enclosures with and without predators as a separate 2 × 2 factorial design.
