Taylor¹ ¹National Rivers Authority, Biology Laboratory, Station Road, St Olaves, Great Yarmouth, NR31 9JA, UK ²ECON, School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, UK (*author for correspondence) Key words: zooplankton, zooplanktivorous fish, macrophyte, refugia, predator/prey interactions, lake restoration Abstract The provision of a refuge from fish predation for large-bodied Cladocera among stands of submerged macrophytes is thought to be an important stabilising mechanism against nutrient-induced phytoplankton increases in clear water shallow lakes. The occurrence of any refuge effect in relation to the seasonal impact of both macrophyte development and recruitment of zooplanktivorous fish was monitored over the summer months (May to September) in three lakes (Cromes Broad, Hoveton Little Broad/Pound End, and Upton Broad) of variable trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover, in the Norfolk Broads in Eastern England. At all sites, Daphnia spp. exhibited a early summer peak of abundance but had declined rapidly by July probably as a result of predation from underyearling fish. In extensive macrophyte stands (Cromes Broad) Daphnia spp. persisted after its elimination in open water, indicating some refuge effect. At sites with macrophyte cover and/or low fish predation pressure, Daphnia spp. was replaced by Ceriodaphnia spp., both with and without Simocephalus sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera, apparently capable of exerting a high grazing pressure on phytoplankton. This occurred, even under high predation pressure from a relatively high density of zooplanktivorous 0+ fish (Cromes Broad), consistent with the refuge hypothesis. In addition, at this site, significant positive associations of cladoceran abundance with increasing macrophyte cover were apparent throughout the summer. From information on the distribution of fish it is suggested that dense macrophytes offer the most suitable refuge through provision of predator-free space. Introduction Eutrophication of shallow freshwater lakes frequently results in increased standing crops of phytoplankton or perhaps filamentous algae. This in turn leads to the decline or loss of submerged macrophytes, typically through shading (Phillips et al., 1978; Scheffer, 1990), with consequent gross changes in biotic structure and function (Moss, 1983; De Nie, 1987; Bronmark & Weisner, 1992). However, there is growing empirical and experimental evidence that stabilising mechanisms associated with the presence of stands of macrophytes, may prevent or reduce increases in algal growth up to a threshold level of nutrient loading (Howard-Williams, 1981; Timms & Moss, 1984; Mitchell et al., 1988; Balls et al., 1989; Andersson et al., 1990; Blindlow et al., 1993; Van Donk et al., 1993; Schriver et al., 1995). Consequently, within a range of nutrient concentration, either macrophytes or phytoplankton may dominate; the alternative stable state hypothesis (Irvine et al., 1989; Scheffer et al., 1993). Several stabilising mechanisms which perpetuate the macrophyte-dominated state have been suggested. These include: allelopathy, the production of com- pounds limiting algal growth by the macrophytes themselves (Wium-Anderson et al., 1982); competition for N, with macrophytes maintaining a competitive advantage over algae through luxury uptake (Balls et al., 1989) and acting as a sink for available nutrients (in both water column and sediments) (Ozimek et al., 1990; Van Donk et al., 1993); prevention of resuspension of sediment and recirculation of fast sinking algae by wind and wave action through calming of the water column (James & Barko, 1990); provision of refuges for grazing zooplankton (Timms & Moss, 1984) and refuges for piscivorous fish acting upon the production (Spencer & King, 1984; Grimm & Backx, 1990) or the distribution (Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) of zooplanktivorous fish thereby reducing predation pressure upon the zooplankton (Hambright et al., 1986, Turner & Mittelbach, 1990). Detailed knowledge of the mechanisms responsible for maintaining clear water and low algal populations in lakes dominated by macrophytes is critical for those lake managers concerned with the sustainable restoration (i.e. reversal of anthropogenic eutrophication) of shallow lakes, particularly if this is to be achieved in a predictable and cost-effective manner (Shapiro, 1990). In restoration programmes, the refuge effect for zooplankton is particularly appealing (Shapiro, 1990). This is due to two reasons. First, after nutrient loading has been reduced to the range where macrophyte dominance is likely to be stable (TP<0.15 mg l\(^{-1}\) or higher if N is strongly limiting-Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990), the removal of zooplanktivorous fish, often termed biomanipulation (Lammens et al., 1990), is often required to enhance populations of grazing zooplankton to reduce algal crops to provide a suitable light climate for macrophyte growth. If this mechanism operates, then it is likely that grazing has some importance in maintaining clear water within macrophyte beds. Second, during the development of macrophyte stands following biomanipulation which may or may not be rapid (Meijer et al., 1994; Perrow et al., 1994, Moss et al., 1996), any stabilising mechanism is of increased value if it also preserves water clarity in the open water surrounding macrophyte stands. The diel migration of large-bodied Cladocera from macrophyte stands to open water to feed provides such a mechanism (Timms & Moss, 1984). Although macrophyte stands have been demonstrated to provide refuges for zooplankton (Schriver et al., 1995; Phillips et al., 1996) the timing of such effects relative to the seasonal development of macrophytes and recruitment of 0+ fish is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to describe the seasonal pattern of use of submerged macrophytes by grazing Cladocera in relation to potential predation pressure from fish and to determine whether the refuge effect is plausible as a mechanism in promoting clear water in beds of macrophytes. This adopted a comparative approach by monitoring zooplankton abundance and community structure, fish abundance and biomass, chlorophyll a concentration (as a index of algal abundance) and macrophyte cover during the macrophyte growing season (May–September) in three lakes of varying trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover. Description of study sites The three lakes studied (Hoveton Little/Pound End, Crones and Upton Broads) are among the Norfolk Broads, a series (around 50) of small (1–124 ha), shallow (0.5–2 m) lakes in eastern England, formed from flooded medieval peat diggings. Most may now be classed as hypertrophic and only four retain their original macrophyte populations (Moss, 1983). The study sites represent a continuum from phytoplankton to macrophyte dominance. The first, Hoveton Little Broad, has been divided into two sections as part of a long term management strategy aimed at evaluating the effects of different restorative actions (Table 1). For the purposes of this study, Hoveton Little Broad, acts as a control section with turbid phytoplankton dominated water and few submerged macrophytes, whereas the other biomanipulated section, Pound End, has clear water and some macrophytes, although these are restricted to bird exclosures. The second, Crones Broad, retains a relatively high nutrient loading but has recently developed an extensive cover of Ceratophyllum demersum L. with Potamogeton freisii Rupr. (Perrow et al., 1997). The third, Upton Broad, being isolated from riverine inputs and surrounded by wet woodland, has largely retained its original character and has a large cover of macrophytes, particularly Najas marina L., with Chara spp., P. pectinatus L. and Zannichellia palustris L. Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll a Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll a was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m² quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m²) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 µm net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 × magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (rs). Chlorophyll a concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- hy3777lk.tex; 5/03/1997; 11:24; v.7; p.3 ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point. The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered. Results Fish The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1. Zooplankton Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.). *Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer. The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2). For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions. Indeed, where fish recruitment is poor or absent, *Daphnia* spp. populations typically persist throughout the summer months (Perrow et al., 1994). Conversely, it is clear that the relatively low overwintering stock of older fish exerted little influence on the development of the *Daphnia* spp. population. Second, in all sites, *Daphnia* spp. was quickly replaced by high densities of other species which is not consistent with food limitation and indeed at no site was the abundance of edible algae (expressed as chlorophyll *a*) apparently limiting. It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that predation by 0+ fish is responsible for the decline in *Daphnia* spp. Moreover, this appears to be readily achieved by a relatively low number of 0+ fish in Upton (prior to the development of macrophytes) and relatively moderate recruitment in Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads. However, *Daphnia* spp. persisted in Cromes Broad for a further month even in the presence of a suite of zooplanktivorous fish at relatively high density. This seems related to the early development of an extensive cover of macrophytes at this site. *Daphnia* spp. showed a positive association with macrophytes (Figure 2) and increasing macrophyte cover (Table 3) at this time, quite unlike the situation in any other site. Such use of macrophytes is consistent with the refuge hypothesis. However, *Daphnia* spp. appeared unable to exploit macrophytes as a refuge over an extensive period. This is in keeping with the behavioural ecology of the group which are typically pelagic and have been shown to avoid macrophytes (Pennak, 1973; Dorgelo & Heykoop, 1985). Recent experiments in the laboratory have shown that a clear trade-off exists, *Daphnia magna* Straus preferring to stay in open water until exposed to the risk of predation from zooplanktivorous fish whereupon it migrates to macrophytes, predation risk clearly outweighing repellency (Lauridsen & Lodge, 1996). However, many common fish species, particularly 0+ cyprinids, are capable of feeding in darkness (Townsend & Risebrow, 1982) and so the risk of predation, although reduced, is still evident. In addition, Daphnia spp. populations may suffer some predation from the fish concentrated in a low density of macrophytes (Figure 3). Therefore, in the face of intense predation pressure from a high density of zooplanktivorous fish, as at Cromes Broad, Daphnia spp. may not be able to persist through time, even with the provision of suitable refuges. Following the decline of Daphnia spp., at those sites retaining at least some macrophyte cover Ceriodaphnia spp. dominated, both with (Pound End) and without Simocephalus sp. (Upton). At Pound End, there was even some partial recovery of Daphnia populations in late summer. In contrast, the connected Hoveton Little Broad, with relatively high numbers of 0+ roach, displayed no replacement of Daphnia spp. with other species or any recovery of populations. The consequence of the presence of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus was the maintenance of large populations (typically >50 l\(^{-1}\), Figure 1) of grazing Cladocera throughout the summer months in Cromes and Pound End. The patterns of habitat use of these species also appeared to be related to the potential predation pressure from fish, thus also consistent with the refuge hypothesis. For example, where predation pressure was presumably low from a low density of 0+ perch as in Upton, Ceriodaphnia spp. was present in both open water and macrophyte beds (Figure 2). Under moderate fish predation pressure in Pound End (0.45 m\(^{-2}\) of 0+ perch and roach), Ceriodaphnia spp. and particularly Simocephalus sp. were more abundant in macrophytes, although Ceriodaphnia spp. also occurred at high density in open water (Figure 2). In contrast, where predation pressure was likely to be intense from a suite of 0+ fish at high density (0.8 m\(^{-2}\)) in Cromes, large populations of both Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. were only maintained through association with macrophytes. Furthermore, under intense predation pressure the abundance of cladocerans was almost always positively correlated with increasing PVI suggesting that increasing cover offered a better refuge (Table 3). What is the mechanism behind the refuge effect? Schriver et al. (1995) demonstrate that a refuge effect may exist at low macrophyte density (15–20% of volume) but that this is dependent on fish density. In the current study, it is suggested that macrophytes may act as refuges for zooplankton at relatively high fish hy37771k.tex; 5/03/1997; 11:24; v.7; p.8 ![Bar chart showing the relative distribution of all fish species in different levels of macrophyte PVI in Cromes Broad in September.](page_320_370_1047_482.png) Figure 3. Relative distribution of all fish species in different levels of macrophyte PVI in Cromes Broad in September. density (Cromes) where macrophyte coverage is extensive and the density of macrophytes is high (Table 1). However, the situation at Pound End suggests that even where the distribution of macrophytes is limited, providing patches of dense macrophytes are available (Table 1), a refuge against moderate predation pressure may be provided. The reasons for this may be that dense macrophyte stands contain relatively few fish (Figure 3). By implication, this suggests that predation risk for Cladocera declines with increasing macrophyte cover. Evidence for this is provided by Phillips et al. (1996), who demonstrated that predation pressure, derived from known numbers of fish with known diet, upon zooplankton declined with increasing macrophyte cover. It is therefore suggested that the formation of predator-free space is the mechanism responsible for the refuge effect. The question is, why do zooplanktivorous fish avoid dense macrophytes? (Engel, 1988). Several plausible mechanisms exist. First, oxygen concentrations (Davis, 1975) and pH (Beklioglu & Moss, 1995) may be unsuitable in macrophyte stands, although there is no evidence that either was limiting in the samples collected during routine monitoring of the study sites. Second, and perhaps more applicable, the foraging efficiency of some fish may decline with increasing habitat complexity (Winfield, 1986; Diehl, 1988). However, when foraging on zooplankton, this is clearly species and size dependent. For example, 0+ perch (Perca fluviatilis L.) may show high feeding efficiency in structured environments unlike 0+ roach (Rutilus rutilus (L.)) (Winfield, 1986), and vegetation may serve as a competitive refuge for perch (Persson, 1993). In support of this, several authors (Hall & Werner 1977; Carpenter et al., 1987; Venugopal & Winfield, 1993) have demonstrated that small fish may associate with macrophytes. However, this is typically a behavioural response to potential predation risk (Savino & Stein, 1982; Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) and not because of enhanced foraging opportunity. Whether small fish take refuge in macrophytes in response to predation risk is dependent on a number of factors including the functional type of predator and prey (Jacobsen et al., 1997). It is perhaps significant that in this study the relative proportion of piscivorous pike increased with increasing macrophyte cover (Figure 3). In addition, the individuals present in these habitats were 0+, the size class most likely to consume 0+ zooplanktivores (Van Densen, 1994). Therefore, a third explanation for the avoidance of dense macrophytes by fish in this study may be that they were exposed to a greater risk of predation in these habitats. This in turn may have led to a reduced predation risk for zooplankton (Turner & Mittelbach, 1990) thereby enhancing the refuge effect. Are refuging Cladocera able to control phytoplankton populations? The presence of large numbers of cladoceran grazers exerting an influence on phytoplankton populations is essential to the value of any refuge effect in explaining the presence of clear water in macrophyte-dominated lakes. Particularly to species other than *Daphnia* spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for *Ceriodaphnia* spp. and *Simocephalus* sp. compared to *Daphnia* spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of *Simocephalus* spp. and *Ceriodaphnia* spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of *Daphnia* spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where *Simocephalus* sp. is absent and the filtering rate of *Ceriodaphnia* spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of *Daphnia* spp. However, it is still comparable with that of *Daphnia* spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of *Ceriodaphnia* spp. and *Simocephalus* sp., it is likely that only *Ceriodaphnia* spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, *Simocephalus* sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of *Daphnia* spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, *Daphnia* may be expected to decline, with *Ceriodaphnia* assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with *Simocephalus* contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of *Daphnia* spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. Essential to the value of the refuge effect as a mechanism promoting the stability of submerged macrophyte populations in shallow lakes, the presence of hy37771k.tex; 5/03/1997; 11:24; v.7; p.10 significant populations of grazing Cladocera seems to contribute to the maintenance of a low phytoplankton standing crop and the attainment of clear water. Moreover, macrophyte-associated species such as Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. appear to make an important contribution to this effect where Daphnia spp. is reduced by fish predation and/or disfavoured by extensive macrophyte cover. The mechanism for the refuge effect in this study appears to be the provision of predator-free space as zooplanktivorous fish appear to avoid dense macrophytes. Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll a Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll a was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m² quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m²) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 µm net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 × magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (rs). Chlorophyll a concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- hy3777lk.tex; 5/03/1997; 11:24; v.7; p.3

ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point.

The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered.

Results

Fish

The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1.

Zooplankton

Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.).

*Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer.

The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2).

For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions.

Discussion

Seasonal interactions between macrophytes, fish, zooplankton and phytoplankton

There is clearly some interaction between extent of macrophyte development, intensity of predation by 0+ fish measured simply as a function of density and the structure and abundance of the cladoceran community and its potential impact on algal abundance (measured as chlorophyll *a*) (Figure 1). The distribution of microcrustacea in the littoral zone of a freshwater lake Michael Paterson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory, 501 University Cres., Winnipeg, Manitoba, R3T 2N6 Canada Received 7 April 1992; in revised form 1 December 1992; accepted 14 January 1993 Key words: littoral zone, microcrustacea, Cladocera, Copepoda Abstract The distribution of microcrustacea in the water column, sediments and on different macrophyte species was examined in the littoral zone of Jack Lake, Nova Scotia, Canada. Large numbers of microcrustacea occurred in association with macrophytes, suggesting that this habitat should receive greater attention in future studies of microcrustacean numbers, biomass, and production. The relative abundance of different microcrustacea varied considerably among sediments, macrophytes and water column samples. Although microcrustacean species composition differed among macrophyte groups, consistent differences in absolute numbers per gram could not be demonstrated. Epiphytic microcrustacean community structure also varied among depth strata in Jack Lake. Few epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea migrated into the water column on a diurnal basis. Introduction The littoral zone of most freshwater lakes supports a diverse and abundant assemblage of microcrustacea that inhabit the sediments (benthos), surface of macrophytes (epiphyton), and water column (zooplankton). Littoral microcrustacea influence algal dynamics and are important food for fish and many invertebrates. Community interactions within the littoral zone are largely unknown. As a first step in understanding the role of microcrustacea in littoral food webs, it is important to determine their distribution in space and time. Information on the distribution of microcrustacea within lakes is important for several reasons. Organisms with overlapping spatial and temporal distributions are most likely to interact on a regular basis. Non-overlapping distributions may reflect strong interactions that prevent co-existence. Details of the distribution of microcrustacea are also essential for the design of littoral sampling programs. For example, decisions concerning the allocation of sampling effort may depend on the relative importance of different habitats to different invertebrates. Finally, the exuviae of one group of littoral microcrustacea, chydorid Cladocera, preserve well in lake sediments and have been frequently used in paleolimnological studies. It may be possible to use information on the habitat preferences of chydorid species to reconstruct longterm habitat changes within lakes. This study examines the distribution of micro- crustacea among different habitats in the littoral zone of Jack Lake, Nova Scotia, Canada. Temporal dynamics are described in Paterson (1991, 1993). The following specific questions are addressed: (1) How do microcrustacean assemblages vary among the water column, sediments, and different types of macrophytes? (2) How does epiphytic microcrustacean community structure vary with water depth? (3) Do epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea move into the water column at night? Diurnal migrations may lead to interactions between benthic and epiphytic microcrustacea and zooplankton. Study site Jack Lake (44° 44' N, 63° 40' W) is a small (3.9 ha), acidic (mean pH = 4.7), oligotrophic, headwater lake located near Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada. Aside from hiking trails and a small access road, the watershed is forested and undeveloped. Jack Lake is devoid of fish. The littoral zone is characterized by highly organic sediments and dense submerged macrophyte growth (Paterson, 1991). The macrophyte assemblage is dominated by Pallavicinia lyellii (Hooker) (a liverwort), Eriocaulon septangulare Withering (Northern Pipewort), Scirpus subterminalis Torrey (Water Bulrush), and Potamogeton confervoides Reichenbach (Alga Pondweed). Floating and emergent macrophytes are restricted to shallow water (< 0.5 m) and include Nymphaea odorata Aiton (Yellow Pondlily), Nuphar variegatum Engelmann (White Waterlily), and Pontederia cordata Linnaeus (Pickerel Weed). Materials and methods Distribution of invertebrates in the shallow littoral zone Invertebrates were collected at 3 week to 1 month intervals from the water column, sediments, and macrophytes. All samples were obtained from water 1 to 2 m deep along the north shore of Jack Lake between August 22 and October 5, 1986 and June 11 and October 8, 1987. A more detailed description of sampling methods is available in Paterson (1991). The water-column overlying submerged macrophytes was sampled haphazardly from a boat with a 10 cm diameter flexible plastic tube (cf. Pennak, 1962). Samples were sieved with a 63 \( \mu \)m screen, preserved in 5% formalin with sugar, and counted without subsampling. A minimum of 10 samples was collected on each sampling date. Benthic invertebrates were collected from a boat using a 3.5 cm diameter corer attached to a metal pole. The uppermost 4 cm of each core and 5 cm of overlying water were drawn off with a wide mouthed pipette, sieved with a 125 \( \mu \)m screen, and preserved in 5% sugar-formalin with rose bengal. At least 5 cores were counted in their entirety for each sampling date. Epiphytic invertebrates were collected by a SCUBA diver who closed a 5.5 l hinged plexiglass box around submerged macrophytes (Downing, 1986). Samples were collected at randomly selected locations along rope transects placed parallel to shore in water 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 m deep. Because most macrophytes in Jack Lake could be completely enclosed within the box, sampling was not stratified vertically within the water column. Between 10 and 18 box samples were collected on each sampling date. Box samples were brought to the surface, unenclosed plant material was trimmed away, and the contents were drained through a 125 \( \mu \)m sieve. In the laboratory, invertebrates were rinsed from macrophytes and preserved in 5% sugar-formalin with rose bengal. Macrophytes were sorted to species, dried at 90 \( ^\circ \)C, and weighed. Material washed from macrophytes was made up to a known volume and repeatedly subsampled until at least 300 microcrustacea had been counted. The above-ground biomass of macrophytes (dry weight) was determined by removing plants within randomly located 929 cm\(^2\) (1986) or 232 cm\(^2\) (1987) quadrats. Biomass estimates for each sampling date were based on 12–20 replicates in 1986 and 19–30 replicates in 1987. Macrophyte data are presented in Paterson (1991). Relationships between the abundance of total Cladocera and Cyclopoida in box samples and the biomass of different macrophytes were examined using multiple linear regression (Neter et al., 1983). Because the abundance of total Cladocera and Cyclopoida in box samples varied systematically between June and October (Paterson, 1991), two temporal variables (year and Julian date) were also included in the regression models. Attempts to develop separate regression equations for each sampling date were unsuccessful. Only 10 to 14 box samples were collected per date and multicollinearity among different macrophytes was occasionally high (Pearson r² as high as 0.8). As a result, estimated regression coefficients were unstable and it was not valid to examine habitat preferences using this approach (Neter et al., 1983). Correlations among independent variables in the combined data set are presented in Table 1. Although several correlations were statistically significant, collinearity was not severe (Wilkinson, 1990). For each sampling date, the mean abundance of epiphytic microcrustacea (no g⁻¹) was multiplied by the biomass of submerged macrophytes (g m⁻²) to estimate numbers per square meter of lake bottom. These estimates are crude, because the use of ratios requires the adoption of several assumptions (Jackson et al., 1990). It was not possible to use regressions to estimate numbers of microcrustacea per m² of lake bottom (Downing, 1986). This was because patterns of collinearity among macrophytes were frequently different in box and quadrat samples. Variation in the relative abundance of microcrustacea in different habitats was summarized using Principal Components Analysis (PCA) (Cooley & Lohnes, 1971; Pielou, 1984). PCAs were undertaken using two correlation matrices. The first used data from 92 macrophyte box samples and 40 sediment samples, whereas the second used only data from the box samples. This second ordination helped to elucidate the influence of macrophyte species composition on invertebrate community structure. All proportions were arcsine square-root transformed (Sokal & Rohlf, 1981) and taxa that occurred in less than 15% of samples were dropped. Each sample was assigned a score on PCA axes so that samples with similar invertebrate assemblages had similar scores. Sample scores reflected the weighting of different taxa on each axis. These weightings were summarized using scaled component loadings that are equivalent to the correlation coefficients between sample scores and the relative abundances of different taxa. Ordinations using absolute abundance data (numbers per box sample) resulted in similar interpretations and are presented in Paterson (1991). All analyses were completed using the SYSTAT statistical package (Wilkinson, 1990). Distribution of epiphytic invertebrates with depth The depth distribution of epiphytic invertebrates was investigated on August 27 1986. Two numbered transects were established from shore to the deepest part of Jack Lake (maximum depth = 7.0 m). Each transect was divided into three sections of different water depths: 0–2 m, 2–4 m, and 4–6 m. Day-night movement of microcrustacea into the water column Nocturnal migration of epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea into the water column was assessed using two different approaches: (1) On May 27 1986, numbers of microcrustacea captured using a 3.5 cm diameter sediment corer were compared with numbers moving upward into funnel traps (Whiteside, 1974; Whiteside & Williams, 1975). Each funnel trap consisted of four 127 mm diameter glass funnels attached to clear bottles filled with filtered lake water and held by a plexiglass frame. For invertebrates to become trapped inside the bottles, they had to move upwards 18 cm through a 10 mm internal diameter stem. Traps were placed mouth-down on open sediments and left for 24 h. (2) On August 18 1988, I compared numbers of invertebrates captured in zooplankton tube samples collected during the day (sampling began at 12.00 h) and at night (sampling began at 24.00 h). All samples were collected in water 1 to 2 m in depth. Principal component analysis indicated that microcrustacean community composition varied between core and box samples (Fig. 2; Table 4). Taxa with high relative abundances in sediments had negative loadings on axis 1 and included Diacyclops nanus Herrick, Macrocylops albidus (Jurine), Disparalona acutirostris (Birge), and Alona cf. affinis Leydig. The relative abundance of microcrustacean species also varied among different macrophytes (Fig. 2; Table 4). Axis 1 of the ordination of box samples was positively correlated with the relative abundance of S. subterminalis and P. convervoides and negatively correlated with P. lyellii, E. septangulare, and Sphagnum sp. (Fig. 2, Table 5). These latter species grow close to the sediment-water interface, whereas P. convervoides and S. subterminalis grow higher into the water column. Hence, different microcrustacea apparently occured within dissimilar vertical strata. Taxa associated with 'tall' macrophytes had strong positive loadings on axis 1 and included Eucyclops agilis (Koch), Chydorus linguilabris Frey, Ophryoxus gracilis Sars, and Acroperus cf. harpae Baird (Table 4). The relative abundance of D. nanus, D. acutirostris, Camptocercus sp., Chydorus brevilabris Frey, and adult M. albidus increased in samples predominated by 'short' macrophytes (P. lyellii). Taxa with positive loadings on axis 2 increased in relative abundance in September and October, whereas taxa with negative loadings were most abundant in June and July. 178 Samples of water lilies (N. variegatum) were collected on only one date in 1986, but contained a unique assemblage of microcrustacea (Fig. 1). Estimates of littoral microcrustacean densities (no m\(^{-2}\)) from Jack Lake were within ranges reported from other lakes where appropriate sampling methods have been used (e.g. Daggett & Davis, 1974; Whiteside et al., 1978; Williams, 1982; Vuille, 1991). The results of this study suggest that epiphytic animals may make important contributions to total microcrustacean productivity. This will be especially true in small lakes, where the relative importance of the littoral zone is high. In Jack Lake, 33% of the total surface area includes water less than 2 m deep. Numbers of epiphytic microcrustacea per m\(^2\) of lake surface area were similar to densities of zooplanktonic crustacea collected at the mid-station of oligotrophic-mesotrophic lakes by Patalas (1971). Because of higher water temperatures, production per unit-biomass (P/B) is probably greater in the littoral zone than in cooler, deeper waters. Substantial numbers of chydorid and macrothricid Cladocera and cyclopoid copepods were also encountered at depths greater than 2 m in Jack Lake. Microcrustacean species composition varied among the sediments and different species of macrophytes in Jack Lake. Similar observations have been made by Quade (1969), Whiteside et al. (1978), Flossner (1985), and DiFonzo & Campbell (1988). There are few records of the distributions of microcrustacean species encountered in this study. In Jack Lake, the relative abundances of D. nanus and D. acutirostris were greatest in sediments. Similar results have been reported by Fryer (1968), Hare & Carter (1976), and Strayer (1985). Several studies have found Chydorus piger Sars and Ilyocryptus sp. to be most abundant in mud habitats (Fryer, 1968, 1974; Whiteside et al., 1978; Flossner, 1985; Strayer, 1985). In Jack Lake, relative abundances of these species were greatest on macrophytes. This suggests that the microhabitat distributions of many microcrustacea may be flexible. As a result, care must be taken in the paleolimnological reconstruction of past habitats using littoral cladoceran remains (cf. Crisman & Whitehead, 1978). Because the results from Jack Lake are correlative, the causes of observed distributions cannot be ascertained absolutely. Some potentially important factors include local variations in algal and detrital food resources, competition, predation, chemical conditions (Pip & Stewart, 1976), and habitat permanence (Hargeby, 1990). Most of the microcrustacea in Jack Lake are herbivores and detritivores (Fryer, 1957; 1968; 1974) and their distributions may reflect spatial differences in food quality and availability. The upright stems of S. subterminalis and P. confervoides grew closer to the water surface and probably supported different algal communities than macrophytes near the sediment-water interface (P. lyellii, E. septangulare). Tall macrophytes in Jack Lake supported dense clouds of filamentous algae, which trapped considerable amounts of fine detritus. D. minutus, B. longirostris, H. gibberum, and D. birgei were dominant in water column samples and are adapted to feed on suspended algae. The occurrence of these zooplanktonic species in box samples probably reflects their presence in water near submerged macrophytes. Densities of these organisms were similar in box and tube samples (Paterson, 1993) and were not correlated with macrophyte biomass. There was no evidence that planktonic microcrustacea were repelled by macrophytes as suggested by Gehrs (1974). Different microhabitats may provide varying degrees of protection from predators. Jack Lake is devoid of fish and the dominant predators are invertebrates (Paterson, 1991). The distribution of invertebrate predators varied among littoral microhabitats (Paterson, 1991). Tanypod chironomids and M. albidus (a cyclopoid copepod) were predominant benthic predators; tanypod chironomids, M. albidus, zygopteran odonates, and water mites were common on all submerged macrophytes; anisopteran odonates were associated with short macrophytes; and Cernotina sp. (a predatory trichopteran) was most abundant on tall macrophytes. The predominant predators in the water column were Chaoborus americanus (Johannsen) and E. nordenskioldi (a predatory copepod). The abundance of microcrustacea in box samples was positively correlated with macrophyte biomass, as has been previously demonstrated by Cyr & Downing (1988a, 1988b). Although community composition varied among macrophytes, there were no demonstratable differences in total microcrustacean densities on different species. These results conflict with those of several other studies (e.g. Cyr & Downing, 1988a, 1988b). In part, the absence of strong differences in microcrustacean densities among macrophytes in Jack Lake may reflect the effects of high sampling variability. More detailed studies may reveal important differences in the ability of different macrophytes to support microcrustacea. Epiphytic microcrustacean community composition varied with water depth. Physical and chemical conditions in the hypolimnion may have directly and indirectly influenced distributions. For example, mean temperatures in the epilimnion and hypolimnion were 16.9 and 10.9 \(^\circ\)C respectively. Oxygen concentrations varied from 11.6 mg l\(^{-1}\) in the epilimnion to 7.1 mg l\(^{-1}\) in the hypolimnion. Microcrustacea may also have been affected by changes in macrophytes with depth. All samples collected in the epilimnion included S. subterminalis and P. confervoides, while all hypolimnetic samples included only an unknown species of moss. Microcrustacean species that declined in the hypolimnion tended to be those that were most abundant on the tall macrophytes (S. subterminalis, P. confervoides) in the shallow littoral zone, whereas microcrustacea with increased densities in the hypolimnion were most common in sediments and on P. lyelli. Food resources almost certainly changed with water depth (e.g. Lalonde & Downing, 1991). Hypolimnetic water in Jack Lake was highly colored in August and light levels declined sharply below 4 m. As a result, there was probably an increased dependence of epiphytic and benthic food webs on detrital resources in the hypolimnion. Inadequate numbers of most predators were collected to assess their depth distributions accurately. M. albidus, water mites, odonates, tanypod midges, and Cernotina sp. were found at all depths, with general decreases of abundance in the hypolimnion (Paterson, 1991). Although nightly vertical movements of epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea have been observed in several studies (e.g. Whiteside, 1974; Evans & Stewart, 1977; Meyers, 1984), few migrated into the water column of Jack Lake. Meyers (1984) suggested that many chydorid Cladocera are facultative planktivores that move upward at night to utilize phytoplankton. In Jack Lake, low edible phytoplankton concentrations may have precluded vertical migration. Nightly decreases of oxygen concentrations in the littoral zone may also have been less than in previously studied lakes. Many epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea show strong vertical movements with declining oxygen concentrations (Meyers, 1980; Tinson & Laybourn-Parry, 1985). Numbers of H. gibberum, D. birgei, and E. nordenskioldi increased in zooplankton samples collected at night. These increases were probably caused by vertical migration of zooplankters from water surrounding submerged macrophytes. Alternatively, transverse movements of animals between the pelagic and littoral zones cannot be ruled out (cf. Davies, 1985). In this study, funnel traps were used to estimate vertical movements of benthic microcrustacea. Funnel traps have been frequently employed to quantitatively estimate littoral microcrustacean abundance (e.g. Whiteside, 1974; Whiteside et al., 1978; Whiteside & Williams, 1975; Meyers, 1984). In Jack Lake, estimates of total microcrustacean abundance obtained using funnel traps were less than 20% of core sample estimates. Although these results suggest that funnel traps underestimate microcrustacean numbers, other researchers have found that funnel traps captured more than 90% of chydorid cladocerans on underlying substrata (Whiteside & Williams, 1975; Meyers, 1984). This indicates that the accuracy of funnel trap estimates may vary among lakes, habitats, and seasons. Before funnel traps are used, care should be taken to compare results with alternative sampling techniques. In summary, the results of this study indicate that the distribution of microcrustacea varies considerably among different habitats (water column, sediments, macrophyte species) and depths. In Jack Lake, large numbers of microcrustacea were associated with macrophytes, suggesting that estimates of epiphytic invertebrates should be included in lake-wide surveys of invertebrate abundance, biomass, and production. This will be especially true for small lakes, where the relative size of the littoral zone is greatest. Acknowledgements I am grateful for the encouragement and support of my supervisor, Dr P. The following specific questions are addressed: (1) How do microcrustacean assemblages vary among the water column, sediments, and different types of macrophytes? (2) How does epiphytic microcrustacean community structure vary with water depth? (3) Do epiphytic and benthic microcrustacea move into the water column at night? Diurnal migrations may lead to interactions between benthic and epiphytic microcrustacea and zooplankton.

Study site

Jack Lake (44° 44' N, 63° 40' W) is a small (3.9 ha), acidic (mean pH = 4.7), oligotrophic, headwater lake located near Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada. Aside from hiking trails and a small access road, the watershed is forested and undeveloped. Jack Lake is devoid of fish. The littoral zone is characterized by highly organic sediments and dense submerged macrophyte growth (Paterson, 1991). The macrophyte assemblage is dominated by Pallavicinia lyellii (Hooker) (a liverwort), Eriocaulon septangulare Withering (Northern Pipewort), Scirpus subterminalis Torrey (Water Bulrush), and Potamogeton confervoides Reichenbach (Alga Pondweed). Floating and emergent macrophytes are restricted to shallow water (< 0.5 m) and include Nymphaea odorata Aiton (Yellow Pondlily), Nuphar variegatum Engelmann (White Waterlily), and Pontederia cordata Linnaeus (Pickerel Weed).

Materials and methods

Distribution of invertebrates in the shallow littoral zone

Invertebrates were collected at 3 week to 1 month intervals from the water column, sediments, and macrophytes. All samples were obtained from water 1 to 2 m deep along the north shore of Jack Lake between August 22 and October 5, 1986 and June 11 and October 8, 1987. A more detailed description of sampling methods is available in Paterson (1991).

The water-column overlying submerged macrophytes was sampled haphazardly from a boat with a 10 cm diameter flexible plastic tube (cf. Pennak, 1962). Samples were sieved with a 63 \( \mu \)m screen, preserved in 5% formalin with sugar, and counted without subsampling. A minimum of 10 samples was collected on each sampling date.

Benthic invertebrates were collected from a boat using a 3.5 cm diameter corer attached to a metal pole. The uppermost 4 cm of each core and 5 cm of overlying water were drawn off with a wide mouthed pipette, sieved with a 125 \( \mu \)m screen, and preserved in 5% sugar-formalin with rose bengal. At least 5 cores were counted in their entirety for each sampling date.

Epiphytic invertebrates were collected by a SCUBA diver who closed a 5.5 l hinged plexiglass box around submerged macrophytes (Downing, 1986). Samples were collected at randomly selected locations along rope transects placed parallel to shore in water 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 m deep. Because most macrophytes in Jack Lake could be completely enclosed within the box, sampling was not stratified vertically within the water column. Between 10 and 18 box samples were collected on each sampling date. Box samples were brought to the surface, unenclosed plant material was trimmed away, and the contents were drained through a 125 \( \mu \)m sieve. In the laboratory, invertebrates were rinsed from macrophytes and preserved in 5% sugar-formalin with rose bengal. Macrophytes were sorted to species, dried at 90 \( ^\circ \)C, and weighed. Material washed from macrophytes was made up to a known volume and repeatedly subsampled until at least 300 microcrustacea had been counted.

The above-ground biomass of macrophytes (dry weight) was determined by removing plants within randomly located 929 cm\(^2\) (1986) or 232 cm\(^2\) (1987) quadrats. Biomass estimates for each sampling date were based on 12–20 replicates in 1986 and 19–30 replicates in 1987. Macrophyte data are presented in Paterson (1991).

The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor. 92 Laurie E. Further predictor variables were added in an attempt to explain a larger proportion of the variance in the full data set and so improve the predictive value of the regression equation: (a) All other water chemical factors are either highly correlated with pH and do not contribute further to explaining the variance once pH has been added, or are of no predictive value *per se*. The composition of the sixteen macroinvertebrate communities were compared by calculating a Jaccard similarity index (\( C_J \)) for each pair of ponds: \[ C_J = j / (a + b - j) \] where \( j \)=number of taxa in common and \( a \) and \( b \)=numbers of taxa in the two ponds (Southwood, 1978). A qualitative index was preferred in view of the very large variance in species abundances. The results are summarized in the similarity half-matrix (Fig. 5a), in which the ponds are arranged in order of pH. A predominance of high Jaccard index values near the diagonal indicates the faunal similarity between most of the ponds adjacent, or close together, in the pH ranking. The faunas of ponds E and R (\( C_J = 0.59 \)) and ponds C and D (\( C_J = 0.52 \)) are the most similar.
